note: Raw verified corpus for slope.json. Six researchers were asked what each living layer of a garden stands on, and — where the evidence genuinely supported it — to propose a hard floor rule: a condition without which a layer cannot work AT ALL. Each claim was then re-checked by an independent sceptic who fetched the same source again, could reject or reword the claim, and judged the floor rule separately under an explicitly harsh standard. 89 of 89 claims survived rejection. 40 floor rules were proposed. 39 were destroyed, in nearly every case by the cited source contradicting the rule in its own next breath. The 40th is adjudicated below and does not survive as evidence either.
method: artbitrage standing-order workflow, 95 agents: 6 topic researchers, 89 adversarial verifiers (one per claim, each judging fact and floor rule separately, each instructed to default to rejection when uncertain).

adjudication.what_happened: One rule was let through: that a garden with no reachable unsealed soil cannot support ground-nesting bees. A different checker in the same run, reviewing a different claim (INV-15), demolished exactly that rule's surface list from a stronger angle — and was right.
adjudication.the_stricter_reading: Decking sits on joists above intact, undisturbed soil, and the cavity beneath it is a known bumblebee nesting and queen-hibernation site. A weed membrane is water- and air-permeable. Artificial grass is typically laid over sand or membrane on undisturbed subsoil. Soil life persists under all three — heavily suppressed, which is a gradient, not a floor.
adjudication.what_actually_survives: Only the narrow, definitional case: a solitary bee cannot excavate a nest tunnel through continuous impermeable cover — poured concrete, asphalt, or mortared paving on a full sub-base. That is true the way it is true that you cannot dig a hole in a rock. It is a definition, not a finding, and the paper cited for it never addressed the question.
adjudication.so_the_count_is: Forty hard rules were proposed from the evidence. Zero survived as evidenced floors. One survives as a definition.
adjudication.why_this_is_recorded: Two of this project's own checkers disagreed, and the stricter one won. Burying that would make this room the thing it is about.

claims.statement: USDA-NRCS publishes a general table of bulk densities at which root growth is affected and restricted, graded by soil texture: the restricting threshold runs from >1.80 g/cm3 on sand and sandy loam down to >1.47 g/cm3 on clay over 45 percent clay. Table 1 gives three columns - ideal, affects root growth, restricts root growth: Sand and loamy sand <1.60 / 1.69 / >1.80; sandy loam and loam <1.40 / 1.63 / >1.80; sandy clay loam and clay loam <1.40 / 1.60 / >1.75; silt and silt loam <1.40 / 1.60 / >1.75; silt loam and silty clay loam <1.40 / 1.55 / >1.65; sandy clay, silty clay and clay loam <1.10 / 1.49 / >1.58; clay over 45 percent clay <1.10 / 1.39 / >1.47. NRCS calls this a "general relationship", and the middle column exists precisely because the effect is a gradient rather than a cliff; the footnote excludes red clayey soils and volcanic ash soils. Note that NRCS's own rows overlap - "clay loam" and "silt loam" each appear twice with different thresholds - so the table is a rule of thumb, not a clean function of texture. For scale, the same guide states that an ideal silt loam has about 50 percent pore space at 1.33 g/cm3 against a particle density of 2.65 g/cm3; on that arithmetic the clay restricting figure of 1.47 corresponds to about 44 percent pore space, and the sandy restricting figure of 1.80 to about 32 percent.
claims.detail: The NRCS Soil Health guide Table 1 gives three columns: ideal, affects root growth, restricts root growth. Sand and loamy sand: ideal <1.60, affects 1.69, restricts >1.80. Sandy loam and loam: <1.40 / 1.63 / >1.80. Sandy clay loam and clay loam: <1.40 / 1.60 / >1.75. Silt and silt loam: <1.40 / 1.60 / >1.75. Silt loam and silty clay loam: <1.40 / 1.55 / >1.65. Sandy clay, silty clay, clay loam: <1.10 / 1.49 / >1.58. Clay over 45 percent clay: <1.10 / 1.39 / >1.47. The footnote excludes red clayey soils and volcanic ash soils. The shorter 2008 NRCS sheet collapses this to Sandy <1.60 / >1.80, Silty <1.40 / >1.65, Clayey <1.10 / >1.47. The physical meaning: a medium-textured soil at about 50 percent pore space sits at 1.33 g/cm3, so the clay restricting figure of 1.47 means pore space has fallen to roughly a third of the volume.

source.name: USDA-NRCS, Soil Health – Bulk Density/Moisture/Aeration, Guides for Educators (May 2019), Table 1

claims.checker_note: verified with corrections - Table 1, its seven rows, its footnote and the source URL are confirmed verbatim against the live May 2019 NRCS guide; but the derived sentence "pore space has fallen to roughly a third" is false (it is 44.5 percent, not 33 percent) and must be removed, "hard table" and "different for every soil texture" must be softened, and the 2008 NRCS sheet line is unverified and should be dropped unless separately sourced
claims.cannot_establish: This is a general relationship, not a species-specific law. NRCS gives no experimental citation inside the sheet, no error bars, and no statement that roots stop dead at the figure — 'restricts' is not 'prevents'. It also cannot be checked by a homeowner without an oven, a scale and a 3-inch core ring, so it is a builder's-spec number, not a garden observation. It does not apply to red clay or volcanic soils.

claims.statement: For woody landscape plants, the bulk densities at which root growth is measurably restricted can fall well below the root-limiting values commonly cited for agricultural soils, and construction work compacts soil into that range. The peer-reviewed ISA review by Day and Bassuk reports root growth of Forsythia ovata 'Nakai' significantly restricted at bulk densities as low as 1.21 g/cm3, and roots "few and entirely confined to the upper third of the pot" at 1.40 g/cm3 and above. Their Austrian pine example is the important one: root penetration was not statistically reduced until 1.6 g/cm3 in a sandy loam, but only 1.4 g/cm3 severely restricted the same species in a silt loam - so there is no single number that travels across soil textures, which is why the authors instead suggest roughly 2.3 MPa penetrometer resistance as an approximate critical limit above which woody root growth would be severely restricted. In a survey of areas to be landscaped near new residential and commercial construction, mean bulk density was 1.56 g/cm3 - a 0.5 g/cm3 increase over adjacent undisturbed ground. (The comparison to NRCS figures is ours, not the paper's; NRCS root-limiting bulk densities are themselves texture-dependent, roughly 1.80 for sandy loam down to about 1.47 for clay.)
claims.detail: The peer-reviewed ISA review by Day and Bassuk reports root growth of Forsythia ovata significantly restricted at bulk densities as low as 1.21 g/cm3, sugar maple roots confined to the upper third of containers at 1.40 g/cm3 and above, and Austrian pine restricted at 1.6 g/cm3 in sandy loam but only 1.4 g/cm3 in the same-textured-family silt loam. They propose roughly 2.3 MPa soil strength as the point above which woody root growth is severely restricted. On a measured urban construction site, bulk density near new building work was 1.56 g/cm3, a 0.5 g/cm3 increase over adjacent undisturbed ground. That single number is the whole story of builder's fill: half a gram per cubic centimetre is the difference between soil and a floor.

source.name: Day, S.D. & Bassuk, N.L., A Review of the Effects of Soil Compaction and Amelioration Treatments on Landscape Trees, Arboriculture & Urban Forestry 20(1)

claims.checker_note: verified with corrections — source live, full text, quotes exact; but the 1.56 g/cm3 figure is a multi-site survey mean rather than one measured site, the NRCS comparison is the site's own inference and not in the source, and the "single number is the whole story" framing contradicts the paper's own texture-dependence argument
claims.cannot_establish: These are individual species in individual experiments, several in containers rather than field soil; they cannot be generalised into a species-by-species table for a UK garden. The 1.56 g/cm3 construction figure is one site, not a survey. The review is from 1994, so more recent work may revise the 2.3 MPa figure.

claims.statement: Penn State Extension gives two numbers you can check on site. Its page on construction-damaged soils says "Most plant root growth is restricted at a penetration resistance of 300 pounds per square inch" — measured with a penetrometer, a rod driven at about an inch per second. And where compaction and drainage are a concern, it says to "pour a gallon of water into a 12-inch-wide, 24-inch-deep hole dug with a shovel. If the water does not drain from the hole in eight hours, consider planting in another location." The page frames compaction damage as gas exchange rather than pure mechanics: compacted soil lacks pore space, so CO2 from root respiration builds up and slows root growth even where roots could physically push through. Two honest caveats: Penn State does not call the water test the most important check — it names a shovel, your hand and a soil test as the best tools, and says always to run a soil test — and it does not treat standing water at eight hours as the end of the matter. It offers French or PVC drains, mounded beds, or another special type of planting as alternatives to moving the tree.
claims.detail: The 300 psi figure (about 2.07 MPa) is the standard agronomic root-limiting soil strength and matches the roughly 2.3 MPa the arboricultural literature proposes for woody plants. Penn State's page on construction-damaged soils frames the problem as gas exchange rather than pure mechanics: compacted soils lack pore space, so carbon dioxide from root respiration builds up and slows root growth even where roots could physically push through. The eight-hour drainage test is the field check that matters most for a homeowner, because it needs nothing but a spade, a hose and a watch, and it tests the actual thing that kills plants in made ground.

source.name: Penn State Extension, Understanding Tree Planting in Construction-Damaged Soils

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: The page does not specify the test hole's depth or diameter, so the eight-hour figure is not a reproducible standard; it also does not say what to do if the site is the only site. Penetration resistance varies enormously with soil moisture — the same ground can read below 300 psi wet and far above it dry — and the page does not state the moisture condition at which to measure.
claims.wall_fell_because:
The cited source refutes the floor in its own next breath. Immediately after the eight-hour sentence, the page says plantings in these areas "may have to be engineered for drainage (e.g., French, PVC, or other drains), planted in mounded beds, or be provided some other special type of planting," and the "Final Strategies" section repeats the drainage-improvement advice. A source that lists four ways to plant successfully on the spot cannot be evidence that a woody layer "cannot stand" there. The verb in the source is "consider," not "do not."

The rule also fails on its own terms. It is a single-event test with unrecorded antecedent conditions — a hole dug the day after heavy rain, or in soil at field capacity, drains differently from the same hole in a dry week, and eight hours is a threshold of concern rather than a physical boundary. Species tolerance spans an enormous range: bald cypress, black gum, red maple, river birch, swamp white oak and willow root and stand in ground that holds water far longer than eight hours, so the outcome depends on what is planted, which the rule does not mention. And the failure mode is a gradient — poor drainage raises the risk of root suffocation and decline over years, it does not make establishment impossible. The BECAUSE clause describes the bathtub effect, which is real and worth stating, but "raises risk, sometimes decisively" is not "cannot work at all."

If a rule is wanted here, it should be phrased as a strong caution that shifts the burden of proof — standing water at eight hours means do not plant a dug pit on that spot unless you change the drainage, raise the planting, or choose a species that tolerates saturation — not as a hard floor.

claims.statement: There is a published five-point spade test — Visual Evaluation of Soil Structure (VESS), SRUC 2012, by Cloy (SRUC), Guimarães (Maringá, Brazil), Batey, and Munkholm (Aarhus, Denmark) — that lets anyone with a garden spade about 20 cm wide and 22-25 cm long read the structural quality of their own soil. You take out a block to full spade depth and break it apart by hand, then match it to the chart's pictures and descriptions. Sq1 friable: aggregates readily crumble with the fingers, mostly under 6 mm, roots throughout the soil. Sq3 firm: most aggregates break with one hand, roots usually grow through the aggregates. Sq4 compact: considerable effort to break aggregates with one hand, mostly over 10 cm, sub-angular and non-porous, all roots clustered in macropores and around aggregates rather than through them. Sq5 very compact: difficult to break up, mostly over 10 cm, angular and non-porous, may contain anaerobic zones, grey-blue colour as the distinguishing feature, and "few roots, if any, and restricted to cracks". Where the roots have gone is one of five things the chart reads, alongside aggregate size and shape, break-up effort, and visible porosity — but it is the one that says plainly what the structure has cost the plants. The chart's own verdict: "Scores of 1-3 are usually acceptable whereas scores of 4 or 5 require a change of management." Layers of differing structure are scored separately and depth-weighted (score times thickness, divided by overall depth), which is how you catch a loose top layer sitting on a compacted one — within the reach of a spade.
claims.detail: Visual Evaluation of Soil Structure, published by SRUC with co-authors in Brazil and Denmark, needs only a garden spade about 20 cm wide and 22-25 cm long. You take out a block to full spade depth and break it apart by hand. Sq1 friable: aggregates crumble in the fingers, mostly under 6 mm, roots throughout. Sq3 firm: most aggregates break with one hand, roots grow through the aggregates. Sq4 compact: considerable effort to break with one hand, mostly clods over 10 cm, sub-angular and non-porous, and all roots clustered in macropores and around the outside of aggregates rather than through them. Sq5 very compact: difficult to break, clods over 10 cm, angular and non-porous, may contain anaerobic zones, grey-blue colour, few roots if any and restricted to cracks. Layers are scored separately and depth-weighted, which is exactly how you catch a good topsoil skin sitting on a dead subsoil.

source.name: Cloy, Guimarães, Batey & Munkholm, Visual Evaluation of Soil Structure (VESS) colour chart, SRUC, 16 Oct 2012

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: VESS was designed and validated for arable fields, not garden beds or made ground with rubble in it, and 'require a change of management' means ploughing or subsoiling, not necessarily that nothing can be planted. Scoring is subjective and the chart itself says scores may fall between categories. It does not convert to a bulk density figure.
claims.wall_fell_because: The cited page contradicts both halves of the rule. FIRST, the "cannot work at all" premise fails on the chart's own Sq5 wording: "Few roots, if any, and restricted to cracks" — roots are present and rooting does occur, through cracks and macropores ("Macropores may be present" is listed under Sq5 porosity). That is severe restriction, a gradient, not a floor. The rule's stated BECAUSE — "the roots visible in the sample have already failed to enter the soil" — misreads the source: what Sq4 and Sq5 record is roots failing to enter the AGGREGATES, being pushed into cracks and macropores instead. Roots in cracks are roots in the soil. SECOND, the "until that layer is physically broken up" necessity is not in the source and is contradicted by it: the chart's prescription for scores 4 and 5 is "require a change of management" — an open category that includes reducing traffic, avoiding working the ground wet, timing, and rooting by deep-rooted species through existing cracks and biopores. The chart never names mechanical loosening as the required or only remedy. THIRD, the rule ignores the depth-weighting the claim itself endorses: because layers are scored separately, an Sq5 layer can sit beneath a friable upper layer, and a shallow-rooted planting can stand perfectly well above it — the chart's own worked example is exactly a two-layer block with a good layer over a worse one. A floor rule that forbids all rooted planting over any Sq5 layer is falsified by the very method it cites. At most the evidence supports: an Sq5 layer means rooting through that layer is largely blocked, the chart calls for a change of management, and anything depending on roots crossing that layer should not be assumed to work.

claims.statement: Water behaves differently at a change of soil texture, and the boundary can trap water and roots above it — but by two different mechanisms, not one. Where fine sits over coarse, water moves down through the fine layer and stops at the interface, crossing only "as pressure increases due to saturation in the finer layer" — a genuine threshold, and the effect deliberately engineered into golf greens and sports pitches, whose rootzones "range from 10 to 12 inches in depth" so the held water stays within reach of roots. Where coarse sits over fine, there is no threshold: water keeps crossing, but "only... at the rate of the underlying finer textured soil", so it backs up in the coarse layer whenever it arrives faster than the fine layer can take it, and drains away once the fine layer catches up. When either happens by accident — typically from topdressing whose particle size is not matched to the soil beneath — the source says "water and roots can be confined to a shallow area". Note the conditional: the same layering that is a design feature at adequate depth becomes a fault at shallow depth.
claims.detail: The Sports Turf Managers Association note (illustrated from A.J. Turgeon) sets out both cases plainly. Fine over coarse gives a perched water table: water moves down through the fine layer and stops when it reaches the coarse medium, crossing only as pressure builds from saturation above. This is deliberately engineered in golf greens and sports pitches, where rootzones of 10-12 inches sit over coarse material to hold water within reach of roots. Coarse over fine gives a temporary water table: water can only leave the coarse layer as fast as the fine layer underneath will take it, so it backs up in the coarse layer until the fine layer catches up. Both produce shallow rooting when they happen by accident — 'water and roots can be confined to a shallow area'. This is why a bag of imported topsoil or compost tipped onto untouched ground makes a shelf, not a soil.

source.name: Sports Turf Managers Association (STMA), Water Tables (images courtesy A.J. Turgeon PhD)

claims.checker_note: verified — every element of the corrected statement is directly quotable from the fetched primary source; the claim as originally worded is overstated in its headline sentence only
claims.cannot_establish: This is a two-page trade note with no citations, no numbers for how high the perched zone sits, and no data on how long saturation persists. It cannot tell you how thick a layer must be before the effect matters, nor how much a partly-mixed transition zone reduces it. It says nothing about plant death, only about where water and roots sit.
claims.wall_fell_because: The proposed floor rule says a free-draining rooting layer "CANNOT EXIST" over an unbroken layer of different texture. The cited source refutes this in its own words. Its "Positive aspects" section states that a fine-over-coarse boundary "is the basic premise for construction of athletic fields and golf greens" and "can provide an ideal growing environment if the rootzone is deep enough to support plant roots" — the exact configuration the rule declares impossible is the industry's deliberate design, and it grows turf. A rule cannot stand on a document whose headline example is the rule being violated successfully. Four further reasons it fails the "cannot work at all" test. (1) That very sentence names the governing parameter: "IF the rootzone is deep enough", generally 10-12 inches. Same physics, same boundary — good rootzone or useless shelf depending on depth. That is a gradient with a depth term, not a floor. (2) The source hedges every negative outcome without exception: "SOMETIMES a perched water table CAN occur", "This CAN happen with topdressing IF the topdressing particle size is not matched", "IF layering occurs, water and roots CAN be confined", "over time a temporary water table CAN form", "This CAN result in shallow rooting". Nothing in the document asserts a necessary consequence, so nothing in it can license a categorical one. (3) The rule's BECAUSE clause is wrong for half the cases it claims to cover. Compost or topsoil over untouched ground is frequently coarse-over-fine, where the source describes rate-limiting, not a saturation threshold — water does cross the boundary continuously. The stated mechanism does not hold in that direction. (4) "Free-draining" is the wrong contrast anyway: a perched layer does drain once the interface tension is overcome, just later and holding more water, which is precisely the retention the greens design is buying. The honest form of this is a warning about degree and depth — an unbroken texture boundary changes how water moves and, if the layer above is shallow, can confine water and roots to it — which is a caution, not a floor.

claims.statement: The USDA-NRCS Urban Soil Primer (Scheyer and Hipple, 2005), a government introduction to urban soils written for homeowners and planning boards, names both halves of this. It defines a perched water table as what happens when "a restrictive layer anywhere in the soil limits waterflow deeper into the soil," so water "builds up, or 'perches,' above the restrictive layer and above the expected water table depth" — and says in the sentence just before it that compaction under heavy weight on wet soil is one way such a restrictive layer forms. It then gives the visible signs: "Compaction below the surface may be evidenced by puddles on the surface or trees that are blown over by heavy winds because of shallow root systems." Two notes of precision: the primer offers those two signs as evidence of subsurface compaction rather than labelling them symptoms of a perched water table directly, and it names both foot traffic and construction machinery as causes — the machinery case being "the use of large machinery to move materials around on a building site when the soil is wet," which "compacts surface and subsurface horizons" and alters "soil drainage, root penetration, and even microbial communities."
claims.detail: The NRCS Urban Soil Primer deals specifically with anthropogenic soils — ground made of fill, dredge, rubble and subsoil placed over topsoil, where the natural horizon order has been reversed. It defines a perched water table as occurring when a restrictive layer anywhere in the profile limits water flow deeper, so water drains down, builds up and perches above the expected water table depth. On compaction it is blunt: because of soil sealing at the surface, vegetation cannot grow in compacted areas, and compaction below the surface may be evidenced by puddles on the surface or trees that are blown over by heavy winds because of shallow root systems. It attributes this to large machinery moving materials on a building site when the soil is wet, which compacts both surface and subsurface horizons and alters drainage, root penetration and microbial communities.

source.name: USDA-NRCS, Urban Soil Primer

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: The primer is descriptive and carries no bulk density figures, no depth-of-compaction figures and no failure rates. Windthrow has many causes, so a fallen tree is a hint, not proof of compaction. It is written for US urban soils; the fill materials and machinery are comparable in the UK but the soil series and rainfall are not.

claims.statement: Dig a hole in slow-draining ground, refill it with looser, richer material, and you have built a bathtub: in wet seasons water moves fast through the backfill, is held back by the tighter native soil around it, and collects in the hole. Chalker-Scott's WSU extension sheet states the consequence plainly — water "accumulates in the planting hole, floods the roots and eventually kills the plant" — and notes the summer mirror image, where the porous backfill wicks its moisture out to the finer soil and cannot draw it back, so the plant droughts unless watered. She adds that roots hitting the wall of the hole behave as they do in a container, circling back into the friendlier backfill instead of establishing outside it, and that the organic fraction rots away until the hole sinks and ponds worse. This is a mechanism argued by an extension horticulturist, not a body of experiments measuring drowned trees; how often it kills, rather than merely fails to help, is still argued over.
claims.detail: Chalker-Scott's WSU extension sheet states the mechanism in two directions. In wet seasons water moves quickly through the amended backfill and is held back by the more slowly draining native soil, so it accumulates in the planting hole, floods the roots and eventually kills the plant. In summer the reverse: the porous backfill wicks its moisture away to the finer native soil and cannot draw it back, so the plant droughts unless irrigated. She also describes root plate deformation at the interface — roots reaching the wall of the hole behave as they do in a container, circling the edge and turning back into the hospitable backfill, so the plant never establishes in the surrounding ground and becomes a hazard as the crown outgrows the root ball. The independent peer-reviewed ISA review corroborates the hydraulic half: it notes that restricted infiltration combined with slow subsurface movement causes water to collect in the bottom of a planting hole dug in compacted soil, flooding tree roots. Organic backfill also decomposes, so the hole sinks over a few years and ponds worse.

source.name: Chalker-Scott, L., The Myth of Soil Amendments, WSU Puyallup Research and Extension Center

claims.checker_note: contested
claims.cannot_establish: This fact sheet cites no studies by name and makes a sweeping claim — "No scientific studies to date show any measurable benefit of soil amendment except in containerized plant production" — that later literature reviews dispute, reporting mixed and sometimes neutral-to-positive results for amended backfill. The bathtub physics is standard and independently supported, but the strength of the root-circling effect, and how much it depends on hole shape, soil type and rainfall, is not established here. No numbers are given for how much amendment, how impermeable the surround, or how long until death.

claims.statement: In one Texas study (Arnold et al. 2007, as reported in the ISA review), small container-grown trees (9.3 L / 3 gal) planted as little as 7.5 cm below grade showed decreased survival and growth in four of five species after three years — on a sandy loam underlain at 15-30 cm by a hard clay pan that was punctured when the planting hole was dug, so the roots of the deeper-planted trees sat partly in clay. Growth increased in some instances for trees planted above grade, which the review suggests may mean the benefit was minimising exposure to the clay pan rather than depth alone. More generally the review says effects of deep planting are typically seen only when root collars are 15 cm or deeper, with 7.5 cm the shallowest depth having any apparent impact in any situation. The BMP threshold — first two structural roots less than 7.5 cm deep, measured 7.5-10 cm out from the trunk — is a criterion for identifying deep root systems in nursery stock.
claims.detail: The ISA review of deep structural roots reports Arnold et al. (2007): small container-grown trees planted as little as 7.5 cm below grade in a sandy loam underlain by a hard clay pan at 15-30 cm depth showed decreased survival and growth in all but one of five species after three years. The hardpan was punctured when the planting hole was dug, which exposed the roots to the clay. Trees planted above grade grew better, suggesting minimising exposure to the clay hardpan was itself the benefit. More generally, effects of deep planting typically appear when root collars are 15 cm or deeper, though effects were sometimes observed at as little as 7.5 cm, and deep planting has been shown to increase formation of girdling roots, though this is species and time dependent. The BMP standard measures depth to the first two structural roots, wanting them less than 7.5 cm deep, measured 7.5-10 cm out from the trunk.

source.name: Causes and Consequences of Deep Structural Roots in Urban Trees, Arboriculture & Urban Forestry 35(4)

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: This is one Texas study on small container stock in a specific sandy loam over clay pan; the review itself says deep structural roots "hinder successful establishment of trees, occasionally enhance establishment, and often have little or no effect". So it cannot be turned into a universal depth law, and the review explicitly notes long-term effects and persistence of girdling roots remain unclear. The climate and species are not eastern England.

claims.statement: Defra's Construction Code of Practice for the Sustainable Use of Soils on Construction Sites (2009) documents, in Case Study 3 (pp. 30-32), a greenfield housing development where 150-200 mm of topsoil was laid in winter 2005 over subsoil that had not been ripped or decompacted after being trafficked by wheeled plant and used to store building materials. The turf was healthy through the first summer; by the onset of winter 2006 — roughly a year after placement — it rapidly failed and the gardens waterlogged, with the topsoil structureless, waterlogged and anaerobic and "virtually no root growth into the topsoil" while the compacted subsoil beneath stayed relatively dry. Eighteen of the twenty-seven gardens had to be remediated by ripping the subsoil with a single-tine ripper on a small tracked excavator, ameliorating the topsoil with washed sand, and replacing all the turf. Defra puts the cost at £90,000. Note that the topsoil had also been independently ruined by stripping and stockpiling it wet, so the case study is not a clean test of subsoil compaction alone.
claims.detail: Defra's Construction Code of Practice, Case Study 3: topsoil stripped and stockpiled wet came back out of the pile as compacted, structureless clods; the subsoil was left in situ and over-compacted by wheeled plant and stored building materials. Topsoil was placed in winter 2005, 150 mm to 200 mm deep, over subsoil that had not been ripped or decompacted, and the gardens laid to turf. The turf was healthy for the first summer, then by the onset of winter 2006 it rapidly failed and the gardens waterlogged. On examination the topsoil was structureless, waterlogged and anaerobic, the dead turf was rotting, there was virtually no root growth into the topsoil, and the subsoil beneath was relatively dry but heavily compacted — water never got that far. Eighteen of twenty-seven gardens had to be remediated by ripping the subsoil with a single-tine ripper on a small tracked excavator and amending the topsoil with washed sand; all the turf was replaced.

source.name: Defra, Construction Code of Practice for the Sustainable Use of Soils on Construction Sites (2009), Case Study 3

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: One anonymised case study in a guidance document, with no site named, no soil analysis published and no control gardens. It cannot tell you the probability of failure on any given new-build plot, nor how much of the failure was the compacted subsoil versus the structureless stockpiled topsoil — the remediation changed both at once. It is UK and directly relevant, but it is a story, not a trial.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule claims the planting layer CANNOT STAND, and the cited case study refutes that on its own evidence. (1) Internal counter-evidence: only "eighteen houses out of twenty-seven" needed remediation — nine gardens on the same site, over the same un-ripped trafficked subsoil, did not. A third of the sample did not fail, which is fatal to a hard floor. (2) Confounded cause: the topsoil was independently destroyed before it ever met the subsoil — heavy loam stripped and stockpiled wet and plastic, "lost its structure", respread as compacted structureless clods. The remediation changed two variables at once (ripped the subsoil AND ameliorated the topsoil with washed sand), so the case cannot isolate un-ripped subsoil as sufficient cause of failure. (3) The turf "was healthy for the first summer" — a layer that establishes and grows for a full season has demonstrably stood for a time; it failed under a wet winter load, which is a durability gradient, not an inability to work. (4) Defra's own "Lessons learnt" uses improvement language, not precondition language: the subsoil "should have been decompacted before spreading the topsoil, to improve rainwater soakage into the substrate." (5) Generality: the outcome depends on subsoil texture, topsoil depth, rainfall and installed drainage; heavy loam over compacted clay through a UK winter is the worst case, not the universal one. The honest version is a strong, expensive, well-documented risk factor — a leading cause of turf failure that can kill a lawn within a year and cost tens of thousands to repair — not a floor.

claims.statement: Defra's construction soils code says topsoil "does not normally perform well below a depth of 400mm from the surface", because self-compaction increases there and the soil's biochemical oxygen demand often outruns the rate of aeration, often producing anaerobic conditions that are detrimental to plant root function. Subsoil has a lower oxygen demand, and the code says it "should, therefore, always be used to create rooting depths in excess of 400mm". So the rule of thumb is: at least 150 mm of topsoil for lawns and mown grass, and up to 400 mm is beneficial for trees and shrubs — but rooting depth beyond 400 mm should be built from subsoil, not from a thicker layer of topsoil. (The code says this of topsoil versus subsoil; it does not discuss compost at that depth, though the same oxygen-demand mechanism would argue against burying it deep.) Deeper is not automatically better: the code's own advice is "Place topsoil too deeply – 'more' is not necessarily 'better'."
claims.detail: Defra's code states that topsoil placement thickness depends on the anticipated rooting depth of the plants and the quality of the subsoil beneath; that trees and shrubs need much greater rooting depth than grasses but this does not have to be made up entirely of topsoil; that topsoil at least 150 mm deep is desirable for lawns and mown amenity grass and can beneficially go up to 400 mm thick for trees and shrubs; but that topsoil does not normally perform well below 400 mm from the surface, where self-compaction increases and biochemical oxygen demand often exceeds the rate of aeration, producing anaerobic conditions detrimental to root function. Subsoil, having lower oxygen demand, should therefore always be used to create rooting depths in excess of 400 mm. Separately the code requires the receiving layer to be decompacted before any soil is spread, and pictures a single ripper tooth used for relieving compaction to a depth of 600 mm, noting deep compaction can only be relieved with heavy ripper equipment and only when the soil is dry to the full working depth, otherwise the tine smears rather than fractures. A toothed excavator bucket is explicitly not an appropriate tool.

source.name: Defra, Construction Code of Practice for the Sustainable Use of Soils on Construction Sites (2009), section 6.1 Soil placement

claims.checker_note: verified as restated — quote is exact and correctly cited; the original wording overstates a hedged "does not normally perform well / often" finding as an absolute "stops working", and adds compost, which the source never mentions in this context
claims.cannot_establish: The 400 mm figure is stated as guidance without a supporting citation, measurement or range, and 'does not normally perform well' is not quantified — no oxygen readings, no failure rate, no timescale. It also does not say what quality of subsoil is required, only that subsoil should be used. Whether the same figure holds for a light sandy topsoil as for a heavy loam is not addressed.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule asserts a hard floor — "the part below 400 mm CANNOT function as rooting medium" — and the source will not carry that weight. Every load-bearing word in the cited passage is hedged: topsoil "does not NORMALLY perform well" below 400 mm; BOD "OFTEN exceeds" the rate of aeration; this "OFTEN results in" anaerobic conditions. Normally/often/often is a probabilistic tendency, and the code's own summary calls it "'more' is not necessarily 'better'" — a degradation, not an impossibility. The 400 mm figure is itself a round rule of thumb ("about" in the claim's own wording), not a measured threshold, and the code makes the outcome conditional on the underlying material and on soil condition rather than on depth alone. The document also gives a counter-instance of the depth-alone logic: manufactured rootzones (e.g. 70% sand / 30% topsoil) are built precisely to be free-draining, so a coarse-textured topsoil placed deep is exactly the case the "self-compaction plus BOD" mechanism would not apply to. The strongest sentence available — "Subsoil... should, therefore, always be used" — is a design SHOULD in a voluntary code of practice, addressed to specifiers, not a claim that deep topsoil is inert. Finally, the rule's scope exceeds the evidence: it names compost, and the source never discusses compost at depth. A floor may only stand where the thing cannot work at all without the condition; this is a well-evidenced gradient, so it belongs in the guidance as a strong default, not as a floor.

claims.statement: On its chalky soils page, under "Correcting problems", the RHS recommends target topsoil depths for when soil is imported onto shallow chalk: at least 10-15 cm (4-6 in) for lawns, 20-30 cm (8 in-1 ft) for borders, and >45 cm (18 in) for shrub beds. It says that on very shallow soils, less than 10 cm (4 in) over chalk, it "may be necessary to increase the growing depth by importing topsoil". The same page states that chalky soils have a pH of 7.1 or above, that both manganese and iron can be "locked up" so they become unavailable to plants, and that it is not practical to reduce alkalinity by adding sulphur because huge quantities would be needed over many years to counter the free calcium carbonate. These are the RHS's horticultural recommendations for chalk soils, not general minimum depths below which planting fails.
claims.detail: On its chalky soils page the RHS states: for lawns the topsoil depth should be at least 10-15cm (4-6in); for borders 20-30cm (8in-1ft); and for shrub beds >45cm (18in). It treats under 10 cm over chalk as the point where importing topsoil becomes necessary to increase growing depth at all. These figures roughly track Defra's — 150 mm for grass, deeper for woody plants — from a completely different direction, which is some corroboration. The same page states chalky soils have a pH of 7.1 or above, that both manganese and iron can be locked up so that they become unavailable to plants, and that it is not practical to reduce alkalinity by adding sulphur because huge quantities would be needed over many years to counter the free calcium carbonate.

source.name: Royal Horticultural Society, Chalky soils

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: These are RHS house recommendations with no cited trial, no species list and no statement of what happens below them — they are minima for good practice, not measured failure thresholds. The page is written for shallow soils over chalk specifically, so applying the figures to a compacted clay subsoil is an extrapolation. The RHS is a charity but also sells plants, seeds and memberships, so it has a general interest in people planting.

claims.statement: Lindsey and Bassuk (Arboriculture & Urban Forestry 17(6):141-149, 1991) derive street-tree soil volume from the water a mature crown transpires, and give a general estimate of 2 cubic feet of soil per 1 square foot of crown projection — a figure they reach by rounding up results computed for six representative US cities, so it is climate-dependent rather than universal. They state that "the depth should be no greater than 3 ft," which is the constraint that matters for a garden: because the required volume is fixed and the depth is capped, the requirement has to be met sideways, by area rather than by digging deeper. Their worked example is a separate, site-specific calculation, not an illustration of the 2:1 rule: for Ithaca NY, a tree with a 20 ft crown diameter (314 sq ft of crown projection) needs about 220 cubic feet of soil to last a 10-day dry period, laid out as roughly 8 ft x 9 ft x 3 ft or 4 ft x 18 ft x 3 ft. The general 2:1 rule applied to that same 314 sq ft crown would instead call for about 628 cubic feet; the paper does not reconcile the two figures. They add that it will be at least 10-15 years before the tree in the example grows large enough to require all the water that volume holds.
claims.detail: Lindsey and Bassuk, in Arboriculture & Urban Forestry, derive soil volume from the water a mature crown transpires. The general estimate is 2 cubic feet of soil per 1 square foot of crown projection. Their worked example: a medium tree with a 20 ft crown diameter has a crown projection of 314 sq ft and needs about 220 cubic feet of soil, laid out as roughly 8 ft x 9 ft x 3 ft or 4 ft x 18 ft x 3 ft — and they state the depth should be no greater than 3 ft. That last constraint is the important one for a garden: extra depth beyond about 900 mm does not count toward the tree's water supply, so the requirement has to be met sideways. They also note the example volume supports the tree for only about 10-15 years before it reaches a size requiring all the water that volume holds.

source.name: Lindsey, P. & Bassuk, N., Specifying Soil Volumes to Meet the Water Needs of Mature Urban Street Trees and Trees in Containers, Arboriculture & Urban Forestry 17(6)

claims.checker_note: verified with correction — source, citation and all quoted figures check out verbatim, but the detail must be rewritten: it wrongly presents the Ithaca-specific 220 ft3 example as the output of the general 2 ft3/ft2 rule (that rule gives 628 ft3 for the same crown), inverts the paper's "at least 10-15 years" into "only about 10-15 years", and attributes to the paper an unstated mechanism that depth beyond 900 mm contributes no water
claims.cannot_establish: The model is water-balance driven and calibrated to US street tree conditions and their reference climate; it does not translate directly to Cambridge's ~557 mm annual rainfall without redoing the water balance, and the paper does not claim it does. It assumes the soil in that volume is actually rootable — it says nothing about compacted or perched volumes, which are counted as available in the arithmetic but are not available in fact.

claims.statement: Above pH 7.5 phosphate ions react with calcium and magnesium to form less soluble compounds, and most other nutrients — micronutrients especially — become less available, with molybdenum the exception (nitrogen, potassium and sulfur are less directly affected, though not unaffected). The fertilizer industry's own guidance lists among its highlights that "iron deficiencies are best addressed by avoiding high pH soils altogether," because soil-applied iron fertilizer is tied up before roots reach it; the same note gives foliar iron as the workaround where a high-pH soil cannot be avoided.
claims.detail: The IPNI/Fertilizer Institute note states most plant nutrients are optimally available between pH 6.5 and 7.5, and that this range is generally compatible with root growth. Nitrogen, potassium and sulfur are less directly affected. Phosphorus is the nutrient most directly affected: at alkaline pH values, greater than pH 7.5 for example, phosphate ions react quickly with calcium and magnesium to form less soluble compounds. Most of the other nutrients, micronutrients especially, are less available above pH 7.5 and are optimally available at a slightly acidic pH of about 6.5 to 6.8; molybdenum is the exception, being more available at moderately alkaline pH. Soils are classed alkaline above pH 7.5 and very alkaline above pH 8. Lowering pH with elemental sulfur or acid is possible but rarely done at field scale because of cost. Their own highlight box says: iron deficiencies are best addressed by avoiding high pH soils altogether.

source.name: Jensen, T.L., Soil pH and the Availability of Plant Nutrients, IPNI Plant Nutrition TODAY (Fall 2010, No. 2), hosted by The Fertilizer Institute

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: The publisher is the fertiliser industry (IPNI, hosted by The Fertilizer Institute), which profits from the sale of soil amendments and micronutrient products — though note the 'avoid high pH soils' advice cuts against that interest. The document is conceptual and gives no curve, no availability percentages and no crop data; 'less available' is not quantified. It does not distinguish high pH from free carbonate, which is the more important variable on chalk.

claims.statement: On chalky ground — pH 7.1 or above with free calcium carbonate in it — ericaceous plants are a bad bet in the open soil, and the RHS says so plainly: iron and manganese get locked up, and it is "not practical to reduce alkalinity in chalky soils by adding sulphur because huge quantities of sulphur would be required over many years". Its advice is to avoid acid-loving plants such as camellias and rhododendrons there unless you will grow them in containers of ericaceous compost. Two honest qualifications. The wall is free lime, not alkalinity as such: the RHS gives real sulphur rates (135-270 g per sq m) for bringing merely neutral or slightly alkaline soil, pH 7.0-7.5, down to pH 6.0-6.5, and says only that "if free lime or chalk is present, the soil cannot realistically be acidified" — you can test which you have by dripping vinegar on a sample and watching for fizzing. And the RHS keeps a page on rhododendrons for alkaline soil listing tolerant species and grafted rootstocks, including Inkarho, rated to tolerate pH up to 7.5 in open ground. So the honest version is: on free-lime chalk, an ungrafted ericaceous planting in unamended open ground will fail, and the failure shows as lime-induced chlorosis — yellowing between the veins, on the youngest leaves first when iron is short. It is a hard practical limit for the ordinary case, with a documented and narrow way round it, not a law of nature.
claims.detail: The RHS growing guide for rhododendrons gives their requirement as soil between pH 5.0 and 6.0, rich in organic matter, and then states the floor directly: if you have alkaline soil, choose plants that will thrive in it, and acid-loving or ericaceous plants such as rhododendrons will not. It adds that reducing soil pH is not simple, and offers only two ways out — grow them as container plants in ericaceous compost, or choose more tolerant species and cultivars. The RHS chalky soils page closes the loop: chalky soils are pH 7.1 or above, manganese and iron get locked up so they are unavailable to plants, it is not practical to reduce alkalinity by adding sulphur because huge quantities would be needed over many years to counter the free calcium carbonate, and gardeners should avoid acid-loving plants such as camellias and rhododendrons unless prepared to grow them in containers. What you see when someone tries anyway is lime-induced chlorosis: yellowing between the veins, and per the RHS chlorosis page iron deficiency shows on the youngest leaves first while manganese and magnesium deficiency start in the older leaves. This matters especially in Cambridge and eastern England, which sit on chalk and chalky boulder clay.

source.name: Royal Horticultural Society, Rhododendron growing guide

claims.checker_note: overstated — verified only for chalky, free-lime soils and for ungrafted stock; "alkaline" and "cannot" are both broader than the source
claims.cannot_establish: 'Will not' is the RHS's editorial judgement, not a cited experiment; the same page immediately offers 'more tolerant species and cultivars', so the floor is a group-level floor with acknowledged exceptions rather than an absolute botanical law. It does not state the pH at which the floor bites, nor distinguish mildly alkaline from genuinely calcareous ground — a soil at pH 7.2 without free lime is a different case from chalk. Raised beds of imported acid soil over chalk are not addressed and are known to revert over time, but this source does not say so.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule overreaches on three axes at once. Soil: it says "chalky OR alkaline", but the RHS's impracticality finding is specifically about free calcium carbonate — it publishes sulphur rates that do work on neutral-to-slightly-alkaline non-calcareous soil, so alkalinity as such is not a floor. Plants: it extends a rhododendron-and-camellia source to azalea, pieris, heather and blueberry with no evidence offered; heather is the visible weak point, since lime-tolerant winter heathers are widely grown, and I could not test it here (search budget exhausted, the RHS heathers guide URL 404s) — an unsourced extension should not be published as a floor. Modality: a floor rule requires "cannot work at all", but the cited organisation's own page /plants/rhododendron/on-alkaline-soil documents the bypass — 'Cunningham's White' and Inkarho rootstocks tolerating pH above 6.0 and up to 7.5 in open ground — and its language throughout is "difficult", "not practical", "costly and difficult to maintain". That is a steep gradient with a known workaround, which is exactly what a floor rule must not be built on. A much narrower rule (free-lime chalk + ungrafted rhododendron/camellia + unamended open ground) could stand, but that is not the rule proposed.

claims.statement: A spoonful of soil and a splash of 5% white vinegar is a valid field test for free lime, and UF/IFAS publishes it as a quantitative one: add the vinegar ten drops at a time, stirring, and count until the bubbling stays weak. Fizzing means free carbonate is present; the drop count tells you roughly how much (under 10 drops is under 2% carbonate, 100-150 drops is 10-16%). That number is the useful part, because the same publication says acidulants such as elemental sulfur have been used successfully on calcareous soils below 3% CaCO3 but will not acidify soil above about 10%. UF/IFAS defines calcareous soils as those holding free calcium carbonate with pH between 7.0 and 8.3, and notes they grow most crops "excluding those requiring acidic growth media, such as blueberry" — but a fizz on its own proves carbonate, not a particular pH, so read it as "measure how much" rather than "the ground is alkaline and beyond help."
claims.detail: The University of Florida IFAS extension publication defines calcareous soils as those that have free calcium carbonate and pH values in the range of 7.0 to 8.3, and describes the household version of the standard acid test: wet a capful of soil with a few drops of water, add white vinegar ten drops at a time, stir, and count. Carbon dioxide released by the reaction shows as bubbles; whether the bubbling is weak or vigorous depends on the quantity and particle size of the carbonate present, and you stop when vigorous bubbling goes weak after stirring. The publication notes that calcareous soils can grow most crops, excluding those requiring acidic growth media, such as blueberry. For a homeowner this is the single most useful observation in this whole set: it costs nothing, needs no meter, and it separates 'slightly alkaline soil' from 'buffered chalk that will defeat every attempt to acidify it'.

source.name: University of Florida IFAS Extension, HS1262: Determination of Carbonate Concentrations in Calcareous Soils

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: The drop-count method is a semi-quantitative estimate of carbonate concentration, not a pH measurement, and a weak fizz does not tell you how much lime is present or how strongly buffered the soil is. It also cannot detect carbonate below its sensitivity, so no fizz does not prove no lime. Household vinegar strength varies, which the publication does not correct for. The 7.0-8.3 range is a definition of the soil class, not a measurement of any particular garden.
claims.wall_fell_because: The cited source refutes the rule rather than supporting it. The proposed floor says that if the ground fizzes at all, no acid-requiring plant layer can stand there because the carbonate buffers against "any practical attempt to acidify it." HS1262's "Acidifying Calcareous Soils" section says the opposite: "Soil acidulants such as elemental sulfur, thiosulfate salts, or fertigation acids such as nitric acid, phosphoric acid, or sulfuric acid have been successfully used to acidify calcareous soils with less than 3% CaCO3," and only "will not acidify soil with high concentrations of CaCO3 (>10%)." Fizzing starts far below 3%, so a large share of fizzing ground is explicitly amendable per the source. This is a gradient over roughly 2% to 60% carbonate, with the source's own practical break at >10%, not a hard threshold at "fizzes." The publication's blueberry line describes calcareous soils as a class and is about crop suitability in that ground, not a demonstration that acid-loving planting cannot work at all — such crops are in practice grown on calcareous sites in pine-bark beds, raised beds and containers, which the rule as written would forbid. Fails the "cannot work at all" bar.

claims.statement: Cambridge University Botanic Garden states that the plants in its Dry Garden "flourish despite us never having provided any supplementary irrigation, even in times of drought", on rainfall it gives as averaging 557 mm annually over the last 30 years, in a local climate it classifies as "semi-arid". The page credits close planting and mulches with conserving soil moisture, and names three visible drought traits: small leaves that reduce water loss (Potentilla fruticosa 'Snowflake'), silvery hairs that trap moisture and reflect heat (Santolina pinnata 'Sulphurea'), and thick fleshy leaves that store water (Aeonium 'Zwartkop'). Fagus sylvatica and Rhamnus alaternus 'Argentovariegata' appear on the page as the garden's hedges, chosen for drought tolerance — not as specimens in the dry beds. This is the garden's own account of its own practice; the page gives no planting date and says nothing about watering-in at establishment or plant losses.
claims.detail: This is the closest documented analogue to a Cambridge garden that exists. CUBG states rainfall has averaged 557 mm annually over the last 30 years and calls the local climate 'semi-arid'. Moisture is conserved by close planting and mulch, not by watering — even in drought years. Plants named on the page as thriving there include Potentilla fruticosa 'Snowflake', Santolina pinnata 'Sulphurea', Rhamnus alaternus 'Argenteovariegata', Aeonium 'Zwartkop' and a Fagus sylvatica. The page attributes survival to small leaves that cut water loss, silvery hairs that reflect heat, and thick fleshy leaves that store water — three visible traits a homeowner can use as a buying filter in a garden centre.

source.name: Cambridge University Botanic Garden — Dry Garden

claims.checker_note: source-declared — CUBG's own unaudited statement about its own garden, quoted accurately from a live page; the "never" and the 557 mm figure both rest entirely on the institution's word, and the page offers no establishment-watering or loss data against which to test it
claims.cannot_establish: The page never says what the soil is, how the ground was prepared before planting, whether plants were watered while establishing, or what died. No failure rate, no mortality figure, no planting date. It is an institution reporting its own management, not an experiment with a control. It also does not claim the ground is compacted or rubble — only that it is dry.

claims.statement: The famous never-watered Beth Chatto gravel garden was mechanically subsoiled to 60 cm, then ploughed, and had compost dug in two spits deep before a single plant went in. The site was a compacted former car park on thin, sandy, gravelly soil. A tractor-drawn subsoiler broke the compaction to 60 cm depth; the beds were then covered with homemade compost, spent mushroom compost and bonfire waste, incorporated to a depth of two spits. Planting was March 1992; every plant was dunked until the rootball was saturated, planted, and watered in with a hose. By spring 1993 the beds were mulched with local 10 mm gravel at 3-5 cm depth. The garden was conceived from the outset as an unirrigated experiment, but the source records watering at planting-in and does not date exactly when watering stopped. 'Right plant, right place' was applied on top of a one-off, whole-area engineering intervention -- not instead of one.
claims.detail: This matters more than any plant list, because the garden is usually cited as proof that you should not touch the soil. The site was a compacted former car park on thin sandy, gravelly soil. A tractor-drawn subsoiler broke the compaction to 60 cm depth. The beds were then covered with homemade compost, spent mushroom compost and bonfire waste, incorporated to a depth of two spits. Planting was March 1992; every plant was dunked until the rootball was saturated, planted, and watered in with a hose. By spring 1993 the beds were mulched with 10 mm gravel at 3–5 cm depth. Only after that did the no-watering regime begin. 'Right plant, right place' was applied on top of a one-off, whole-area engineering intervention — not instead of one.

source.name: Beth Chatto Gardens — Gravel Garden Creation and Maintenance

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: There is no control plot, so this cannot establish that the subsoiling rather than the plant choice is what made the garden work — only that both were done. It cannot establish that 60 cm is the required depth, nor that the same treatment works on construction rubble rather than sand and gravel. The garden runs a commercial nursery selling drought-tolerant plants, so it has an interest in the story being tellable.

claims.statement: Across 225 studies worldwide, cover crops cut soil bulk density by 3.2% and penetration resistance by 11.8% — and found no significant change in soil pH. (The largest effect in the same analysis was water infiltration, up 37.2%; water stable aggregates rose 15.9% and total porosity 6.1%. A 3.2% fall in bulk density is small: green manure is a slow structural improver and a large infiltration improver, not a decompaction tool.)
claims.detail: Yan & Arthur, Geoderma 460 (2025), article 117436, a global meta-analysis of 225 studies covering 15 soil properties. Your figures are confirmed exactly: bulk density −3.2%, penetration resistance −11.8%, water stable aggregates +15.9%. It extends further: total porosity +6.1% and water infiltration +37.2% — infiltration is by far the biggest effect and the one most relevant to a bed that sheds rain. Crucially, the analysis found no significant change in air permeability, saturated hydraulic conductivity, soil pH, electrical conductivity or cation exchange capacity. A 3.2% fall in bulk density is a small number. Green manure is a slow structural improver and a large infiltration improver; it is not a decompaction tool and not a pH tool.

source.name: Aarhus University research portal — Yan & Arthur, Geoderma (2025), DOI 10.1016/j.geoderma.2025.117436

claims.checker_note: verified — figures confirmed exactly against the live cited source; the pH clause must be weakened from "changed pH not at all" to "found no significant change in pH"
claims.cannot_establish: These are means from mostly arable farmland, not garden beds and not construction rubble. I fetched the repository record and abstract, not the full text (ScienceDirect returned 403), so I cannot report confidence intervals, sample variance, over what number of years these effects accrued, or at what soil depth they were measured. A mean effect says nothing about whether your bed is in the responsive half.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule claims impossibility ("cannot fix it") from a null average effect, which the evidence does not support. A meta-analysis finding no statistically significant pooled change in pH means the mean effect could not be distinguished from zero across 225 heterogeneous studies — not that cover crops are incapable of moving pH in any given soil. Three specific failures: (1) the pool mixes acidic, neutral and alkaline soils and many cover crop types, so offsetting effects yield a null average; the alkaline-soil subgroup is not reported as separately null. (2) The same abstract states effects varied by climate, management and soil texture — the paper itself says context governs outcomes. (3) Soil pH is strongly buffered and shifts slowly, so a null across typical few-year trials is fully consistent with "too slow and too small to detect in a trial window," not with a mechanical barrier. Alkalinity is normally carbonate- or irrigation-water driven, where the obstacle is buffering capacity — a question of how much amendment is needed, i.e. a gradient, not a floor. The honest form is a planning heuristic ("do not rely on green manure to correct alkalinity; it is not a pH tool"), which is guidance, not a hard floor.

claims.statement: AHDB, the UK levy board, advises that cover crop roots should not be relied on to remove a compaction pan. Its guidance describes deep roots as acting like a "tillage tool", creating channels later crop roots can use, "alleviating soil compaction and improving soil structure" — then adds: "However, do not expect rooting action to get rid of compaction pans. These should be removed with targeted sub-soiling and followed by cover crops to keep compaction at bay and retain the structure created by the cultivation." AHDB sets rooting targets as shallow (0-20 cm), deep (20-40 cm) and very deep (over 40 cm), and says to avoid short-duration cover crops where the target is very deep. This is guidance rather than a cited trial result — the page gives no date and no references — and its wording is "do not expect", not "cannot". Treat it as the recommended sequence for a pan (loosen mechanically, then hold the structure biologically), not as proof that roots never penetrate a pan.
claims.detail: AHDB (the UK statutory levy board) describes deep roots as acting like a 'tillage tool', creating channels that later roots reuse, alleviating compaction and improving structure. But it then draws a hard line: rooting action will not get rid of compaction pans; those need targeted sub-soiling, and cover crops should follow to hold the structure created. AHDB classifies rooting targets as shallow 0–20 cm, deep 20–40 cm, very deep over 40 cm, and warns that short-duration cover crops will not reach the very deep band. This is the same sequence Beth Chatto actually used: machine first, biology after. The two independent sources agree, which is why this is the firmest finding in the whole set.

source.name: AHDB — Cover crops improve soil structure

claims.checker_note: verified-as-guidance (source live, quote exact; it is undated advisory guidance with no cited trials, and the claim's "cannot" overstates AHDB's "do not expect"; the Beth Chatto corroboration is unverified and should be dropped)
claims.cannot_establish: This is synthesised guidance, not a single trial with numbers — the page gives no measured penetration resistance thresholds, no depths at which a pan counts as a pan, and no figures for how long biological maintenance holds. It is written for arable fields worked by machinery, not for a small garden bed where hand-forking may substitute for a subsoiler. It does not say a garden fork is or is not sufficient.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule asserts a hard floor — green manure alone CANNOT remove a pan — but the evidence is one undated guidance page whose own wording is deliberately softer: "do not expect rooting action to get rid of compaction pans" is advice against relying on an outcome, not a finding that the outcome is impossible. The page cites no trials, so there is nothing behind it establishing impossibility. Three further reasons it is a gradient, not a floor. First, "compaction pan" is not one thing: a shallow plough pan a few centimetres thick and a cemented iron pan differ by orders of magnitude in what roots can do, and the guidance does not distinguish them. Second, the same page grants that deep roots do alleviate compaction and create reusable channels — so root action sits on the same axis as the pan, working partially, rather than being categorically excluded by it. Third, AHDB's own depth framing gives the game away: it warns against short-duration cover crops where the target is very deep, which is a statement about timescale and species choice, i.e. that roots reach less far in less time, not that they are barred. That is the signature of a degradation, not a floor. As a practical default the advice is sound and worth publishing; as a mechanical rule with "cannot" in it, it claims more than the source will bear.

claims.statement: University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension introduces radish bio-drilling as something "often touted," then qualifies it: "Observations suggest, however, radish root growth can be restricted by compaction zones," and radish roots "often follow the path of least resistance, finding an older root or earthworm channel (bio-pore), to navigate downward." Extension leaves the payoff open — this "may, or may not, offer soil health benefits unique to radish." The same page adds two cautions: radish sown too early (July) sets seed and becomes a weed concern, and seeding radish alone is not recommended due to erosion concerns, so it should go in with a cereal or grass. Note this is reported field observation, not a cited study, and Extension says roots can be restricted by compaction — not that they are stopped by it.
claims.detail: University of Wisconsin–Madison Extension notes radish is 'often touted' to alleviate compaction by bio-drilling, then immediately qualifies it: observations suggest radish root growth can be restricted by compaction zones, and roots frequently follow the path of least resistance — an old root channel or an earthworm biopore — rather than boring new ones. The page goes further and says the approach may or may not offer soil health benefits unique to radish. Two practical cautions: radish sown too early (July) sets seed and becomes a weed problem, and it is not recommended to sow radish alone because of erosion risk — it should go in with a cereal or grass. Radish also winterkills, which is the point: the dead taproot leaves a channel.

source.name: University of Wisconsin–Madison Extension — Crops and Soils, Radish

claims.checker_note: contested
claims.cannot_establish: This is an extension summary reporting observations, not a controlled trial, and it does not quantify at what penetration resistance radish roots stop. Wisconsin's climate and sowing calendar are not eastern England's — the July/August sowing window and reliable winterkill do not transfer directly. It cannot establish that radish is useless, only that the strong version of the bio-drilling claim is not supported. I could not open the USDA NRCS or University of Maryland radish fact sheets to cross-check depth figures.

claims.statement: In 4 m deep soil-filled rhizotrons, chicory (Cichorium intybus) rooted below 3 m within about 4.5 months of transplanting. Deuterium-labelled water injected at 2.3 m showed measured water uptake below 1.7 m in 2016 and below 2.3 m in 2017, contributing significantly to the plant's total water use. But neither topsoil drying nor competition from shallow-rooted neighbours increased that deep uptake, and it could not compensate for the topsoil water that was lost. Deep roots buy access, not immunity. (Rasmussen, Thorup-Kristensen & Dresboll, Plant and Soil 446:275-290, online Nov 2019.) Caveat worth keeping: these were narrow 1.2 x 0.3 m columns of prepared soil, not garden ground — compaction, stones or a water table can cut this depth short. [REMOVED as unsupported by the cited source: the sentence about a companion Copenhagen study with trace-element tracers at 2.3 m and nitrogen-15 at 3.5 m. This paper used deuterium only, at 2.3 m. Also removed: the claim that this is the best-evidenced rooting-depth figure for any garden-available species.]
claims.detail: Rhizotron study in 4 m deep soil columns (Plant and Soil, 2019). Chicory (Cichorium intybus) rooted below 3 m within 4.5 months. Measured water uptake occurred below 1.7 m in 2016 and below 2.3 m in 2017 and contributed significantly to total water use. A companion Copenhagen study recorded chicory taking up trace-element tracers placed at 2.3 m and nitrogen-15 placed at 3.5 m — proof the roots were genuinely functional at depth, not just present. The honest finding: neither surface drying nor competition increased deep water uptake, and deep uptake could not compensate for lost topsoil water. Deep roots buy access, not immunity. This is the best-evidenced rooting-depth figure I could obtain for any garden-available species.

source.name: Plant and Soil — Uptake of subsoil water below 2 m fails to alleviate drought response in deep-rooted chicory

claims.checker_note: verified — headline claim fully supported verbatim by the cited source; publish only with the companion-study tracer sentence and the "best-evidenced" superlative removed
claims.cannot_establish: The soil was packed into rhizotron columns, not compacted construction rubble — this says nothing about whether chicory can penetrate a builder's pan or a brick layer. Danish climate, agricultural cultivars, irrigated establishment. It cannot establish that chicory leaves usable channels behind, nor that a garden bed is deep enough for 3 m roots to matter. Nobody appears to have tested bio-drilling in rubble at all.

claims.statement: The RHS says there is little evidence that adding extra organic matter to the bottom of a planting hole helps, and that the practice can hinder establishment: the organic matter decomposes and may cause the plant to sink. Elsewhere on the same page it notes that planting too deep is a common cause of tree death. It also states that it is not beneficial to apply fertiliser at planting time. Its positive instructions are mechanical rather than nutritional: dig a hole no deeper than the roots but ideally at least three times the diameter of the root system; break up compacted hole sides with a fork before planting; square holes aid root penetration at the corners on heavy soils; firm gently, avoiding compacting the soil into a hard mass. It allows that a mycorrhizal inoculant may help trees and shrubs establish — but warns that if you use one, do not apply fertiliser at all, because phosphorus can suppress the fungus.
claims.detail: The named mechanism is specific: the organic matter decomposes, loses volume, and the plant sinks — ending up too deep, which is a common killer of trees and shrubs. The same page says it is not beneficial to apply fertiliser at planting time. Its positive instructions are all mechanical rather than nutritional: dig a hole no deeper than the roots but at least three times the diameter of the root system; if the sides of the hole are compacted, break them up with a fork before planting; square holes aid root penetration at the corners on heavy soils; firm gently without compacting into a hard mass. On poor soils it allows that a mycorrhizal inoculant may help — but warns not to apply fertiliser alongside it, because phosphorus suppresses the fungus.

source.name: RHS — Trees and Shrubs: Planting Guide

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: 'Little evidence' is a statement about the state of research, not a demonstration of harm; the page cites no specific trials. It cannot establish how much sinking occurs or over what period. It also does not address the different question of improving a whole bed, and the RHS's own drought-gardening page gives apparently opposite advice for whole-bed preparation — see notes.

claims.statement: In a controlled two-year trial, amending backfill gave no shoot-growth advantage over plain native soil, and one amendment set trees back. Balled-and-burlapped red maple (Acer rubrum) were planted into four backfills: native soil; 50:50 aged pine bark and soil; 50:50 proprietary landscape media and soil; and 100% proprietary media. The media-and-soil mix did increase fibrous root growth inside the planting hole at five months, but that did not translate into more shoot growth. Aged pine bark induced nitrogen deficiency symptoms and reduced shoot growth in the first year. By two years, shoot growth did not differ between any treatment. The authors' own conclusion: "The data support use of native soil in backfilling planting holes." One species, one site, two years -- experimental evidence from a single trial, not guidance, and not proof that amendment never helps anywhere.
claims.detail: Published in Arboriculture & Urban Forestry (21:5, 247). Balled-and-burlapped red maple (Acer rubrum) were planted into four backfills: native soil; 50:50 aged pine bark and soil; 50:50 proprietary landscape media and soil; and 100% proprietary media. The media-and-soil mix increased fibrous root growth inside the planting hole at five months but did not increase shoot growth. Aged pine bark induced nitrogen deficiency symptoms and reduced shoot growth in the first year. By two years, shoot growth did not differ between any treatment. The paper's own conclusion is that the data support using native soil to backfill planting holes. This is experimental evidence, not guidance, and it points the same way as the RHS.

source.name: Arboriculture & Urban Forestry — Effect of Backfill Amendment on Growth of Red Maple

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: One species, one site, two years — nothing here about long-term effects, about shrubs or perennials, or about eastern England. Red maple is not a dry-alkaline-ground plant. Two years is short for a tree. It cannot establish that amendment is harmful in general; the honest reading is that it bought nothing, and that the wrong amendment (raw bark) cost something. It also cannot establish anything about pre-planting whole-bed treatment.

claims.statement: Acid-loving plants are hard to keep alive on alkaline ground, and a pocket of ericaceous compost is not a durable fix on its own. The RHS says rhododendrons grow best at pH 4.5-6.0, that on limey soil iron gets "locked up" and unavailable, and that acid organic matter "alone will not bring about any appreciable reduction in soil pH" — because where soil is naturally alkaline, holding an artificially low pH is "both costly and difficult", the pH of the soil moisture gradually raising it back up. On soils approaching pH 7.0 the RHS calls a raised bed the most reliable method: at least 30 cm of ericaceous compost over an isolating lime-free drainage layer such as sharp sand (or polythene punched with drainage holes), or a container of ericaceous compost. It is not, however, the only thing the RHS endorses: it also suggests ericaceous material plus a dressing of sulphur at planting, chelated iron on neutral to slightly alkaline soils, tolerant species, and plants grafted on lime-tolerant rootstocks — Inkarho-grafted rhododendrons "appear to tolerate soils with a pH up to 7.5". This page covers rhododendrons; do not extend it to camellia, pieris, blueberry or heathers without a source of their own.
claims.detail: The RHS states rhododendrons need pH 4.5–6.0, and that on alkaline ground iron is chemically locked and unavailable, causing chlorosis. Adding ericaceous material alone will not appreciably reduce soil pH, especially where the soil and groundwater are alkaline; maintaining an artificially low pH is described as costly and difficult to maintain, because moisture chemistry gradually pushes the pH back up. The only approaches the RHS endorses are full physical isolation: a raised bed with a minimum depth of 30 cm of ericaceous compost above isolating drainage material, or growing entirely in a container of ericaceous compost. This is the single hardest boundary in this research, and it applies to the whole calcifuge group — rhododendron, azalea, camellia, pieris, blueberry, most heathers.

source.name: RHS — Rhododendrons on Alkaline Soils

claims.checker_note: supported-but-overstated (core mechanism verified; the "only full isolation works" absolutism, the stitched verbatim quote, and the extension to the whole calcifuge group are not supported by the cited page)
claims.cannot_establish: The page is written about rhododendrons; I am extending it to other calcifuges by shared mechanism, which is reasonable but not directly sourced here. It gives no timescale for how fast a treated hole reverts, and no pH figure at which the raised-bed method starts to fail. It cannot establish anything about lime-tolerant rhododendron rootstocks, which exist and which the page's mention of 'limited success' may allude to.
claims.wall_fell_because: The cited page refutes the "cannot / only" structure of the rule rather than supporting it. Three passages on the same page describe non-isolation routes that the RHS says can work on above-neutral ground: "Ericaceous compost, chopped bracken and pine needles at planting, plus a dressing of sulphur, may also enable rhododendrons to be grown"; "With neutral or slightly alkaline soils chelated iron can be used"; and rhododendrons grafted on the Inkarho rootstock "appear to tolerate soils with a pH up to 7.5" — which is alkaline ground with no isolation at all. The raised bed is introduced as "the most reliable method", a ranking among options, not a precondition. The negative evidence is itself cost-and-difficulty language ("both costly and difficult to maintain") and rate language ("will gradually raise the pH over time") — a gradient of decline and maintenance burden, not an impossibility. The rule's stated mechanism also fails: the RHS's own isolating layer is sharp sand or "polythene with holes punched through", i.e. deliberately not a seal, so "breaking contact" is not what makes the raised bed work.
