This is a strong, high-failure-rate gradient worth stating as guidance, but it is not a hard floor.

claims.statement: You cannot practically acidify chalky ground — the free calcium carbonate would need huge quantities of sulphur over many years.
claims.detail: The RHS defines chalky soils as pH 7.1 and above, typically 7.1–8.0. They are free-draining with poor moisture retention, often shallow, stony and light. Added organic matter decomposes rapidly, which makes them hard to keep fertile — directly relevant to any plan built on repeated compost dressings. Both manganese and iron become locked up, causing chlorosis. The page states plainly that reducing alkalinity with sulphur is not practical, because huge quantities would be required over many years to counter the free calcium carbonate. The framing to take from it: alkalinity is not a problem to solve, it is a specification to design to. Calcicoles such as Syringa tolerate lime; calcifuges such as Rhododendron will not thrive.

source.name: RHS — Chalky soils

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: Eastern England is 'tending to alkaline' but not necessarily true chalk — mortar-rich construction rubble raises pH by the same free-lime mechanism but the buffering capacity may be far lower and could decline over years as the mortar weathers. This page cannot establish what your specific bed's pH is or how strongly buffered it is; only a test can. It gives no named plant list of its own.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule overreaches the evidence in two ways. First, it invents scope: the page never mentions mortar or concrete rubble, and those are materially different from chalk soil. Rubble is a finite, physically removable inclusion with no chalk bedrock or carbonate-bearing groundwater behind it, whereas a chalk soil sits on an effectively unlimited reservoir; the sulphur needed scales with the carbonate present, so a patch of builder's rubble may well be practically amendable or simply dug out. Extending an RHS sentence about chalky soils to "the ground contains free calcium carbonate" in any amount is the claimant's leap, not the source's. Second, the source states impracticality — cost, quantity, and years — not impossibility, and the underlying variable (carbonate content, hence buffering capacity) is a continuum from a trace at pH 7.2 to deep chalk at pH 8.0, not a threshold. That is a gradient dressed as a floor. "Any plan that depends on acidifying the soil cannot stand" also sweeps in things the page does not rule out, such as ericaceous compost in containers or raised beds, and it is not needed to justify the design conclusion the claim actually wants, which is plant selection. A rule this could support, if one is wanted: WHEN the soil itself is chalk or limestone derived and effervesces in vinegar THEN a plan whose success depends on durably lowering that ground's pH in situ should be treated as unfunded, BECAUSE the RHS states the sulphur required is impractical in quantity and must be sustained over many years. That version is honest; the proposed one is not.

claims.statement: Mount Etna broom (Genista aetnensis) is listed by the RHS for chalk, clay, loam and sand; acid, alkaline or neutral pH; well-drained soil; full sun; exposed or sheltered sites; and it is marked drought resistant. Cultivation guidance is "grow in poor but well-drained soil in full sun". Hardiness H5 (hardy in most of the UK even in severe winters, -15 to -10) and it holds an Award of Garden Merit. Ultimate height and spread 4-8 m over 10-20 years, so it does structural work. Note that the RHS also says it will not regrow from old wood and responds badly to hard pruning. (Its nitrogen fixation as a legume is a reasonable inference, not something the RHS page states; the Beth Chatto gravel garden attribution needs its own source before it is published.)
claims.detail: This is the strongest structural candidate I verified for exactly your ground. RHS lists soils as chalk, clay, loam and sand; pH acid, alkaline or neutral; moisture well-drained; any aspect; exposed or sheltered. Hardiness H5, meaning hardy in most of the UK through severe winters, and it holds an Award of Garden Merit. Ultimate height and spread 4–8 m over 10–20 years, so it does real structural work rather than groundcover. Cultivation notes call for poor but well-drained soil in full sun, with strong drought resistance and no need for enriched soil. It is a legume, so it fixes its own nitrogen — which is why low fertility is not a handicap to it. Beth Chatto grew it in the gravel garden.

source.name: RHS Plants — Genista aetnensis

claims.checker_note: verified — every RHS-rated attribute confirmed against the live cited page; two side-facts in the supporting detail (nitrogen fixation, Beth Chatto) are unsourced by that page and must be cited separately or dropped
claims.cannot_establish: RHS plant profiles describe soil texture and pH tolerance; they say nothing about compaction or rubble. Tolerating chalk is not the same as tolerating a compacted mortar-rubble pan. H5 is a winter-cold rating only. It cannot establish survival rate, nor what happens in the first two summers before roots are down, nor whether the nitrogen fixation actually establishes on a rubble bed lacking the right rhizobia.

claims.statement:
Italian buckthorn (Rhamnus alaternus 'Argenteovariegata') is RHS-rated for chalk and sand, for acid, alkaline or neutral pH, and is flagged drought resistant: an AGM evergreen reaching 2.5-4 m in 20-50 years, hardiness H5 (hardy in most of the UK even in severe winters, -15 to -10C). Evergreen structure that stands through winter is rare among genuinely drought-tolerant plants, which is what makes it worth the caveat. The caveat: RHS lists its exposure as sheltered only, and says it is "not reliably hardy and needs some shelter in the colder more exposed areas." The same entry, though, calls it "valuable for coastal planting" and lists Coastal among its suggested locations, so the RHS limit is cold combined with exposure rather than wind on its own. On a cold, open fen-edge site, treat it as a warm-wall plant rather than an open-ground one.

[Separately: if the Cambridge Botanic Garden Dry Garden example is kept, it needs its own citation to a CUBG source naming the plant. The RHS page does not support it, and it was not verified here.]
claims.detail: This is one of the plants Cambridge Botanic Garden actually names in its unwatered Dry Garden, so it has both a specification and a working example behind it. RHS: soils chalk, clay, loam, sand; pH acid, alkaline or neutral; moist but well-drained or well-drained; south or west facing; hardiness H5; Award of Garden Merit; evergreen; ultimate size 2.5–4 m over 20–50 years. Evergreen structure that stands through winter is rare among genuinely drought-tolerant plants, which is what makes this worth the caveat. The caveat is that RHS lists exposure as sheltered, and notes it is not completely hardy and benefits from shelter in colder, exposed districts. On an open, windswept fen-edge site this is the wrong plant; against a warm wall it is the right one.

source.name: RHS Plants — Rhamnus alaternus 'Argenteovariegata'

claims.checker_note: verified for the RHS specification and the sheltered-exposure caveat; unverified for the Cambridge Botanic Garden Dry Garden example, which the cited source does not support
claims.cannot_establish: 'Sheltered' in the RHS exposure field is a categorical rating with no wind-speed threshold behind it, so I cannot say how exposed is too exposed. Cambridge Botanic Garden is a walled, urban, relatively sheltered site — its success there does not transfer to an open plot. Nothing here addresses compaction or rubble, and the 20–50 year maturity figure means no quick structure.

claims.statement: Olympian mullein (Verbascum olympicum) is specified by the RHS for alkaline, poor, well-drained soil in full sun, and the RHS adds: "In fertile soils, it grows large and needs support." It is a case where enriching the ground works against the plant rather than against planting technique. RHS lists soils as chalk and loam, pH alkaline, moisture well-drained, aspect south-facing, exposure exposed, hardiness H6 (hardy across all of the UK and northern Europe), and calls it a drought-tolerant plant. Height 1.5-2.5 m, spread 0.5-1 m; RHS describes it as "a short-lived perennial, usually dying after flowering", so it is a pioneer rather than a permanent fixture. It carries the RHS Plants for Pollinators mark. Improve the ground and you get a bigger plant that has to be held up.
claims.detail: This is the clearest published case of soil enrichment being counterproductive to a specific plant rather than to planting technique. RHS lists soils as chalk and loam, pH alkaline, moisture well-drained, aspect south-facing, exposure exposed, hardiness H6 (hardy across all of the UK and northern Europe) — a tougher exposure and cold rating than either woody plant above. Height 1.5–2.5 m, spread 0.5–1 m, short-lived perennial that typically dies after flowering, so it works as a self-renewing pioneer rather than a permanent fixture. Grey-woolly stems and leaves are the drought adaptation CUBG describes. It is an RHS Plant for Pollinators. Feed it or improve the ground and you get a taller plant that needs staking.

source.name: RHS Plants — Verbascum olympicum

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: Flopping is a performance problem, not death — this establishes that fertility is unhelpful here, not that it is fatal, so it is not a floor rule. The page does not give rooting depth, does not say the plant will self-seed and persist, and says nothing about germination on rubble or gravel. Being short-lived, its long-term presence depends on seedlings establishing, which is unevidenced here.

claims.statement: The RHS advises watering newly planted trees, shrubs and perennials regularly, particularly through the first year and longer depending on size at planting, explicitly including plants sold as drought tolerant; large tree specimens may need it for up to three years. The drought-tolerant label describes an established plant, not a newly planted one. How long that dependency lasts is something you can shorten: plant small (9 cm perennials, small trees and shrubs) because young plants establish faster, plant in March or September while the soil is warm, skip fertiliser because it forces soft growth that dries out, and mulch Mediterranean-style plantings with 5-7.5 cm of gravel. (If the Beth Chatto gravel garden is mentioned, mention it honestly: every plant was soaked and hosed in at planting, and the garden has not been irrigated since — that is an argument for watering in well at planting, not for a year of watering.)
claims.detail: The RHS says to water newly planted trees, shrubs and perennials regularly, particularly in the first year or longer depending on size at planting, explicitly even if they are described as drought tolerant; large specimens may need watering for up to three years. This is corroborated by practice: every plant in the Beth Chatto gravel garden was dunked until the rootball was saturated and hosed in at planting. The RHS mitigations all reduce how long that dependency lasts: plant small (9 cm pots for perennials, small trees and shrubs) because young plants establish faster; plant in March as the soil warms or September while it is still warm, giving root growth time before winter; avoid fertilisers because they force soft growth that dries out; and mulch Mediterranean-style plantings with 5–7.5 cm of gravel.

source.name: RHS — Drought-Resistant Gardening Tips

claims.checker_note: verified as RHS guidance (quote is verbatim, URL live); the Beth Chatto corroborating detail is unverified and should not be published as support
claims.cannot_establish: No volumes, no frequency, no trigger for when to stop — 'regularly' is undefined, and the one-to-three-year range is broad. It cannot establish what happens if you do not water, only that the RHS advises against relying on that. It also does not distinguish a rubble bed, where a rootball may sit in a dry pocket with no capillary contact to surrounding soil, from ordinary garden ground.
claims.wall_fell_because: The evidence is prescriptive advice, not a demonstration of total failure. Nowhere does the RHS say an unwatered new planting dies; it says water "regularly" and that large trees "may need" up to three years — hedged language describing a raised failure rate and slower establishment, which is a gradient. The page's own structure proves it is a gradient: the requirement scales with size at planting (9 cm perennial at one end, three-year tree at the other), and a floor does not have a dial on it. Rainfall is the uncontrolled confound — in a temperate maritime climate a small autumn-planted perennial can be met entirely by rain through its first season, which is why RHS recommends September planting in the first place. The claim's own example is the standing counter-example: the Beth Chatto gravel garden was watered in at planting and never irrigated after, first growing season included, and it worked. At most the evidence supports a much narrower floor — soak the soil and rootball at planting — and even that is a practice recommendation rather than a proven hard limit. "A zero-watering plan cannot work in the first growing season" overstates it into a law.

claims.statement: About three quarters of all wild bee species nest in the soil, and spend much of their life cycle underground. (Antoine & Forrest 2021, Ecological Entomology — the review's opening sentence.) What those bees need varies enormously between species: soil texture, compaction, moisture, temperature, ground-surface features and proximity to flowers all matter differently to different bees, and the review is explicit that there is little quantitative information on any of it. There is no single correct bee soil. If the site also wants to say these bees are underground as egg, larva, prepupa and pupa and above ground as adults for only a few weeks, that needs its own source — it is not in this review's abstract.
claims.detail: A peer-reviewed review of ground-nesting bee habitat (Antoine & Forrest, Ecological Entomology) opens by stating that roughly 3/4 of wild bee species nest in the soil. These bees are underground for most of the year as egg, larva, prepupa and pupa, emerging as adults for only a few weeks. The same review is blunt that requirements vary enormously between species — soil texture, compaction, moisture, temperature, ground-surface features and distance to flowers all matter differently to different bees. There is no single 'correct' bee soil; what is constant is that there must be soil they can dig into.

source.name: Antoine & Forrest (2020/21), 'Nesting habitat of ground-nesting bees: a review', Ecological Entomology — abstract via Semantic Scholar API

claims.checker_note: verified — cited quotation is exact and the URL resolves; publish with "much of their life cycle" rather than "most of their lives", and drop or separately source the life-stage detail
claims.cannot_establish: I fetched the abstract only, not the full text (Wiley returned 402). It does not give a UK-specific proportion, does not name a minimum patch size of bare soil, and does not give a compaction threshold in measurable units.
claims.proposed_wall: WHEN no unsealed soil is reachable anywhere in the garden — every surface is paving, decking, artificial grass, concrete or a permanent weed membrane — THEN the ground-nesting bee layer cannot stand BECAUSE these bees must excavate a tunnel into soil to nest at all.

claims.statement: On farms around Ottawa, Canada, ground-nesting bees were more abundant and more species-rich on plots with more bare ground and more sand. Cavity-nesting bees showed no relationship with any measured soil property, which the authors take as evidence that the soil associations are direct rather than a side-effect of something unmeasured. Sand, slope, compaction and bare ground were all significant predictors of which species were present, though they explained only a small share of the variation, because each species responds its own way; slope alone was linked to lower overall diversity. These are associations from a two-year field survey, not effects from a manipulation.
claims.detail: Antoine, Normandin & Forrest (2025) sampled 131 plots on 35 farms over two years and collected 8,661 ground-nesting bees of 100 species. Abundance and species richness both rose with the percentage of bare ground and the percentage of sand. Cavity-nesting bees showed no relationship with any soil variable, which is the control that shows the soil effect is real and direct rather than a side-effect of something else. Sand percentage, slope, compaction and bare ground were all significant predictors of community composition, but only a small share of variance was explained, because each species responds its own way.

source.name: Antoine, Normandin & Forrest (2025), 'Associations between soil characteristics and ground-nesting bees on farms', Insect Conservation and Diversity — abstract via Semantic Scholar API

claims.checker_note: verified with caveats — figures and findings match the cited abstract exactly, but the evidence is correlational (observational survey, not manipulation) and regional (one Canadian farming area), so "raise" should read "were higher with" and the direct-effect inference is the authors' suggestion rather than a demonstrated result
claims.cannot_establish: Abstract only; full text paywalled. The study is farmland near Ottawa, Canada — not a UK garden, and not chalky eastern-England soil. It gives no threshold percentage of bare ground, and no penetrometer reading above which bees fail. It cannot tell you that adding bare ground to a specific garden will produce nests.

claims.statement: Most of the UK's roughly 240 solitary bee species nest underground, and ground-nesting species tend to favour light, dry soil in a sunny spot — bare earth on a south-west facing slope or a footpath — though the Tawny Mining Bee will nest in short turf. Cite both Buglife posts: "Bare ground experiments to help save rare bees and wasps" (24 May 2025, https://www.buglife.org.uk/blog/bare-ground-experiments-to-help-save-rare-bees-and-wasps/) for the 240 species, the "most are fossorial and nest in cavities underground" line, the warm-dry-bare-soil requirement, the six- and eight-tonne mini diggers across eight sites, and the rotational winter bare-ground creation; and "Gardening for Solitary Bees" (Beth Barber, 23 May 2025, https://www.buglife.org.uk/blog/gardening-for-solitary-bees/) for the siting advice and the Tawny Mining Bee short-turf exception. Do not attribute the siting advice to the bare-ground page, and note the bare-ground project's focal species is the Tormentil Mining Bee, not the Tawny.
claims.detail: Buglife, the UK invertebrate conservation charity, states there are around 240 solitary bee species in the UK and that while some are aerial nesters using stems, dead wood, walls and bee hotels, most are 'fossorial' and nest in cavities underground. Their siting advice is specific: light, dry soils in a sunny spot, such as bare earth on a south-west facing slope or a footpath, although the Tawny Mining Bee will use short turf. Their bare-ground restoration work used six- and eight-tonne mini diggers across eight sites, and they recommend rotational small-scale bare-ground creation each winter — that is, bare ground is something actively made and re-made, not something that appears by leaving a garden alone.

source.name: Buglife — 'Bare ground experiments to help save rare bees and wasps'

claims.checker_note: source-declared (two Buglife sources required — the siting-advice half belongs to a second URL)
claims.cannot_establish: Buglife is a conservation charity giving guidance, not reporting a controlled experiment on this page, and 'most' is not a number. Nothing here proves a garden-scale patch works, gives a minimum area, or says how sunny is sunny enough. The south-west-facing advice is a rule of thumb, not a measured optimum.
claims.wall_fell_because: The sources describe a strong preference, not an absolute requirement. Buglife's wording is gradient language throughout: ground nesters "tend to favour" light, dry soils in a sunny spot; the bare-ground post says unchecked vegetation makes conditions shady and damp and therefore unsuitable for the rare target species, which supports "much worse", not "cannot work at all". Neither page states that ground-nesting bees are absent from shaded ground, and neither tests permanently shaded sites. The stated mechanism is also too strong: soil in shade still warms with ambient air temperature, and some mining bees are associated with woodland and shaded banks. Permanent shade plainly makes a poor bee bank and the honest line is that it will attract few or no ground-nesters — but that is a steep gradient, not an evidenced hard floor, and this rule as written would be published as a certainty the cited evidence does not carry.

claims.statement: Deadwood is not a minor habitat, but the number usually quoted for it should be quoted carefully. Buglife's 2011 factsheet "Scottish Invertebrate Habitat Management: Deadwood" states that "it has been estimated that 13% of all species of plants and animals known in the UK are directly dependent on deadwood habitats", citing Antrobus et al. 2005. That reference, in the factsheet's own list, is the Deadwood Habitat Action Plan Technical Appendix to the Birmingham and Black Country Biodiversity Action Plan — a local action plan, not a national census. So the headline percentage is a figure passed onward, not a fresh count of UK species. The dependence is large and well established; the precise share rests on a secondary citation and is worth naming as such.
claims.detail: Buglife's habitat management guide and their Scottish deadwood factsheet both state that an estimated 13% of all species of plants and animals known in the UK are directly dependent on dead and decaying wood, citing Antrobus et al. (2005). Their public gardening page instead says 'nearly two thousand invertebrates in Britain depend on deadwood'. The Woodland Trust gives a third number: around 650 UK beetle species require deadwood at some point in their lifecycle. These are not reconcilable as stated — 13% of the roughly 70,000 known UK species would be several thousand — so the honest position is that deadwood dependence is large and well established, and the headline percentage is a repeated secondary citation rather than a fresh count.

source.name: Buglife (2011), 'Scottish Invertebrate Habitat Management: Deadwood' — PDF fetched and text extracted locally

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: I did not reach Antrobus et al. (2005), the primary source — it is a Birmingham and Black Country Biodiversity Action Plan technical appendix, not a peer-reviewed paper. I cannot verify how the 13% was derived, what species list it used, or why the same charity publishes 'nearly two thousand' elsewhere. Do not present any single number as settled.

claims.statement: Buglife's habitat management guide says standing dead wood "tends to be more valuable for saproxylic species than fallen timber, as it rots from the inside rather than from the outside, creating quite different conditions and microhabitats", and that "soft, red rotten heartwood is the sole habitat of some of our rarest and most threatened saproxylic invertebrates" — felling trees with heart-rot "could result in the extinction of these specialist species". It also says continuity is what matters most, because "many are poor colonisers and cannot travel far to find suitable habitats". Note the guide values fallen wood too, and asks for it to be left where it lies in a range of sun and shade; its argument is that a steady supply of decaying wood over time beats a one-off deposit, not that a log pile is worthless.
claims.detail: Buglife's habitat management guide states that standing dead wood tends to be more valuable for saproxylic species than fallen timber, because it rots from the inside rather than the outside and so makes different conditions. It also says soft, red rotten heartwood is the sole habitat of some of our rarest and most threatened saproxylic invertebrates, and that felling or removing trees with heart-rot could cause their extinction. Crucially it says many saproxylic species are poor colonisers that cannot travel far, so continuity of habitat over time — a supply of new decaying wood every year, and trees growing on to replace those that die — is what matters, not a single stack of logs.

source.name: Buglife, 'Managing dead and decaying wood habitats' Habitat Management Guide (Back from the Brink / Ancients of the Future) — PDF fetched and text extracted locally

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: This is charity management guidance aimed at woodland, parkland and wood pasture, not gardens. It gives no measured comparison of species counts between standing and fallen wood, no minimum trunk diameter, and no evidence about what a domestic garden can or cannot hold. It does not say a garden log pile is worthless — only that it is a different and lesser thing.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule looks like a tautology ("sole habitat absent, therefore species absent") but four things break it, three of them from the source's own text. (1) The guide defeats "cannot be present": section (g) says "Many of the insects associated with dead and decaying wood microhabitats only use them in their larval form. As adults, many require pollen and nectar", and asks for nectar sources "in close proximity" to decaying wood. So adult heartwood specialists can be genuinely present in a garden with no heart-rot at all — feeding on umbellifers, passing through. What is barred is breeding, not presence. As written the rule is false, and a "cannot be present" floor that means "cannot complete its lifecycle" is a different rule. (2) The WHEN condition is unobservable. Heart-rot is internal — the very sentence the claim rests on says standing dead wood "rots from the inside rather than from the outside". Nobody can establish from a garden that a tree lacks heart-rot; a floor rule keyed on a hidden state cannot be applied. (3) "no tree old or large enough" is the wrong proxy, and the same document undercuts it: page 1 says "trees can start producing wounds and small sections of decaying wood from a young age", and section (k) describes veteranisation — deliberately damaging young trees to start decay early. Heart-rot follows wounding and fungal entry, not a size threshold. (4) The BECAUSE clause "a log pile does not produce it" is unsupported by the source, which never says that. The standing/fallen contrast in the guide is about how decay proceeds, not about fallen wood being incapable of holding red rot — a veteran trunk that falls carries its heart-rot with it. Finally, the rule invents "the heartwood-specialist saproxylic group" as a bounded category; Buglife names no species and draws no such boundary, so there is nothing to test the floor against. This is a strong gradient with a near-definitional core, not a publishable hard floor.

claims.statement: PTES's log-pile instructions for stag beetles are specific: wood from any broadleaved tree, logs "at least the thickness of an adults arm", "partially bury the logs in the soil so that they don't dry out", and "site the logs in partial shade if possible to prevent them drying out" — their diagram marks the buried portion approx. 50cm below ground level. Their stated reason: stag beetles "rely on decaying wood that is in contact with the soil, both to feed on as larvae and in which to lay their eggs", and the larvae "develop underground in rotting wood for several years". Note what this does and doesn't say. Soil contact is the requirement; burial is how you get it — the same leaflet says "a single log on or in the soil will be appreciated". Partial shade is offered as "if possible", not a rule. And a dry, raised log pile is not a dead loss: PTES say it still serves fungi, other deadwood invertebrates, small mammals, basking reptiles and solitary bees — it just isn't stag beetle habitat. Siting matters too: most female stag beetles don't travel more than 20m, so a pile far from any existing population is unlikely to be colonised. All of the above is PTES's own instruction and stated reasoning, not a measured result.
claims.detail: PTES specify: use wood from any broadleaved tree, logs at least the thickness of an adult's arm, sited in partial shade to stop them drying out, and partially buried in the soil — their diagram shows roughly 50cm below ground level. Their stated reason is that stag beetle larvae rely on decaying wood in contact with the soil, both to feed on and to lay eggs in, and develop underground for several years. Buglife's 2025 deadwood pile leaflet agrees on siting: a cool, shady part of the garden, logs plus bark plus dead leaves, new logs added yearly as old ones rot, and a 'stumpery' of vertical half-buried logs particularly favoured by stag beetles. Note the dispersal limit: most female stag beetles do not travel more than 20m, so an isolated pile in a landscape with no other deadwood will not be found.

source.name: People's Trust for Endangered Species — 'Build a log pile for stag beetles' — PDF fetched and text extracted locally

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: Conservation-charity leaflets, not experiments — there is no trial here comparing buried against surface log piles, and no evidence a garden pile raises stag beetle numbers. Climate/geography flag: stag beetles are largely south-east England and the Thames corridor, so Cambridge is at the edge of range and a log pile there may never be colonised. Buglife says shady; the management guide says a range from shaded to sun-exposed — the two are advice for different audiences, not a measured optimum.
claims.wall_fell_because: Fails on scope and on evidence type. Scope: the rule covers "the buried-deadwood group (stag beetle and relatives)", but the leaflet speaks only of the stag beetle, Lucanus cervus. The extension to relatives is where it breaks — Britain's lesser stag beetle, Dorcus parallelipipedus, routinely breeds in standing dead trunks, stumps and dead branches that are not in soil contact, so the stated floor is false for the group as drawn. Evidence type: for L. cervus alone the leaflet's "they rely on decaying wood that is in contact with the soil" is close to a floor, but it is a charity's declarative habitat guidance in a public leaflet — it asserts dependence, it does not demonstrate zero occupancy without soil contact, and this claim's own status is source-declared. A floor rule needs the stronger footing. The leaflet also cuts against the rule's condition as written: it says "a single log on or in the soil will be appreciated", so a log merely lying on soil qualifies, and the mechanism at stake is soil CONTACT, not depth. A narrower, honest version would survive as source-declared rather than as a floor: PTES state that stag beetle larvae need decaying wood in contact with soil, so deadwood kept entirely on hard surfaces or raised clear of the ground is not, by their account, stag beetle habitat.

claims.statement: A bumblebee queen can live up to 12 months and spends up to half of that dormant. The Bumblebee Conservation Trust says queens hibernate in a variety of places — well-drained soft soil, leaf litter, log piles, open compost heaps, hollow trees or under bark — that they can excavate more than 10cm into soil, and that they often choose north-facing spots, so less winter sun reaches them and the ground does not warm enough to wake them early.
claims.detail: The Bumblebee Conservation Trust states that queens hibernate in well-drained, soft soil, leaf litter, hollow trees or under bark, that they can excavate to a depth of more than 10cm, and that they often choose north-facing spots so less winter sun reaches them and the ground does not warm enough to wake them early. A queen can live up to 12 months and spends up to half of that dormant. The practical consequence is that the hibernation site is invisible: it is under the ground you are about to dig over, repot on, or turn compost on in winter and spring. This is a genuinely counter-intuitive requirement — the cold, shaded, unimproved north side of a garden is doing work, not sitting idle.

source.name: Bumblebee Conservation Trust — 'How to help hibernating bumblebees'

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: Charity guidance, not a cited study — no sample sizes, no survival rates, no measurement of how many queens are lost to autumn digging. It does not establish that a garden without such a bank loses its bumblebees, only that the bank is where they go. Species vary and this page does not distinguish between them.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule is contradicted by its own cited source. The same BBCT page lists leaf litter, hollow trees, inside tree bark, log piles, open compost heaps, raised beds and longer grass/moss as hibernation sites, and BBCT's garden advice is to build log piles and leave compost undisturbed precisely so queens have somewhere to go. Ground that is sealed, compacted or membraned removes the excavation option and makes a site much worse, but it does not make a hibernaculum impossible — a log pile or compost heap on a paved yard still works. The rule's stated mechanism ("they overwinter by excavating over 10cm into soil") also misreads a "can excavate to more than 10cm" capability as an obligatory depth. This is a strong gradient, not a hard floor.

claims.statement: Leaving healthy herbaceous and hollow-stemmed plants unpruned until early spring is one of the standard autumn recommendations for overwintering insects. The RHS advises it directly — hollow dry stems can provide homes for insects over winter — and the timing is what gives it force: cutting the border down in autumn removes that shelter in one afternoon, while the insects are inside and immobile. The RHS presents this alongside about a dozen other winter measures without ranking any of them, noting that carrying out even a few makes a difference. Combined with INV-07 (queens under the soil) and INV-06 (rotting wood), the pattern is that much of what an invertebrate garden needs in winter looks, to a tidy eye, like a job not yet done.
claims.detail: The RHS advises leaving healthy herbaceous and hollow-stemmed plants unpruned until early spring, because these provide homes for overwintering insects. The mechanism is simple: hollow dry stems are the winter shelter, and cutting the border down in October removes it in one afternoon while the insects are inside and immobile. Buglife's garden advice adds the litter layer — leave dead leaves where they are, as they feed worms and other decomposers. Combined with claim INV-07 (queens under the soil) and INV-06 (rotting wood), the pattern is that almost everything an invertebrate garden needs in winter looks, to a tidy eye, like a job not yet done.

source.name: Royal Horticultural Society — 'Wildlife: helping through winter'

claims.checker_note: source-declared for the practice only — the RHS sentence is verbatim and the URL is live; the "single decision that matters most" ranking is unsupported editorial inference and must be dropped, "seedheads" must be dropped from the insect-shelter framing, and the source's "can provide" hedge must be restored
claims.cannot_establish: This is advice, not evidence — the RHS page gives no study, no counts of insects lost to autumn cutting, and no comparison of autumn versus spring cutback. I could not reach Xerces Society or Butterfly Conservation pages on overwintering (both returned 403), so I have no source here that breaks overwintering down by life stage or species group. Treat the size of the effect as unquantified.

claims.statement: The RHS Plants for Bugs experiment found that planting density matters within every plant-origin group: regardless of where the plants came from, the more densely a scheme is planted or allowed to grow, the more invertebrates it supports — a result RHS states for plant-dwelling invertebrates and, for overall abundance, for ground-active ones too. One documented exception: ground-dwelling spiders were more numerous in sparser plantings. And "regardless of origin" does not mean origin is irrelevant — native plantings still supported the most plant-dwelling invertebrates, with near-native around 10% fewer and southern-hemisphere around 20% fewer.
claims.detail: Plants for Bugs ran four years across 36 garden-like plots of 3m x 3m, 18 at RHS Wisley and 18 at RHS Deers Farm, each planted with 14 species from one of three zones (British native, northern hemisphere near-native, southern hemisphere exotic), sampled by pitfall trap, suction sampling and flower observation every six weeks March to October. Around 80,000 invertebrates and over 300 species were counted. The RHS states plainly that regardless of plant origin, the more densely a planting scheme is planted or allowed to grow, the more invertebrates it will support. This is the finding gardeners most often skip past, because it is about quantity of vegetation rather than about which plants are morally correct.

source.name: Royal Horticultural Society — Plants for Bugs project page

claims.checker_note: verified-with-correction
claims.cannot_establish: The RHS ran the study and publishes the summary, so this page is not independent. Density was measured as the plots filled out, not manipulated as an experimental treatment with set spacings, so this cannot give you a plants-per-square-metre number. Wisley is Surrey on acid sandy soil, not alkaline eastern England, and 3m x 3m plots are not a whole garden.

claims.statement: Plants for Bugs did not conclude "natives only" — it concluded "mostly native". In the plant-dwelling-invertebrate arm, the RHS reports that near-native (northern hemisphere) planting schemes support "only marginally fewer invertebrates... (less than 10% fewer)" overall and across three of the four functional groups, and that exotic (southern hemisphere) schemes "will still support a good number of invertebrates, albeit around 20% fewer than British natives." The same page adds the practical version of that gap: to match a native plot you would need about a fifth more near-native vegetation, or about a quarter more exotic vegetation. Two reversals usually left out, from the companion ground-active page: exotic schemes "may support relatively more ground-active invertebrates in winter", because hardy exotic plantings hold more evergreens, and ground-active spiders "were found in greater numbers among sparser plantings" — the one group running against the density rule. The peer-reviewed pollinator arm (Salisbury et al. 2015, Journal of Applied Ecology) concluded gardens should be planted "biased towards native and near-native species but with a selection of exotics to extend the flowering season." The RHS's own headline advice remains to plant predominantly British natives. Cite both pages: https://www.rhs.org.uk/wildlife/plants-for-plant-dwelling-invertebrates and https://www.rhs.org.uk/wildlife/native-non-native-plants-for-ground-invertebrates
claims.detail: The RHS reports that planting schemes based on near-native (northern hemisphere) plants support only marginally fewer invertebrates — less than 10% fewer overall and across three of four functional groups — while exotic (southern hemisphere) schemes still support a good number, around 20% fewer than British natives. They add two reversals that are usually left out: schemes based on exotic plants may support relatively more ground-active invertebrates in winter, because hardy exotic plantings contain more evergreens; and ground-active spiders were found in greater numbers among sparser plantings, the one group that goes against the density rule. The peer-reviewed pollinator arm (Salisbury et al. 2015, Journal of Applied Ecology) concluded gardens should be planted with a variety biased towards native and near-native species but with a selection of exotics to extend the flowering season.

source.name: Royal Horticultural Society — 'Native and non-native plants for plant-dwelling invertebrates' (Plants for Bugs results)

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: These percentages come from the RHS's own summary pages, not from a paper I could open — the peer-reviewed abstract I fetched (Salisbury et al. 2015) covers flower-visiting insects only and gives direction, not percentages. The trial used specific 14-species assemblages, so 'exotic' means those plants, not all southern-hemisphere plants. It says nothing about trees, which is where the native-plant effect is strongest (see INV-13).

claims.statement: The evidence that garden pesticides harm garden wildlife is thin. A 2026 preregistered rapid review (Papworth et al., Ecological Solutions and Evidence 7(2) e70263) searched Web of Knowledge, Scopus, Conservation Evidence and Environmental Evidence and found just four studies for the UK and Ireland that met its criteria — all observational, all on birds and invertebrates. They reported either no significant effect or negative effects; none reported a benefit, and none assessed soil or water quality. Being observational, they show association rather than cause, and the authors note that habitat quality around gardens may interact with pesticide use. The authors' own reading is that this is "some evidence" of harm — enough that they recommend environmental NGOs keep promoting chemical-free gardening, while calling for research on other species groups and on soil and water. ("Four studies" is what this bounded search surfaced, not a census of all research that exists.)
claims.detail: A 2026 preregistered rapid review (Papworth et al., Ecological Solutions and Evidence) searched Web of Knowledge, Scopus, Conservation Evidence and Environmental Evidence for studies on herbicide and pesticide use in domestic gardens in the UK and Ireland. Four observational studies met the criteria, all on birds and invertebrates. They reported either no significant effect or negative effects; no study assessed impacts on soil or water quality. The authors conclude that because they found some evidence of negative impact, environmental NGOs should continue promoting chemical-free gardening. Separately, outdoor use of metaldehyde slug pellets was banned in the UK from 31 March 2022 over risks to birds and mammals — a legal fact, not a judgement call. Buglife's position is that they actively encourage people not to use pesticides or insecticides because they are harmful to all invertebrates; the RHS says we all have a duty to avoid neonicotinoids and other pesticides but still allows use 'where there is no reasonable alternative'.

source.name: Papworth et al., 'Do herbicides and pesticides in domestic gardens threaten wildlife in the United Kingdom and Ireland?', Ecological Solutions and Evidence — abstract on Royal Holloway research portal

claims.checker_note: supported — not contested. The claim is a direct report of a peer-reviewed 2026 paper and is stated near-verbatim in its own abstract; no one disputes the count. "Contested" mislabels the uncertainty: what is thin and uncertain is the underlying evidence base, which is precisely what the claim says. Publish as supported, with the weaker wording. The metaldehyde ban, Buglife and RHS items in the DETAIL are separately true or plausible but are NOT carried by this citation and each need their own source.
claims.cannot_establish: Four observational studies is a very weak base and observational studies cannot establish cause. I read the abstract, not the full text (Wiley returned 402). This cannot tell you that any particular product harms any particular garden, cannot rank products, and cannot support a claim that occasional targeted use makes a garden dead. Anyone claiming strong proof either way is going beyond the evidence — the review's own framing is that the evidence for this very common pro-environmental behaviour is limited.

claims.statement: A garden pond drying out in summer is usually not the disaster it looks like. Freshwater Habitats Trust report that around 40% of lowland countryside ponds dry out in drought years, and that their surveys find ponds which occasionally dry out are among the richest of all, because many creatures are adapted to it: most flying adults (water beetles, pond skaters, backswimmers) leave and return, most mayflies, caddis and damselflies on one-year cycles have already emerged, and zooplankton have resistant eggs. What is genuinely lost is snails, shrimps, water slaters, leeches and flatworms, plus younger dragonfly nymphs if the mud bakes hard. Two honest caveats. First, that richness finding comes from countryside ponds; the Trust says there is "still too little information" about how garden pond communities withstand drought and calls its garden advice a best estimate, partly because lined garden ponds often hold little silt, so there may be no damp sediment to burrow into. Their garden verdict is the weaker "unlikely to be a complete disaster". Second, standing water is not only an invertebrate requirement — amphibian larvae and fish depend on it too; the same page notes younger amphibians perish when a pond dries. Heat is a separate hazard: water reaching 35°C, possible in a sunny pond on a 30°C air day, can kill tadpoles and crustaceans outright.
claims.detail: Freshwater Habitats Trust states that around 40% of lowland countryside ponds dry out in drought years, and that ponds which occasionally dry out are among the richest of all, because many creatures are adapted to it. In a drying pond, most flying adults (water beetles, pond skaters, backswimmers) leave and return; most mayflies, caddis and damselflies with one-year cycles have already emerged; zooplankton have resistant eggs. What is genuinely lost is snails, shrimps, water slaters, leeches and flatworms, plus younger dragonfly nymphs if the mud bakes hard. They flag one real garden-specific risk: lined garden ponds often have little silt, so there may be no damp sediment for creatures to burrow into. Heat is a separate hazard — water reaching 35°C, possible in a sunny pond on a 30°C air day, can kill tadpoles and crustaceans outright.

source.name: Freshwater Habitats Trust FAQ — 'What to do if your pond is drying out' (2013) — PDF fetched and text extracted locally

claims.checker_note: partly verified — supporting detail and the quoted statistic verified verbatim against the fetched source; headline overstated, with one clause ("only required by the aquatic invertebrates") false and contradicted by the cited page, and a countryside finding applied to gardens without the Trust's own hedge
claims.cannot_establish: The Trust says openly that 'in the garden there is still too little information about how wildlife communities withstand drought' and that their garden advice is a best estimate, not measured. The 40% figure is for countryside ponds, not lined garden ponds. Climate flag: eastern England around Cambridge is the driest part of the UK (~557mm/yr), so summer drying should be treated as the normal case there, not the exception — which strengthens the case for rainwater butts and for a shaded pond.
claims.wall_fell_because: The cited evidence cannot support this floor, and in the relevant range it argues the opposite. The whole document is about ponds losing their water temporarily, and its finding is that the aquatic invertebrate layer largely survives that: adults fly out and return, one-year-cycle species have already emerged, zooplankton eggs sit out the dry period, and the Trust notes pond animals "can re-colonise new ponds so incredibly quickly". A pond can therefore hold no standing water for a substantial part of summer and the layer still stands — which directly falsifies the rule as phrased ("no standing water at any point in spring or summer"), since a pond dry from July onward satisfies neither a floor breach nor a collapse. On the genuinely absolute case — a garden with no water at all across the entire season — this source is simply silent; it never addresses it, so the evidence offered does not establish the floor it is cited for. Beyond the evidence gap, the rule is close to a definitional restatement dressed as an empirical finding: "no water anywhere, ever, therefore no aquatic animals" is true by the meaning of "aquatic", not by observation, and a floor rule should carry information. It also overreaches in scope: it generalises from obligately aquatic larval stages of a few named insects to "the aquatic invertebrate layer" as a whole, and some of the taxa named (caddis, stoneflies) are largely running-water animals for which a damp seep or bog, not standing water, is the relevant habitat — while adult water beetles and pond skaters can still be present in a waterless garden in transit. If a floor is wanted here it must be stated as the narrow, near-tautological life-cycle constraint (aquatic insects cannot complete larval development without water of some kind persisting long enough for that species' cycle) and cited to life-history sources, not to this FAQ.

claims.statement:
Water source shifts the odds, not the outcome. The 2023 Freshwater Habitats Trust / Amphibian and Reptile Conservation garden pond guide puts clean water first: "Rainwater is usually best, as tap water often has high levels of dissolved nitrogen and phosphorus. These nutrients will discourage aquatic plants and encourage growth of algae and duckweeds." Note the hedges — "usually", "often", and elsewhere "In many parts of Britain, it is better not to use tap water." The guide still lists "the minimal amount of tap water to keep the pond going" as a fair drought option, and it says new ponds get temporary algal blooms anyway that "settle down within a season or two". Tap water raises the risk; it does not decide the pond.

The guide's harder numbers carry no such hedging, and they are the useful part: "The greatest variety of plants and animals live at the very edge of the pond, often in just a couple of centimetres of water" — so gently shelving natural edges matter more than depth. "Unless you are keeping fish, the deepest areas need to be no more than 25-30 cm (1 foot) deep." And if you go deeper: "try to make sure its surface area is five to 10 times the maximum depth, otherwise there is a good chance you'll suffer from deoxygenation."
claims.detail: Freshwater Habitats Trust and Amphibian and Reptile Conservation's 2023 garden pond guide puts clean water first: rainwater is usually best, as tap water often has high levels of dissolved nitrogen and phosphorus, which discourage aquatic plants and encourage algae and duckweed. Their other specifications are unusually concrete: the greatest variety of plants and animals live at the very edge, often in just a couple of centimetres of water, so gently shelving natural edges matter more than depth; unless keeping fish the deepest area need be no more than 25-30cm; if you want it deeper, make the surface area five to ten times the maximum depth or expect deoxygenation. Their drought FAQ notes that below about 2mg/l nitrate tap water is probably safe, but that almost anywhere in the south and east of England the tap will add nitrate and often phosphate that is then hard to remove.

source.name: Freshwater Habitats Trust / Amphibian and Reptile Conservation / World of Water (2023), 'Creating Garden Ponds for Wildlife' — PDF fetched and text extracted locally

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: This is a charity guidance booklet, not a trial — it gives no experiment comparing rainwater-filled with tap-filled ponds, and no invertebrate counts. The 2mg/l nitrate figure is their rule of thumb. It also cannot tell you your own supply: hard, nitrate-bearing water in the Cambridge area needs checking against the water company's published quality report, not assumed.

claims.statement: Caterpillar supply for birds comes disproportionately from a few tree taxa: a ten-year survey of ten tree taxa at 44 Scottish woodland sites found oak, birch and willow yielding similarly high caterpillar numbers, with peak abundance and total biomass highest on oak, and caterpillar abundance rising with the density of oak foliage in a stand but not with the density of any other taxon. The same study notes that where oak is absent, birch and willow can support comparable caterpillar abundances. (The blue-tit breeding link, the 2,300-species figure and the US chickadee comparison rest on separate sources not checked here.)
claims.detail: Macphie et al. (2024, Oikos) surveyed ten tree taxa across 44 Scottish woodland sites over a decade and found oak, birch and willow yielding similarly high numbers of caterpillars, with peak abundance greatest on oak; oak density within a wood correlated with caterpillar abundance while other taxa did not. A 2026 Ecology paper from the University of Glasgow (Branston et al.) found that along an urban gradient, blue tits with more oaks nearby laid more eggs, laid earlier, and bred more successfully, and the team measured more caterpillar food where there were more oaks; they recommend maximising native broadleaf planting rather than fast-growing non-native conifers or decorative specimens. The Woodland Trust states UK oaks can support more than 2,300 species. The US parallel (Narango, Tallamy & Marra, PNAS 2018) is stronger still: caterpillar and spider abundance fell as non-native plant biomass rose, and Carolina chickadee populations were only sustainable below about 30% non-native plant biomass.

source.name: Macphie, Samplonius, Hadfield, Pearce-Higgins & Phillimore (2024), 'Tree taxon effects on the phenology of caterpillar abundance and biomass', Oikos — abstract via Semantic Scholar API

claims.checker_note: verified for the caterpillar/tree-taxon half, with wording tightened; the blue-tit, Woodland Trust and PNAS elements remain unverified pending their own sources
claims.cannot_establish: Abstract only. This is Scottish semi-natural woodland, not a Cambridge garden, and 'non-native' garden shrubs were not tested — the comparison is between native tree taxa. The Narango 30% threshold is Carolina chickadees in Washington DC suburbs and must not be quoted as a UK number. None of these establish that a small garden can grow an oak, or what a garden-scale substitute (birch, willow, hawthorn) delivers in caterpillar biomass. The Glasgow finding I have from a university press release, not the paper itself.

claims.statement: The RHS states that more than 4.5 million UK front gardens contain no plants at all, and that a quarter of front gardens are now totally paved over. A sealed front garden is therefore common — roughly one in four — not rare; it is not, however, the default: three quarters are not fully paved. The RHS page gives no survey year, sample size or methodology, so both figures are the RHS's assertion rather than a measurement we can trace.
claims.detail: RHS front garden research states that more than 4.5 million front gardens contain no plants at all, and a quarter of front gardens are now totally paved over. This matters for every claim above at once: a fully sealed surface removes the nesting substrate (INV-01), the hibernation substrate (INV-07), the deadwood-soil contact (INV-06), the vegetation density that drives ground-active invertebrate abundance (INV-09) and any possibility of standing water reaching the soil. It is the cleanest example of the distinction between a living system and a purchased surface: paving, decking and artificial grass are bought once and then support nothing, whereas every layer described here requires an ongoing supply — new deadwood each year, re-made bare ground each winter, stems left standing each autumn.

source.name: Royal Horticultural Society — front garden research (Greening Grey Britain)

claims.checker_note: source-declared — quoted verbatim from a live RHS page, but that page cites no study, year, sample size or method, so it is an attributed assertion, not a traceable measurement
claims.cannot_establish: The page I fetched gives no survey year, sample size or method, and the RHS is campaigning on this topic. It does not measure invertebrate loss from paving — the link between paving and invertebrate absence in this claim is my inference from INV-01 and INV-07, not something this source demonstrates. A later RHS figure reported in the press (42% of all garden space paved) I did not fetch and have not used.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule fails on its own terms because it names four surfaces as equivalent sealers and at least two of them do not seal. DECKING sits on joists above intact, undisturbed soil; the cavity beneath it is a well-known bumblebee nesting and queen-hibernation site, so a decked garden is close to the opposite of the rule's prediction for two of the four named layers. A weed MEMBRANE is water- and air-permeable and thin; ARTIFICIAL GRASS is typically laid over sand or membrane on undisturbed subsoil. Soil detritivores persist under both — heavily suppressed, which is a gradient, not a floor. The rule would hold, as something close to a physical definition, only for the narrow case of continuous impermeable cover (poured concrete, asphalt, mortared paving on a full sub-base) and only for the layers that require an exposed soil surface — a solitary bee cannot excavate a burrow through concrete, and deadwood cannot touch soil it cannot reach. Even that narrowed version is definitional rather than evidenced, and the cited source supplies none of it: the RHS page is a prevalence statistic and contains no mechanism, no taxa and no measurement of what sealed ground supports. A floor rule published as a hard "cannot stand" must not rest on a source that never addressed the question.

claims.statement: Hedgehog Street — the campaign run by the People's Trust for Endangered Species and the British Hedgehog Preservation Society — publishes one recommended size for a hedgehog gap: 13cm x 13cm, "about the size of a CD case", small enough to keep nearly all pets out. Its guidance is to make it where the boundary meets the ground: cut the base of a fence, remove a brick from the bottom of a wall, or dig a channel underneath. 13cm is the size the campaign says is sufficient for any hedgehog, not a measured minimum below which a hedgehog cannot pass. Cite two pages, not one: the CD-case wording is at https://www.hedgehogstreet.org/made-hole-fence-hedgehogs-yet/ and the ground-level instruction at https://www.hedgehogstreet.org/help-hedgehogs/link-your-garden/ . Do not claim the developer guidance repeats the figure unless a live developer document is found — the obvious URL 404s.
claims.detail: Both organisations behind the Hedgehog Street campaign — the People's Trust for Endangered Species and the British Hedgehog Preservation Society — publish the same single figure: a 13cm x 13cm square hole cut or dug at the base of a fence or wall. The size is chosen deliberately: big enough for an adult hedgehog, too small for most dogs. It must reach ground level, because a hedgehog cannot climb a smooth vertical boundary. The same 13cm figure is repeated in the campaign's guidance to housing developers. A gravel board can be cut, or a hole dug under a wall.

source.name: Hedgehog Street (PTES and British Hedgehog Preservation Society)

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: I found no experimental study establishing 13cm as a threshold — no published test of what percentage of hedgehogs pass a 10cm, 13cm or 15cm gap. It is a sensible convention agreed by two specialist charities, not a measured minimum. It also cannot establish that one gap is enough: neither charity states how many gaps per boundary.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule turns a sufficient size into a necessary one, which the source does not support. Hedgehog Street's own words are that 13cm x 13cm "is sufficient for any hedgehog to pass through" — a recommendation with deliberate margin, chosen partly to exclude pets, not a measured body-width threshold. A garden whose boundaries have only 10cm gaps fails the rule's condition ("no gap at least 13cm x 13cm") yet hedgehogs would still get through, so the rule would declare a working layer dead. That alone disqualifies it as a floor. Two further leaks: the stated BECAUSE ("a hedgehog cannot climb a solid vertical boundary") is narrower than the condition — hedgehogs do climb wire mesh, chain-link and rough or mortared walls, so "every boundary meets the ground with no 13cm gap" does not entail "cannot enter"; and gardens are routinely entered by routes the condition never mentions — open or gappy gates, driveways, alleyways, hedge bases, and open frontages. This is a steep gradient (access falls sharply as boundaries seal to the ground), not a hard floor. A rule that could survive would be much weaker and would drop the number, e.g. "WHEN every boundary is solid to the ground with no gap at all AND no gate or frontage is left open THEN hedgehogs cannot enter on foot" — but that is not what was proposed.

claims.statement: A hedgehog ranges over far more ground than any one garden. The peer-reviewed assessment of Hedgehog Street (Gazzard et al. 2021) reports mean nightly distances of 861m for males and 514m for females in urban Bristol, and cites estimates that an individual may visit up to 20 gardens in a night and that urban hedgehog populations need up to 90 hectares of suitable habitat to be sustainable. A typical UK garden is about 190m2 (0.02 hectares) — a few hundredths of a percent of that 90 hectares. A single garden can still feed, shelter and even house an individual hedgehog; what it cannot do on its own is sustain a population. So the thing a garden contributes is connectivity, and connectivity is a property of a block of gardens rather than of any one of them.
claims.detail: Hedgehog Street gives average home ranges of 10-20 hectares and average nightly movement of about 2km, up to 3km for males in the breeding season. The peer-reviewed assessment of the campaign cites mean nightly distances of 861m for males and 514m for females in urban Bristol, notes that individuals may visit up to 20 gardens in a night, and states that urban hedgehog populations need up to 90 hectares of suitable habitat to be sustainable. A typical UK garden is around 0.02 hectares. That is roughly one thousandth of a single animal's range. Provision for hedgehogs is therefore a property of a block of gardens, never of one garden.

source.name: Gazzard, Boushall, Brand & Baker (2021), PLOS ONE 16(11): e0259537

claims.checker_note: verified-with-correction (quotes accurate and source live; conclusion overstated, and the 10-20ha and 1-2km figures are not in the cited source)
claims.cannot_establish: It cannot establish that a hedgehog will not visit or feed in an isolated garden — it can, if it can get in. It cannot establish a minimum number of connected gardens, and the 90ha figure is a population-level estimate, not a threshold any one householder can meet or verify.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule's BECAUSE clause is a gradient argument dressed as a floor, and it proves too much. "One garden is a thousandth of a range" is equally true of EVERY garden — if being a thousandth meant the layer cannot stand, Hedgehog Street itself could never stand, since its whole logic is that thousandths aggregate across a block. Range-to-garden ratio establishes insufficiency, never impossibility. The WHEN clause is separately over-broad: "opens onto no other garden or green space" is not the same as "sealed". A garden fronting a pavement or street has no garden or green-space neighbour yet is entirely reachable — hedgehogs routinely traverse pavements, verges and roads, which is precisely why road mortality is a documented cause of death. The rule would therefore strike out gardens hedgehogs demonstrably use. The cited paper's own data actively undercuts the floor framing: only 5.0% of gardens were totally inaccessible, and most boundaries were already traversable via naturally occurring holes, so access is usually already present. A genuine but much narrower floor does exist nearby — a garden with no ground-level gap on any boundary cannot be physically entered, so hedgehog provision inside it does nothing at all — but that is an ACCESS floor resting on physical reachability, not the RANGE floor that was proposed, and it would need to be stated and evidenced as such.

claims.statement: Gazzard et al. (2021) asked Hedgehog Street householders about their own gardens. By their own report, only 5.0% were completely inaccessible to hedgehogs, and purpose-cut highways had opened just 3.2% of previously inaccessible back gardens (though 11.4% of all boundaries were passable only via a cut hole). 48.0% of registered Hedgehog Champions had made at least one highway, against 6.1-29.8% of non-Champions. Among those who had not cut one, the most-cited reason was that the garden was already accessible (51.1%); boundary ownership or having to talk to a neighbour came second (12.6%). Two caveats the authors raise themselves: accessibility was self-reported, and they cite earlier work finding a 70-80% gap between what householders believe is accessible and what surveyors actually find; and their respondents were markedly more wildlife-minded than the public, so the participation figures are probably optimistic. The honest reading is narrower than "the barrier is neighbours, not fences": among people already inclined to help, cutting a hole is often not the limiting step, and needing a neighbour's agreement is a real but second-order friction rather than the dominant obstacle.
claims.detail: Gazzard et al. surveyed householders and found only 5.0% of gardens were totally inaccessible to hedgehogs, and that just 3.2% of neighbouring gardens could be reached only via a purpose-cut highway. 48.0% of registered Hedgehog Champions had made at least one highway; among non-Champions it was 6.1-29.8%. The most common reason for not making one was that the garden was already accessible (51.1%); the second was boundary ownership or having to talk to a neighbour (12.6%). This is the honest reading: cutting a hole is usually not the limiting step, and a scheme that depends on the neighbour's consent has a social floor as well as a physical one.

source.name: Gazzard et al. (2021), PLOS ONE — 'A barrier too far?'

claims.checker_note: verified-with-caveats — figures accurate and quoted correctly; framing overstated (self-reported accessibility the authors distrust, self-selected wildlife-friendly sample, and 12.6% inflated into "the barrier")
claims.cannot_establish: Accessibility was self-reported by householders, who may overestimate it; the study cannot establish that the gaps people believed existed were genuinely usable. It also cannot establish whether making highways changes hedgehog numbers — no population outcome was measured.

claims.statement: Plastic entanglement caused 1.4% of hedgehog admissions to British wildlife rescue centres — 184 cases across 44 of 52 responding centres — and 46% of those entangled hedgehogs died. Netting was the commonest entangling material (114 of 184 cases, 62%), most likely because it is deployed low to the ground in gardens, allotments and farmland, though most hedgehogs caught in netting did recover (69 of 114). The deadliest materials were elastic and hair bands, with an 85% fatality rate. More cases came from urban than from other habitats. The authors note the true entanglement rate is higher than these figures, since people often free hedgehogs without contacting a centre and entangled animals are harder to find than road casualties. The BHPS advises keeping pea and fruit netting a foot (30cm) clear of the ground so a hedgehog can pass underneath, and storing sports and football netting away when not in use or raising it securely.
claims.detail: A study of 52 British wildlife rescue centres found that plastic entanglement caused 1.4% of hedgehog admissions (184 cases across 44 centres) and that 46% of entangled hedgehogs died. Netting was the commonest material, 114 of 184 cases (62%); elastic and hair bands killed 85% of the hedgehogs they caught. More cases came from urban than rural areas. The BHPS gives the practical rule: keep pea and fruit netting 22-30cm (9-12 inches) clear of the ground so a hedgehog passes underneath, and remove or lift sports and football netting when not in use.

source.name: Thrift & Nouvellet et al. (2023), Animals 13(15):2448

claims.checker_note: verified-with-correction
claims.cannot_establish: 1.4% of admissions is not 1.4% of hedgehogs — rescue-centre data only counts animals someone found and carried in, so it cannot estimate how many die entangled and unnoticed. It also cannot separate garden netting from agricultural and sports netting.
claims.wall_fell_because: The evidence shows a gradient hazard, not a hard floor, and the paper undercuts the rule from three directions. Entanglement accounted for 1.4% of admissions, not a collapse of the population using gardens. Netting cases MOSTLY RECOVERED (69/114), so ground-level netting is a raised risk, not an absorbing trap — hedgehogs demonstrably pass through such gardens and survive encounters. And the authors make no netting recommendation at all; their stated recommendation is a national incident database. The study also cannot estimate encounter rates or population-level impact, so nothing in it supports "cannot stand". Two further overreaches: "netting of any kind" exceeds a study that only observed garden/agricultural/allotment netting deployed low, and if any material warranted a floor rule it would be elastic and hair bands at 85% fatality, not netting at roughly 39%. Correct framing is a strong recommended mitigation (raise netting a foot, store sports nets), not a precondition without which the hedgehog layer cannot exist.

claims.statement: A pond or pool with sheer sides can trap a hedgehog and drown it; give it a way out. The British Hedgehog Preservation Society: "Hedgehogs are good swimmers but can become trapped in ponds or pools with sheer sides. Keep water levels topped up, provide a gently sloping edge or place half submerged rocks and ramps in the water as an escape for them." Hedgehog Street asks for the same gently sloping edge — stones or chicken wire will do — "to ensure they won't drown". BHPS separately asks for ramps in cattle grids and covers over ground holes. (Sloping edges are also the standard advice for amphibian access, but that comes from pond-conservation sources, not from BHPS — cite it separately or leave it out. Water butts, cattle troughs and open drains are our own extension of the principle and carry no citation.)
claims.detail: The BHPS states that hedgehogs swim well but become trapped in ponds or pools with sheer sides. The remedy they publish is concrete: keep water levels topped up, provide a gently sloping edge, or place half-submerged rocks and a ramp — chicken wire over a board works — so anything that falls in can walk out. Hedgehog Street repeats it: at least one side must slope gently. This is the same requirement amphibians have, which is convenient: one shelving edge serves both. It applies equally to swimming pools, cattle troughs, uncovered gullies and open drains.

source.name: British Hedgehog Preservation Society, 'A guide to helping hedgehogs'

claims.checker_note: source-declared for ponds and pools (verbatim on the live BHPS page, independently corroborated by Hedgehog Street); the water-butt, cattle-trough, gully and open-drain hazards and the amphibian overlap are uncited inference and should be marked as such or dropped
claims.cannot_establish: I found no published count of hedgehog drownings in garden ponds, and no experiment establishing the maximum wall angle or minimum ramp width a hedgehog can climb. The charity's advice is mechanistically obvious but not quantified.
claims.wall_fell_because:
The rule claims a hard floor — "both layers CANNOT STAND" — but the evidence describes a preventable risk, not an absolute barrier. Three failures:

(1) Wrong quantifier on the trigger. "ANY standing water in the garden with vertical sides and no ramp" fires on a water bowl and a steep-sided bird bath — and BHPS's point 3 actively tells you to put out clean water in bowls. A floor rule that condemns the thing the same source recommends is not a floor rule. The hazard depends on depth and on the drop from rim to water surface (BHPS's own first remedy is "keep water levels topped up"), which is a gradient, not a threshold.

(2) The source language will not carry it. "Can become trapped" is a risk statement. Gardens with sheer-sided ponds do support hedgehogs; the ones that fall in die, the ones that do not, do not. That is a serious and cheaply-fixed danger — strong recommendation, real design duty — but it is not "the hedgehog layer cannot stand".

(3) The amphibian half has zero evidence behind it. Neither fetched page mentions amphibians. A floor rule cannot assert that a layer collapses when nothing in the citation speaks to that layer at all.

Demote to a strong published recommendation with the source's own imperative wording, or rewrite the trigger to something the evidence actually bounds — e.g. water deep enough to swim in, with sides the animal cannot climb — and drop the amphibian clause until it is separately cited.

claims.statement: Outdoor use of metaldehyde slug pellets has been unlawful in Great Britain since the phase-out deadline of 31 March 2022. Defra announced the ban on 18 September 2020, taking into account advice from the UK Expert Committee on Pesticides and the Health and Safety Executive about the risks metaldehyde poses to birds and mammals; the release states that "the risks metaldehyde poses to the environment and to wildlife are too great". Ferric phosphate is an authorised alternative, alongside cultural methods. This is a legal fact, not a preference — an old tub of blue metaldehyde pellets in a shed cannot lawfully be used, and Defra's advice is to dispose of garden quantities through local authority waste facilities rather than use them up. (Note: the ban is about risks to wildlife generally; the cited source says nothing about hedgehogs specifically. The separate point that any pesticide programme starves hedgehogs by removing their invertebrate food is a BHPS argument and needs its own citation — it is not carried by this Defra source.)
claims.detail: Defra banned outdoor use of metaldehyde following advice from the UK Expert Committee on Pesticides and the Health and Safety Executive, citing risks to birds and mammals. The deadline for outdoor use was 31 March 2022; ferric phosphate is the permitted alternative. This is a legal fact, not a preference — old tubs of blue metaldehyde pellets in a shed cannot lawfully be used. Separately, the BHPS notes the wider point that any pesticide programme damages hedgehogs indirectly by removing their food: herbicides reduce earthworms in lawns, insecticides reduce beetles and caterpillars. A hedgehog eats invertebrates; a sterile garden starves one whether or not it poisons it.

source.name: Defra / GOV.UK news release

claims.checker_note: verified — cited source fetched, live, un-withdrawn, and directly supports the claim; two wording points softened and the BHPS paragraph flagged as needing its own source
claims.cannot_establish: The ban was justified on risk to birds and mammals generally; it does not establish that metaldehyde was measurably killing garden hedgehogs, and the evidence for direct hedgehog poisoning by pellets is weaker than the popular claim suggests. Ferric phosphate is permitted but not proven harmless.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule mixes a genuine legal binary with a functional claim the evidence does not reach. What the source establishes is a hard floor on a PRACTICE: using metaldehyde outdoors in Great Britain is unlawful, full stop, no gradient. What the rule asserts is that the PROVISION "cannot stand" — and nothing on that page supports it. The release never mentions hedgehogs; it cites risks to birds and mammals in general, and it is silent on whether any wildlife provision ceases to function in a garden where metaldehyde is used. Concretely: a gap cut in a fence still passes hedgehogs, a nest box still shelters one, a dish of water still works, whether or not the owner also scatters blue pellets. The pellets are a separate harm running alongside a provision that still does its job — that is a degradation, and for hedgehogs specifically an indirect and contested one (the direct secondary-poisoning risk to hedgehogs is much weaker than the folk claim), not a floor that voids the provision. If the site wants this as a floor rule, scope it to the act rather than the provision: "using metaldehyde outdoors in Great Britain is unlawful and must be stopped" is a true hard rule and survives on its own terms. As written — one practice voiding a whole provision — it fails the cannot-work-at-all test.

claims.statement: Bonfire heaps and strimmers are a serious danger to hedgehogs, and the British Hedgehog Preservation Society gives specific physical instructions to prevent it. Material collected for a bonfire "should be re-sited just before the fire is to be lit, even then, the base should be lifted up with poles or broom handles (not a fork!) and a torch shone in to look (and listen) for any wildlife or pets in need of rescue before lighting" — and once checked, "light from one side only to allow an escape route for anything you may have missed". Before cutting, "check areas thoroughly for hedgehogs and other wildlife before strimming or mowing". The society notes elsewhere in the same guide, of traffic, that "a hedgehog's natural defence mechanism is to roll into a ball — this is no match for a vehicle"; that the same defence is equally useless against a rotary blade or a fire is our inference, not the society's stated reason. The guide does not give a seasonal window for these risks, and does not single out long grass or hedge bottoms.
claims.detail: A hedgehog's defence is to roll into a ball and stay put. That defence is fatal against a rotary blade or a fire. The BHPS instruction is specific and physical: material collected for a bonfire should be moved to a fresh spot immediately before lighting, and even then the base should be lifted with poles or broom handles — not a fork — and a torch shone underneath while listening. For cutting, check thoroughly before strimming or mowing, especially in long grass and under hedge bottoms. The risk window is the whole active season, and heaps left standing for days are exactly the kind of dry, sheltered nest site a hedgehog chooses.

source.name: British Hedgehog Preservation Society, 'A guide to helping hedgehogs'

claims.checker_note: Mixed: source-declared for the handling instructions (bonfire re-siting, poles/torch/listen, light from one side, check before strimming or mowing); reasoned inference for the lethal mechanism, since the cited page attaches the roll-into-a-ball defence only to vehicles. Two DETAIL specifics — "long grass and under hedge bottoms" and "the whole active season" — are unsupported by the cited page and should be cut or re-sourced.
