claims.cannot_establish: No fetched source quantifies how many hedgehogs die in bonfires or to strimmers per year in the UK. The mechanism is not in doubt but the scale is unmeasured, so this cannot be ranked against road deaths or starvation.
claims.wall_fell_because: A rule was proposed, but the evidence supports a strong risk, not a hard floor — and the cited page contradicts the rule in its own words. BHPS gives a graded mitigation ladder whose last rung is "light from one side only to allow an escape route for anything you may have missed": the society explicitly contemplates that an animal you failed to find may still get out. That is the opposite of "cannot escape fire". The rule is also probabilistic at root — a heap burned where it stands harms a hedgehog only if one happens to be in it, and most heaps at most times hold none; the advice is precautionary precisely because you cannot know which. The honest strong version is that burning in place removes the only reliable way to check, so the risk becomes unbounded and unknowable — an excellent reason to follow the practice, but a gradient, not a floor. The rule is additionally narrower than the claim it is meant to support (it drops strimmers and mowers entirely) and conflates the practice with the outcome.

claims.statement: Amphibians spend much of the year on land, not in the pond. Natural England's planning guidance for great crested newts reflects this: damage to terrestrial habitat within 50m of a pond is normally high impact, 50-250m normally high to medium, and beyond 250m normally low — and an assessor "must look at other GCN habitats within 500m because GCN move and are unlikely to stay in one place."
claims.detail: Natural England's planning guidance for great crested newts treats terrestrial habitat within 50m of a pond as normally high impact if damaged, 50-250m as medium to high, and requires assessment of habitat within 500m because newts move. The ARG UK habitat suitability index scores terrestrial habitat "within approximately 250 m from the pond", scoring it 'poor' (0.33) when amenity grassland or arable covers the area, and 'none' (0.01) where there is no suitable habitat at all. Froglife lists what counts at garden scale: log and stone piles, long grass, compost heaps, gaps under sheds and decking. Newts overwinter in those places, not in the water.

source.name: Natural England / GOV.UK, great crested newts planning guidance

claims.checker_note: verified for the distances and the 500m quote; wording narrowed — "core" is not the guidance's term, and the source is species-specific planning guidance for great crested newts rather than general amphibian or garden guidance. The ARG UK HSI scores and Froglife list in the supporting detail remain unverified.
claims.cannot_establish: These distances are for great crested newts, a protected species unlikely to appear in a small garden pond; they are a planning convention derived from dispersal studies, not a measured requirement for common frogs, toads or smooth newts. It cannot establish how much land habitat one garden pond needs.
claims.wall_fell_because: The evidence supports a steep gradient, not a floor, and the cited page contradicts the rule on its own terms. (1) The guidance's central proposition is that newts MOVE, which is exactly why habitat must be assessed out to 500m. The rule's trigger is "no rough grass, log pile or stone pile anywhere ADJOINING" — a radius far tighter than 50m, let alone the 250m and 500m bands the guidance actually works in. A pond ringed by paving can still be reached from terrestrial habitat tens or hundreds of metres away, which is the precise scenario the 500m rule exists to catch. (2) The rule contradicts its own supporting detail: the Froglife list cited in support names "gaps under sheds and decking" as terrestrial refuge, so decking reaching the pond edge appears simultaneously as a disqualifying condition and as habitat. (3) The HSI as described scores absent terrestrial habitat 0.01, not 0 — a multiplicative suitability index deliberately floored just above zero so that the total degrades sharply without ever nullifying. A source that refuses to write zero is telling you it is not a floor. (4) The page nowhere states that a site lacking terrestrial refuge cannot support newts at all; it assigns "normally high impact" to damage there, which is a statement about harm caused, not about impossibility of occupation. Honest form would be a strong warning that the amphibian layer is badly weakened and unlikely to hold a breeding population unaided — not a hard floor saying it cannot stand.

claims.statement: The standard UK habitat index (ARG UK Advice Note 5, 2010, after Oldham et al. 2000) scores fish harshly: absent 1.0, possible 0.67, "small numbers of crucian carp, goldfish or stickleback" 0.33, and "dense populations of fish known to be present" 0.01 - the floor, the same score given to polluted water or no terrestrial habitat at all. But the floor bites less than it looks. The index is a geometric mean of ten factors, so dense fish alone caps a pond at 0.63, still the "average" band. Only with a second bad factor - a garden pond under 50 square metres, which scores 0.05 for area - does the score fall to about 0.47, into the "poor" band where 3% of 248 ponds surveyed in south-east England held great crested newts. And the note is explicit that this is not a verdict: the HSI "is not a substitute for newt surveys", and "the system is not sufficiently precise to conclude that... any pond with a low score will not" support newts. The honest tension is not between competing field evidence but inside the standard itself. Froglife's public advice is flat - "we advise that you don't introduce fish to your wildlife pond", they eat spawn and larvae and compete with tadpoles - yet the index's own authors were tentative, writing that the effect of fish varies "not in a manner that can be predicted readily", that goldfish and carp "in some conditions, appear to be benign", and that the national amphibian survey holds "many records of great crested newt populations surviving, probably in suppressed numbers, in the presence of fish". They kept the harsh score anyway because the overall correlation "cannot be ignored". One thing that looks like counter-evidence is not: the same survey (Swan & Oldham 1993) found fish presence correlated with HIGHER amphibian frequency across its whole data set, but that effect disappeared once garden ponds were excluded - garden ponds almost never dry out (about 5%), which suits fish and amphibians alike. For great crested newts specifically that survey found lower abundance in ponds with fish. So: a hard number resting on a soft, species-dependent effect its own authors flagged as unpredictable.
claims.detail: The ARG UK habitat suitability index — the standard UK tool, from Oldham et al. (2000) — scores fish as: absent 1.0, possible 0.67, small numbers of crucian carp, goldfish or stickleback 0.33, and dense populations 0.01. The index is a geometric mean of ten factors, so a dense fish population caps the whole score at about 0.63 even if everything else is perfect; combine that with a garden pond under 50 square metres (which scores 0.05 for area) and the score falls below 0.5, the band where only about 3% of surveyed ponds held great crested newts. Froglife's advice is flat: don't introduce fish, they eat spawn and larvae and compete with tadpoles. But the national amphibian survey (Swan & Oldham 1993) found fish presence correlated with HIGHER amphibian frequency overall, an effect traced to garden ponds being less likely to dry out. So fish are bad, but pond permanence confounds the raw correlation.

source.name: ARG UK Advice Note 5: Great Crested Newt Habitat Suitability Index (2010), after Oldham et al. 2000

claims.checker_note: supported (numbers verified verbatim against the cited PDF); but NOT "contested" - the apparent conflict is a documented confound that the source itself resolves, so the honest label is "supported, with the standard's own stated uncertainty"
claims.cannot_establish: I could not find evidence that fish make newt breeding impossible — only that they make it much less likely. The national survey's positive fish-amphibian correlation is a real published result and I could not fully resolve it. Nor could I verify the smooth newt urban study (Lissotriton vulgaris) directly. Because 'cannot work at all' is not established, no floor rule is claimed here.

claims.statement: A pond wants a gently sloping edge — Froglife calls this "the most important factor", along with native vegetation, so animals can enter and leave the water — and a deeper section of at least 60cm, which Froglife recommends so amphibians can lie dormant on the bottom in icy weather. Holding water into late summer is a separate matter, and it is what a dry-county garden gets wrong. Great crested newt larvae hatch two to four weeks after laying and do not leave the water until around August (Froglife), so a pond that dries in July loses that year's cohort. The ARG UK Habitat Suitability Index scores a pond that dries annually at 0.1 and one drying three years in ten at 0.5, against 1.0 for one that dries no more than two years in ten — note that the same index rates rare drying (1.0) above never drying (0.9), because permanence lets fish in. So the target is not "never dry": it is "not every year, and not before the young are out". Cambridge gets roughly 557mm of rain a year, spread fairly evenly, but summer evaporation far outruns it, and a small, shallow, unshaded pond is the one that fails first. Depth and surface area, not aesthetics, buy the margin. Top up with rainwater rather than tap water — Froglife gives this advice for holding a pond's level while work waits for autumn — which on alkaline ground also avoids adding hardness and nutrients.
claims.detail: Froglife names the sloping side as "the most important factor", with native vegetation, so animals can enter and leave the water; a deeper section of at least 60cm gives somewhere to lie dormant; a wildlife pond should ideally exceed 2m x 2m; top up with rainwater rather than tap water. Great crested newt larvae hatch two to four weeks after laying and do not leave the water until around August, so a pond that dries in July destroys that year's cohort. The ARG UK index scores a pond that dries annually at 0.1 and one that dries in three years out of ten at 0.5, against 1.0 for one that dries no more than twice in ten years. This is the climate-specific item for eastern England: Cambridge's roughly 557mm annual rainfall, with the deficit falling in summer, means a shallow, unshaded, small pond can be dry by mid-July. Depth and surface area, not aesthetics, are what carry a pond through a Cambridgeshire August. On alkaline ground, rainwater collection also avoids adding more hardness and nutrients.

source.name: Froglife, 'Creating or improving ponds'

claims.checker_note: verified with correction — Froglife quotes exact and URL live; the drying/August half is true but rests on two sources that must be cited separately (Froglife's great crested newt page, ARG UK Advice Note 5), and "must not dry" needs weakening to "must not dry every year"
claims.cannot_establish: The August metamorphosis date is for great crested newts; common frog tadpoles usually leave earlier and toads later, so a single date is a simplification. I found no source giving a minimum pond volume that survives an eastern England summer, so the Cambridge-specific inference about drying is mine, not a published threshold.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule claims a hard floor and the evidence refuses it — in one case explicitly. ARG UK Advice Note 5 scores an annually-drying pond at 0.1, not 0, and states in its own limitations section that the index "is not sufficiently precise to conclude that any particular pond with a high score will support newts, or that any pond with a low score will not do so." That is the cited authority denying exactly this inference. Froglife's page cuts the same way: "Common frogs often choose unlikely places, such as puddles, to lay their eggs" and "Any size of pond will be beneficial to wildlife, even if it doesn't attract amphibians", plus "even tiny ponds and bog gardens will be used by local wildlife". The 30cm threshold appears in no source I fetched — it is invented, not derived; Froglife's only depth figure is 60cm and it is given for winter dormancy, not summer drying. The rule is also a conjunction of four soft conditions (under 30cm AND small AND unshaded AND not topped up), each a gradient, and its consequent is weather-contingent rather than structural: a shallow pond in a wet Cambridge summer does not dry, so the layer plainly can stand in some years. Common frog tadpoles also typically metamorphose in June-July, ahead of the August deadline the rule is built on. This is a real degradation — a shallow unshaded pond is a worse breeding site, sometimes a failed one — but degradation is not a floor.

claims.statement: Nestlings are fed insects, not seed — a feeder keeps adults going but supplies nothing to a brood. Narango, Tallamy & Marra (2018, PNAS) followed Carolina chickadees across 159 residential sites near Washington DC and found that as non-native plant biomass rose, caterpillars and spiders declined, birds shifted onto less preferred prey, and the number of young produced fell. Modelled population growth stayed above replacement only below about 6% non-native biomass on average, and populations could not be sustained above about 30%: "Properties landscaped with nonnative plants function as population sinks for insectivorous birds." The mechanism is that over 90% of herbivorous insects specialise on one or a few native plant lineages, so non-native planting breaks the food chain one link below the bird. Two honest qualifications: this is a gradient, not a switch — birds in non-native yards still fledged some young, they just did not fledge enough to replace themselves — and the unit measured was a 0.79-hectare, 50-metre-radius patch spanning several properties, about one chickadee territory. A single caterpillar-free garden on a leafy street is not what was tested; its birds feed next door.
claims.detail: Narango, Tallamy & Marra (2018, PNAS) followed Carolina chickadees breeding in residential yards and modelled population growth against the proportion of non-native plant biomass in each territory. Yards dominated by non-native plants had lower arthropod abundance; birds shifted onto less preferred prey such as spiders and produced fewer young. Mean population growth was only sustainable at under about 6% non-native plant biomass, with the wider threshold for population persistence around 30% non-native. Their conclusion is blunt: "Properties landscaped with nonnative plants function as population sinks for insectivorous birds." The mechanism is that over 90% of herbivorous insects specialise on one or a few native plant lineages, so non-native planting breaks the food chain one link below the bird. A feeder full of sunflower hearts does not substitute: it feeds adults, not broods.

source.name: Narango, Tallamy & Marra (2018), PNAS 115(45):11549-11554

claims.checker_note: verified with correction — source live, quotes exact, but the absolute "cannot fledge chicks" is unsupported and the finding is territory-scale, not garden-scale
claims.cannot_establish: This is a single species (Carolina chickadee) in the eastern United States. The <6% figure cannot be transferred to a Cambridge garden or to blue tits — no equivalent UK threshold exists that I could verify. It also cannot establish that feeders are useless, only that they do not feed nestlings.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule asserts a hard floor ("the breeding-bird layer cannot stand"), but the evidence is a continuous relationship between non-native plant biomass and population growth rate, with degraded output at every step rather than a cliff. Three specific failures. (1) No zero point was demonstrated: birds still fledged young in non-native-dominated yards; what collapsed was net replacement, not reproduction. (2) The authors themselves disclaim the far end of the curve, exactly where the rule wants to plant its floor — "large uncertainty at high nonnative percentages due to low sample sizes, given that chickadees rarely occupy these sites." A floor rule resting on the thinnest data in the study is the weakest possible use of it. (3) Scale mismatch defeats the rule outright: the measured unit is a 50-m-radius, 0.79 ha patch covering several properties, and the paper records family groups foraging outside the assessed area entirely, so a caterpillar-free garden embedded in a planted neighbourhood can and does fledge chicks on food gathered elsewhere. Additionally the stated condition ("no plants that host caterpillars") is close to unachievable — lawn and non-native evergreen carry reduced, not zero, arthropod loads, which is precisely the paper's finding. This is a gradient dressed as a floor.

claims.statement: In the British built environment, swifts, house sparrows and starlings depend heavily on cavities in buildings, and re-roofing and the replacement of soffits and fascias seals those cavities up. Government planning guidance (Planning Practice Guidance, Natural Environment, Paragraph 017, Ref ID 8-017-20250609) states that "swifts rely on urban cavities for nesting, and the national loss of suitable nesting sites through building renovation has been part of the reason for the species' decline", and that "Developments should include integrated nest boxes (commonly known as swift bricks) where possible, with the general aim across a development of a minimum of one nest box per unit." The same guidance notes those boxes "can provide important habitat for other species as well as swifts, such as starlings and sparrows" — though the provision runs one way: swifts cannot use sparrow bricks and terraces.
claims.detail: The RSPB states plainly that gardens are short of natural holes: trees are usually too young to have cavities, and "we tend to patch up holes in our buildings". Swift Conservation's nest brick paper attributes the major declines in swift, house sparrow and starling to "the loss of nesting sites on existing buildings due to re-roofing and replacement of soffits and fascias", and states swifts have declined by nearly 60% in twenty years. Crucially, the species are not interchangeable: "Swifts are unable to use sparrow bricks and terraces." As of the current national planning practice guidance, England now expects integrated nest boxes: "Developments should include integrated nest boxes (commonly known as swift bricks) where possible, with the general aim across a development of a minimum of one nest box per unit."

source.name: Ministry of Housing / GOV.UK, Planning Practice Guidance — Natural Environment, Paragraph 017 (Ref ID 8-017-20250609)

claims.checker_note: partly verified — the quoted planning guidance is verbatim and the URL is live; the surrounding "nest only in building cavities" and "removes the nest site absolutely" are unsupported by this source and factually false as stated
claims.cannot_establish: That nest sites are scarce does not prove they are the limiting factor — food supply and migration mortality also drive swift and sparrow declines, and I found no experiment showing that adding boxes raises regional populations. The 60% swift decline figure comes from an advocacy document (Swift Conservation), not a fetched official statistic.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule rests on a premise the cited source does not state and that is false: these three species do not nest only in building cavities. Even read narrowly as "this building offers no nest site", the rule's own condition list is incomplete — externally mounted swift boxes and sparrow terraces at height are the standard, well-evidenced retrofit and work with no cavity, no eaves gap and no integrated brick, so the listed conditions are one route among several rather than a floor. House sparrows will also use ivy, hedges and creepers on and around the building; starlings will take a box on a nearby tree. And the source itself is gradient language throughout — "part of the reason" for decline, "where possible", "general aim" — which describes more or fewer nest sites and therefore more or fewer pairs, not a threshold below which the layer stops existing. Fewer cavities is a degradation, not a hard floor.

claims.statement: A feeder is a shared mouth: trichomonosis, spread by regurgitated food and contaminated food and water, cut greenfinch breeding numbers by 35% in Britain's worst-affected region between 2006 and 2007 — nationally the fall that year was 15% — with chaffinch down 21% in the same region, together more than half a million birds. Dunnocks, which feed in the same gardens but rarely carried the parasite, did not decline. Robinson et al. did not test feeder cleaning itself; they flagged transmission at garden feeders as the thing still to establish. Regular cleaning, moving feeders, fresh water, and stopping feeding when sick birds appear are the mitigations advised by the RSPB and Garden Wildlife Health — sensible precaution downstream of this finding, not a result of it.
claims.detail: Robinson et al. (2010, PLOS ONE) documented the emergence of Trichomonas gallinae in British finches in 2005, epidemic by 2006. Greenfinches fell 35% in the high-incidence region between 2006 and 2007 — over half a million birds nationally — and chaffinches 21%, while dunnocks (a control) showed no significant decline. Garden Wildlife Health, funded by Defra and the Welsh Government, names the affected species: pigeons and doves, plus gregarious seed-eaters including house sparrow, siskin, goldfinch and bullfinch. Transmission is via regurgitated food and contaminated food or water. What actually reduces it: clean and disinfect feeders regularly, rotate feeder positions between several sites, provide fresh drinking water daily, and — when sick birds appear — stop feeding entirely for two to four weeks to make the flock disperse, and empty the bird bath. The RSPB now advises weekly cleaning, says flat bird tables carry the greatest risk, and recommends stopping seeds and peanuts between 1 May and 31 October because the finches that eat them are the most susceptible.

source.name: Robinson et al. (2010), PLOS ONE 5(8):e12215

claims.checker_note: verified-with-corrections — numbers exact and source live, but the decline must be stated as regional (35% high-incidence region / 15% national), the half-million must be attributed to greenfinch and chaffinch combined rather than greenfinch alone, the uncleaned-feeder causal clause must be marked as inference from mitigation guidance rather than a finding of Robinson et al., and the Garden Wildlife Health details plus "flat bird tables carry the greatest risk" remain unsourced pending a live fetch
claims.cannot_establish: The paper itself says the role of feeders is not proven: "further studies are required to assess the relative importance of these transmission routes." So the hygiene measures are precautionary, not demonstrated to reduce transmission by a measured amount. No fetched source quantifies how much cleaning frequency changes infection rates.
claims.wall_fell_because: This is a gradient dressed as a floor, and the cited paper is the wrong evidence for it. Robinson et al. never manipulated or measured feeder cleaning, feeder rotation, or continued feeding after sick birds appeared — none of the rule's three conditions is a variable in the study, so the study cannot show what happens in their absence. Worse, the paper's own comparison cuts against a hard floor: declines were "less pronounced or absent in these species in regions where the disease was found in intermediate or low incidence." Feeders in those regions were no cleaner; what differed was disease incidence. Millions of irregularly cleaned British feeders have operated for decades without epidemic collapse, and greenfinch numbers rose c. 60% from the mid-1980s to 2006 across exactly that feeding culture. So an uncleaned feeder is a raised risk conditional on the pathogen being present and prevalent — not a thing that "cannot stand". The strongest element, stopping feeding when a sick bird is seen, is the closest to a genuine floor and is real advice, but it is outbreak-response guidance from RSPB/GWH about reducing harm during an epidemic, not a demonstration that the feeder layer is a net source of harm at all other times. Binding all three conditions together with "or" makes it fail harder: "never moved" alone is plainly a gradient. A floor rule here would need evidence that feeders without hygiene are net-negative for bird populations in general, and no such evidence was offered.

claims.statement: Domestic cats bring home wildlife in enormous numbers, but prey counts alone cannot show an effect on prey populations. The Mammal Society reports about 2.04 prey items per outdoor cat per month in the 2003 UK study (Woods et al., surveyed 1997) and about 1.5 per month in a 2025 estimate (Lockwood et al.), which across roughly 7.45 million outdoor-going UK cats works out at around 140 million prey items a year. It states the caveat plainly: "the scale and mechanics of this ecological impact cannot be ascertained purely from the numbers of prey", "the weakest and most vulnerable animals are more prone to being predated on by cats", and common prey such as shrews and voles have "the highest breeding rates designed to compensate high mortality rates". That is a limit on what prey counts prove, not a claim that cats are harmless — the same page warns cats can be devastating for vulnerable species such as ground-nesting birds. On what works, a randomised trial (Cecchetti et al. 2021, Current Biology) found that high-meat, grain-free food cut prey brought home by 36% and five to ten minutes of daily object play by 25%; Birdsbesafe collar covers cut birds by 42% with no discernible effect on mammals; bells had no discernible effect; and puzzle feeders made things worse, increasing prey by 33%. A night-time curfew helps too, by reducing opportunity. Food and play work on the cat's motivation to hunt; the collar cover works on its success, and a curfew on its opportunity.
claims.detail: The Mammal Society reports the 2003 UK estimate of about 2.04 prey items brought home per outdoor cat per month, and a more recent 2025 estimate of about 1.5 per month across roughly 7.45 million outdoor cats, giving around 140 million prey items a year. It then states the honest caveat directly: the weakest and most vulnerable animals are more likely to be taken, so it is hard to know how many would have died anyway, and common prey such as shrews and voles breed at rates designed to absorb high mortality. On what works, the Exeter trial (Cecchetti et al. 2021, Current Biology; 355 cats, 219 households, 12 weeks) found meat-rich food cut prey brought home by 36%, five to ten minutes of daily object play by 25%, and Birdsbesafe collar covers cut birds by 42% with no effect on mammals. Bells had no discernible effect. A night-time curfew also helps. Note these measures reduce the cat's motivation rather than its ability.

source.name: The Mammal Society, 'Feline the pressure: domestic cats and wildlife'

claims.checker_note: contested on the population-impact half only — the prey counts and the trial's effect sizes are settled, well-sourced numbers; what remains debated is whether garden predation is additive to or compensatory for other mortality
claims.cannot_establish: Nothing here establishes that cats cause population declines in garden birds, nor that they do not — the compensatory-versus-additive question is open. Prey brought home is a biased proxy for prey killed. The Cecchetti percentages come from a press release of a paywalled paper I could not open, so I could not check confidence intervals.

claims.statement: The Met Office projects that UK winters will continue to become wetter and summers drier on average, "though natural variability will mean we will continue to see individual years that don't follow this trend", and that the rain that does fall in summer will likely be more intense than at present — rainfall from a summer event that currently occurs about once every two years is expected to increase by around 25%. Annual totals are not shrinking: 2011-2020 was 9% wetter than 1961-1990 across the UK, and heavy-rainfall days in England and Wales are projected to rise from about 7 a year now to 9 at 2C of warming. A drier summer punctuated by heavier downpours is therefore the projected direction of travel, and a garden that must both absorb a sudden 30mm and survive a long dry spell is planning for the trend rather than for a freak. The Met Office does not itself state that drought and flood in the same year is "the expected pattern", nor that summer rain will arrive in fewer events or after longer dry gaps — that reading is ours, drawn from the two projections above.
claims.detail: The Met Office states that "winters will continue to become wetter and summers drier, though natural variability will mean we will continue to see individual years that don't follow this trend", and that "rain that does fall in summer will likely be more intense than what we currently experience". It quantifies this: rainfall from a summer event that typically occurs once every two years is expected to increase by around 25%. It also records 2011-2020 as 9% wetter than 1961-1990 across the UK. This is the mechanism behind the same-year whiplash: total water is not falling much, but its arrival is concentrating into fewer, heavier events separated by longer dry gaps. A garden therefore needs two opposite abilities at once — somewhere to put a sudden 30mm, and something living that survives eight weeks without any.

source.name: Met Office — UK and global extreme events: heavy rainfall and floods

claims.checker_note: verified with caveat — all quoted figures exact and the source page live; the same-year drought/flood framing and the "fewer events, longer gaps" mechanism are the author's inference, not Met Office statements, and "fewer events" runs against the page's own projection of more heavy-rainfall days
claims.cannot_establish: It does not give figures for eastern England or Cambridge specifically, does not say when any individual garden will flood, and the 25% figure is a projection from models, not an observation.

claims.statement: Ponds punch far above their size. Comparing the National Pond Survey (156 sites) with one of the largest British river invertebrate surveys (614 sites), ponds held more invertebrate species in total than rivers — 398 against 368 — with 72 Nationally Scarce species against 41 and 21 Red Data Book species against 13, from a quarter as many survey sites. Water beetles alone: 170 species in ponds against 100 in rivers. About two thirds of Britain's freshwater plants and animals can be found in ponds. And the standard UK conservation definition of a pond (Pond Conservation Group, 1993) starts at one square metre — "man-made or natural waterbodies between 1m2 and 2 ha in area which hold water for 4 months of the year or more" — a definition the Trust calls "deliberately broad", including "even very small waterbodies, which can sometimes have a high conservation value". [Drop "the single richest habitat you can add per square metre": the source never says it, and the totals are a species pool across many sites, not richness per unit area. Say "official definition" only if you cite the statutory/BAP wording; the factsheet credits the Pond Conservation Group. The 50%-lost and 80%-poor-state figures are not in this factsheet — cite them separately or cut them.]
claims.detail: Freshwater Habitats Trust's factsheet compares the National Pond Survey (156 sites) with one of the largest British river invertebrate surveys (614 sites): ponds held 398 invertebrate species against rivers' 368, with 72 Nationally Scarce species against 41, and 21 Red Data Book species against 13. Water beetles alone: 170 species in ponds against 100 in rivers. Ponds achieved this from a quarter the number of survey sites. The Trust defines a pond as a waterbody "between 1m2 and 2 ha in area which hold water for 4 months of the year or more", and states the definition "is deliberately broad and includes even very small waterbodies, which can sometimes have a high conservation value". The Trust also states elsewhere that two-thirds of freshwater species can be found in ponds, that 50% of UK ponds were lost in the 20th century, and that 80% of those remaining are in poor state.

source.name: Freshwater Habitats Trust — The value of ponds for wildlife (factsheet)

claims.checker_note: overstated — underlying figures verified verbatim in the cited source, headline superlative unsupported
claims.cannot_establish: The species table compares two differently-designed national surveys, not matched sites, so it shows ponds are comparably rich — not that any one garden pond will be. It says nothing about how a pond in a suburban garden performs versus a countryside pond.

claims.statement: For a wildlife pond without fish, the Freshwater Habitats Trust / ARC booklet recommends the deepest area be no more than 25-30 cm (1 foot), because "this keeps all of the pond well oxygenated and well lit". It is a recommendation with a stated escape clause, not a ceiling: if you want it deeper, the same paragraph says make the surface area five to ten times the maximum depth, "otherwise there is a good chance you'll suffer from deoxygenation problems". The booklet also says the greatest variety of plants and animals lives at the very edge, "often in just a couple of centimetres of water", so the design consequence is a very gently shelving edge fringed by grasses rather than a bowl — grasses trailing into the water head its list of the best places to find pond animals. (The precise "1-2 cm" figure, the "roughly 50% shallows" proportion, and the description of deep water as a "specialist habitat" come from other Freshwater Habitats Trust pages, not from this booklet — cite them separately or drop them.)
claims.detail: The Freshwater Habitats Trust / Amphibian and Reptile Conservation garden pond booklet says: "Shallow ponds are great. Unless you are keeping fish, the deepest areas need to be no more than 25-30 cm (1 foot) deep. This keeps all of the pond well oxygenated and well lit." The Trust's garden pond hub adds that "most garden ponds are too deep for their area" and recommends "roughly 50% shallows, and the deep area is not more than 30 cm", explicitly rejecting the standard 50-60cm advice as fish-pond advice. Its management factsheet goes further: "Most people think of shallow water as 10-30 cm deep. Pond naturalists think of shallow water as only 1-2 cm deep, and always head for this part of the pond first because, surprisingly, it is usually the richest part of any waterbody for pond animals." Deep water is described as "one of the more specialist pond habitats, used by a relatively small number of species". The design consequence is a very gently shelving edge, not a bowl — and grasses trailing into the water, which the Trust calls "one of the richest of all habitats in a pond".

source.name: Freshwater Habitats Trust / ARC / World of Water — Creating garden ponds for wildlife (2023)

claims.checker_note: partly verified — the 25-30cm depth recommendation, the gently-shelving-edge consequence and the grasses-trailing point are verified verbatim against the cited PDF; the "50% shallows" figure, the exact "1-2cm" richest-zone number and the "specialist habitat" description are absent from the cited source and remain unverified (their claimed home page 404s)
claims.cannot_establish: No controlled trial is cited comparing 30cm and 60cm garden ponds. The booklet is co-published with World of Water, an aquatics retailer, and carries a 'shopping list'. The depth advice runs against retail interest (deeper ponds sell more liner), so bias here is against interest, but the document is guidance, not a study.

claims.statement: Fish and a wildlife pond pull against each other in a small garden, but the conservation bodies stop well short of calling it impossible. The Freshwater Habitats Trust / ARC booklet says fish "will usually overwhelm small garden ponds and eat smaller animals, including frog and newt tadpoles", and can pollute the water unless you install filters — then, rather than prohibiting them, it tells you how to keep both: dense plant cover, grassy edges, refuges the fish cannot reach, or a separate fish pond, which it calls "the best of both worlds". The same booklet treats a fish pond as a legitimate variant with different requirements (deeper than the 25-30 cm it recommends otherwise, plus filtration and winter oxygenation), and notes that Common Toad tadpoles, being toxic, "sometimes live undisturbed in fish ponds". The honest summary is that stocking fish costs you a great deal of what a small wildlife pond would otherwise hold — not that the two cannot coexist.
claims.detail: The FHT/ARC booklet says: "In the wild, fish are a natural part of the wildlife of some pond types. But they will usually overwhelm small garden ponds and eat smaller animals, including frog and newt tadpoles. They can also pollute the water unless you install filters." It then offers mitigations rather than a prohibition — dense plant cover, grassy edges, refuges fish cannot reach, or a separate fish pond. The UCL/FHT/Natural England guide is blunter for new ponds — "Do not add plants, fish or other animals" — and notes that ponds heavily stocked with fish, particularly Common Carp, "often have brown murky water and support few plants other than water-lilies", so "ponds used for intensive angling are often poor for wildlife". The same guide lists ponds that will not be stocked with fish as a criterion for the ponds most worth restoring. Practically: a fish pond is a different object with a different purpose, and stocking one converts the other.

source.name: Freshwater Habitats Trust / ARC / World of Water — Creating garden ponds for wildlife (2023)

claims.checker_note: verified with the framing weakened — the cited quote is exact and the URL is live, but "close to incompatible" overstates a source that offers mitigations and calls the mitigated result "the best of both worlds"; the DETAIL's UCL/FHT/Natural England quotes are uncited and entirely unverified, and should be separately sourced or cut before publication
claims.cannot_establish: Because FHT itself offers workarounds, this is NOT a floor rule — I deliberately left mechanical_rule empty. I found no quantified study in these sources measuring amphibian or invertebrate loss against fish stocking density in garden-sized ponds.

claims.statement: Clean water is what the evidence base calls essential. The UCL / Freshwater Habitats Trust / Natural England guide puts it in its key messages: "Clean water is essential for wildlife; create, restore, resurrect and manage ponds where water is unpolluted." It names nutrients — elevated nitrogen and phosphorus from drains, ditches and spray-drift — as one of the main things degrading UK ponds, alongside outright loss and scrub encroachment. Size is not a threshold: the guide's first key message is that a variety of ponds, "deep, shallow, large, small", is best for wildlife. Separately, Freshwater Habitats Trust's garden pond advice discourages mains tap water — "Most tapwater is not fit to use in a pond because it's full of nutrients" — because it is usually high in dissolved nitrogen and phosphorus, which discourage aquatic plants and encourage algae and duckweed. Its booklet suggests setting up water butts "a couple of months before you dig your pond" so rainwater is ready, while allowing a minimal amount of tap water as a top-up if you must. And if you are digging: "Do not spread topsoil in or around the pond. Topsoil is very rich in nutrients: it pollutes ponds and encourages growth of rank vegetation."
claims.detail: The UCL / Freshwater Habitats Trust / Natural England pond guide lists among its key messages: "Clean water is essential for wildlife; create, restore, resurrect and manage ponds where water is unpolluted." It identifies nutrients — elevated nitrogen and phosphorus from drains, ditches and spray-drift — as a principal reason UK ponds are in poor condition. FHT's own advice says most tap water "is not fit to use in a pond because it's full of nutrients", and the garden booklet advises setting up water butts "a couple of months before you dig your pond" so you have rainwater ready. The same guide warns "Do not spread topsoil in or around the pond. Topsoil is very rich in nutrients: it pollutes ponds and encourages growth of rank vegetation" — which matters directly to anyone digging a pond and heaping the spoil beside it. The Newt Conservation Partnership reports that 95% of its created clean-water ponds showed no evidence of nitrate or phosphate pollution, with Great Crested Newts present at 90% of mature sites.

source.name: UCL / Freshwater Habitats Trust / Natural England — Guide to the restoration, creation and management of ponds

claims.checker_note: verified with correction — the cited guide supports the clean-water and nutrient half verbatim, but says nothing about tap water; that half must cite FHT's Garden Pond Advice Hub (https://freshwaterhabitats.org.uk/advice-resources/garden-pond-advice-hub/) and the Creating Garden Ponds 2023 booklet (https://freshwaterhabitats.b-cdn.net/app/uploads/2023/06/Creating-Garden-Ponds_2023.pdf). Drop "or age" as unsupported, soften "not size" to "size is not a threshold", and soften "wreck" to match FHT's own hedged wording.
claims.cannot_establish: I found no measured threshold — no mg/l of phosphate above which a garden pond fails. FHT hedges on tap water ("usually best" to use rainwater, "in many parts of Britain" avoid tap), so I could NOT establish a hard floor for tap-water filling and left mechanical_rule empty. Tap water chemistry also varies by supplier, and in hard-water eastern England the relevant issue is nutrients, not the chlorine most popular advice mentions.

claims.statement:
A wildlife pond and a drainage feature are best built as two separate things. The leading UK pond guidance — Sayer, Biggs, Greaves & Williams (2023), "Guide to the restoration, creation and management of ponds", published by UCL with the Freshwater Habitats Trust, prompted by Natural England and endorsed by the RSPB, FWAG, the British Dragonfly Society and others — says it plainly in its Key Messages: "Do not create and restore ponds for wildlife and use them for other activities such as angling, duck shooting, natural flood management or pollution interception as this reduces their ability to support wildlife", and "Ensure new ponds are not fed by streams, ditches or drains." Under the heading "Other activities that can damage ponds" it lists "using ponds for pollution interception, irrigation, sustainable urban drainage or for natural flood management purposes", and on creating a new one: "If you want to make a wildlife pond – make it just for wildlife. Do not create ponds that are multifunctional... All these uses will significantly compromise a pond's potential as a wildlife habitat." If a pond already has such a use, the guide's advice is to make a second pond for wildlife rather than ask the first to do both.

The cleanest water sources it names are groundwater and "surface water that drains from unpolluted areas" up-hill of the pond. Piped inflows are warned against for two reasons: drains and ditches "usually bring in polluted water and silt, which fills the pond up reducing its lifespan by an order of magnitude", and "Road run-off contains pollutants that will negatively impact the ecology of the pond."

Two honest limits. First, the guide is written for farmland and landscape-scale work; it never mentions roofs, downpipes or gardens, and it is not statutory national guidance. Applying it to a garden downpipe is our reading of "drains" and "sustainable urban drainage", not a line in the document. Second, its own verdict on multi-purpose ponds is a heavy discount rather than a disqualification: they "often bring only limited wildlife benefits, despite assertions to the contrary, especially where they are polluted". So the honest layout — a rain garden or soakaway taking the roof, sited away from a pond fed by rain, clean local sheet flow or groundwater — is what the guidance points to, not what it spells out.
claims.detail: This is the sharpest and least-known finding. The UCL/FHT/Natural England guide states: "Do not create and restore ponds for wildlife and use them for other activities such as angling, duck shooting, natural flood management or pollution interception as this reduces their ability to support wildlife." Elsewhere: "Ensure new ponds are not fed by streams, ditches or drains", and a list of damaging uses that names "using ponds for pollution interception, irrigation, sustainable urban drainage or for natural flood management purposes". The clean water a wildlife pond needs is rain falling on it plus surface water "that drains from unpolluted areas" — not a downpipe. Road runoff is called out as containing pollutants. So the honest garden layout is two separate things: a rain garden or soakaway that takes the roof, sited away from the pond, and a pond fed only by rain and clean local sheet flow. Selling one hole as both is the purchased-surface move.

source.name: UCL / Freshwater Habitats Trust / Natural England — Guide to the restoration, creation and management of ponds

claims.checker_note: verified with corrections — quotes exact and load-bearing, but "roof", "national guidance", the Natural England co-attribution, and the binary "stops being a wildlife pond" are not supported by the source and must be softened
claims.cannot_establish: This is written for countryside and farmland ponds; the guide does not quantify how much roof runoff is too much, and does not test a domestic garden case. It is possible a clean roof on a low-traffic site is less harmful than agricultural drainage — that comparison is not made anywhere I could fetch. Treat this as strong guidance from the leading UK body, not a measured dose-response.
claims.wall_fell_because:
The rule claims a hard floor ("cannot stand"), and the source will not carry it — the guide's own language is a gradient throughout. Its stated consequences are "reduces their ability to support wildlife", "significantly compromise a pond's potential", "can have negative impacts" and, decisively, "'multi-purpose' ponds OFTEN bring only LIMITED wildlife benefits... ESPECIALLY where they are polluted" (p13). "Often", "limited" and "especially" each concede that a drainage-fed pond still supports some wildlife; the guide grades ponds as better and worse for wildlife, it never declares a category of pond to be no longer a wildlife pond. The same gradient logic appears where it recommends a 10 m minimum buffer in intensive farmland while admitting it is "unlikely to be sufficient to eliminate all nutrient and pesticide inputs from agriculture" but "will still benefit the pond and its wildlife" — explicitly partial benefit, explicitly not nothing.

The rule also fails on its own trigger list. Its first named condition is "roof", and the word "roof" does not appear anywhere in the 48 pages I extracted; neither does downpipe, gutter or garden. A floor rule cannot fire on a condition the cited evidence never discusses, and roof water is not established by this source to be equivalent to road water (which the source DOES call out by name).

An honest narrower version would be a labelling rule, not a floor: WHEN a pond is fed by a stream, ditch, drain or road runoff THEN it should not be described as a clean-water wildlife pond, BECAUSE the guidance defines the clean sources as groundwater and surface water from unpolluted areas and says such inflows "usually bring in polluted water and silt". That constrains what you may call it, which the source does support. It does not support the assertion that the wildlife layer cannot exist at all.

claims.statement: Life arrives in a new pond fast, and you do not have to stock it. The Freshwater Habitats Trust says that in spring "pond animals will arrive often within minutes, including water beetles and pond skaters - and dragonflies will often find your new pond in just a few days", and that "more often than not amphibians will arrive within the first year". Shropshire Wildlife Trust's Dr Cath Price writes that "within two or three years a clean water pond can be as rich in species as one fifty years old" - note "can be", and note "clean water": the timescale depends on the pond not being loaded with nutrients, which is why FHT warns against filling from the tap. On intervention, the sources agree that stocking is unnecessary rather than forbidden: "It isn't necessary to plant a pond", "there is no need to plant your pond: be patient and plants will naturally colonise", and Dr Price likewise says "it really isn't necessary to introduce plants" - though FHT and Shropshire both still allow a few local, native, wild-sourced plants if you want them. The warning about non-native species and pollutants is aimed specifically at moving sludge or material between ponds. What none of the sources say is that an unplanted pond gets rich faster; the case for leaving it alone is that stocking is unnecessary, that it risks importing pollutants and non-natives, and that the bare early substrate is itself habitat for early-stage specialists - Dr Price names common darter dragonflies and mayflies on "inorganic sands" - which disappear once the pond matures.
claims.detail: This is the honest answer to the timescale question, and it is unusually good news. Freshwater Habitats Trust: "In the spring, pond animals will arrive often within minutes, including water beetles and pond skaters – and dragonflies will often find your new pond in just a few days. More often than not amphibians will arrive within the first year." Shropshire Wildlife Trust's Dr Cath Price puts the maturity point at "within two or three years a clean water pond can be as rich in species as one fifty years old". The UCL/FHT guide corroborates the order of magnitude from restoration work: expect algal blooms and discoloured water for some months, but "after 6 months and sometimes less than this, the water should start to clear", and "within two years it can be near impossible to know that any restoration works took place". All three sources say the same thing about intervention: "Do not add plants, fish or other animals" — introducing species is unnecessary and "risks introducing non native species and disease". The bare muddy substrate of the first few years is itself a scarce habitat that some rare species need, so planting it out destroys a stage.

source.name: Freshwater Habitats Trust — Pond FAQs

claims.checker_note: source-declared
claims.cannot_establish: None of these is a peer-reviewed colonisation study with counts and error bars — they are charity guidance summarising practitioner experience. The two-to-three-year figure comes from a single Wildlife Trust blog (fetched: shropshirewildlifetrust.org.uk/blog/dr-cath-price/natural-succession-pond) and I could not trace it to a published dataset. 'As rich as a fifty-year-old pond' is not defined (species count? which taxa?). Rate will also depend on how many other ponds are within flying distance — an isolated urban garden may be much slower, and none of the sources model that.

claims.statement: A pond dropping about half a metre over the summer is normal, not a failure to fix. Freshwater Habitats Trust calls the belief that levels must stay stable "a persistent myth": "Seasonal drawdown is a predictable event in the vast majority of ponds. Indeed, natural ponds typically have a water level drop of about half a metre during the summer months." The exposed drawdown zone is "one of the most important areas of a pond, and is an exceptionally rich habitat for plants, invertebrates, amphibians, birds and even small mammals" — many marginal wetland plant seeds need exposure to air before they can germinate, and dragonflies such as the Southern Hawker lay their eggs into the damp exposed mud. Complete drying is natural too, at least in the wild: around 40% of lowland countryside ponds dry out in drought years, and the Trust's surveys find that ponds which occasionally dry out are among the richest of all. On topping up, the Trust is more cautious than a slogan allows. It says whether to top up "is a personal decision"; the objection to a hose is the nitrate, phosphate and disinfection chemicals in tap water, not the topping-up itself, so rainwater from a butt is preferred where you have it — but "if you regularly fill your pond with tapwater, just carry on", and it advises topping up if the water reaches 35C or to save valuable marginal plants. It also warns that a lined garden pond is not a wild pond: there may be too little damp sediment for creatures to burrow into, and snails, shrimps, leeches and younger amphibians will likely die if it bakes dry. So: don't panic at a falling level, and prefer rainwater to the tap — but doing nothing is a sensible default, not a rule. [Cite the drawdown material to "What makes a good wildlife pond?"; cite the drying/top-up material separately to the Trust's FAQ "What to do if your pond is drying out". Drop the "do not reach for the hose" quote — I could not find it in any Trust source.]
claims.detail: Freshwater Habitats Trust calls stable water levels "a persistent myth": "Seasonal drawdown is a predictable event in the vast majority of ponds. Indeed, natural ponds typically have a water level drop of about half a metre during the summer months." The exposed drawdown zone is "one of the most important areas of a pond, and is an exceptionally rich habitat for plants, invertebrates, amphibians, birds and even small mammals" — many marginal wetland plant seeds need exposure to air before they can germinate, and dragonflies such as Southern Hawker lay into damp exposed mud. On complete drying: "For many ponds, drying up from time to time is perfectly natural and harmless or beneficial" and "annual drying out of ponds has been a natural process for hundreds of millions of years... the pond will recolonise quickly." The Trust's summer instruction is explicit: "If you want to top up, use rain water, and do not reach for the hose." This matters enormously in a drought year in eastern England: the correct response to a shrinking pond is usually nothing.

source.name: Freshwater Habitats Trust — What makes a good wildlife pond?

claims.checker_note: partly verified — the drawdown half is verbatim-exact in the live cited source; the drying-out and hose half is absent from that source, partly unverifiable, and overstated against what the Trust actually says
claims.cannot_establish: 'Many ponds' is not all ponds — the guidance does not say which garden ponds can safely dry and which cannot, and it does give rescue instructions (move creatures to buckets or shaded mini-ponds) for ponds that dry hard, which implies losses do occur. Fish, if present, will die. No figure is given for how frequently drying can be tolerated before species are lost locally.

claims.statement: A container pond needs a way out as well as a way in. The Wildlife Trusts' mini-pond guidance treats the exit as a build step, not a nicety: "Use logs or stones to create a range of depths and a slope for creatures to climb in and out", and "If your container isn't sunk in you'll need a ramp from the ground outside the pond." A washing-up bowl, large plant pot or disused sink counts, at 20-30cm deep, filled with rainwater, one or two plants, and nothing moved in from another pond — "Don't introduce frogs, fish or even water from another pond as this can spread disease." The guidance says damsel and dragonflies, frogs and newts will use even a small one. Note what this source does and does not say: it prescribes the slope and the ramp, but it does not state that animals drown without them — that is our inference, not their finding.
claims.detail: The Wildlife Trusts' mini-pond guidance accepts a washing-up bowl, large plant pot or disused sink, specifies 20-30cm deep, and makes the exit condition explicit: "Use logs or stones to create a range of depths and a slope for creatures to climb in and out", and "If your container isn't sunk in you'll need a ramp from the ground outside the pond." Freshwater Habitats Trust makes the same point from the other end when describing temporary holding containers — you must make "sure there is somewhere where amphibians can rest and climb out (or they can drown)". Other conditions: fill with rainwater, one or two plants is enough, and "Don't introduce frogs, fish or even water from another pond as this can spread disease." The Wildlife Trusts claim damselflies, dragonflies, frogs and newts will use even a small pond. The honest caveat for scale: FHT's own definition of a pond begins at 1 square metre, and a washing-up bowl is roughly a tenth of that — so a container sits below the smallest unit the conservation evidence base actually studies.

source.name: The Wildlife Trusts — How to create a mini pond

claims.checker_note: supported — the exit route (slope, logs or stones, outside ramp) is stated outright on the cited page; only the drowning consequence and the "worse than no pond" framing are inference, and the two Freshwater Habitats Trust sentences in DETAIL are unverified and should not be published as quoted
claims.cannot_establish: I found NO study measuring what a container pond actually supports versus a dug pond, and no evidence that a sub-1m2 container sustains a breeding amphibian population rather than merely being visited. The claim that mini ponds host frogs and newts is a charity assertion, not a measurement. A container also has no drawdown zone and no gently shelving margin — the two habitats FHT names as richest — so on FHT's own reasoning it cannot deliver the main thing a pond delivers.
claims.wall_fell_because: This is a degradation, not a floor. Three failures against the "cannot work at all" test. (1) The cited page never says a rampless container kills anything, never says drowning, and never says worse than no pond — the whole BECAUSE clause is absent from the evidence. (2) The habitat function does not go to zero without an exit: the same page has the pond colonised by damselflies and dragonflies, which fly in to lay, whose larvae live submerged and emerge by climbing plant stems (the guidance already puts one or two plants in), plus water beetles, water snails and other aquatic invertebrates that never need to reach dry ground. A steep-sided rampless tub is a worse pond, not a non-pond. (3) The drowning risk is real but partial — it bears on animals that fall in and cannot swim out (hedgehogs, small mammals, amphibians crossing the garden), and the strongest evidence offered for it is the FHT line about temporary holding containers, i.e. amphibians deliberately confined in a bucket, which is a different situation from an open garden container and which could not be verified at source anyway. A floor rule that would forbid the layer from standing needs the "not at all" case; this has "less well, and with a specific hazard to specific animals". Keep it as a strong build instruction with the hazard named, not as a floor.

claims.statement: All four RHS rain garden figures are on the page verbatim — but three of them carry conditions that the bare numbers hide. Sizing: "Allow the rain garden to constitute 20% of the roof area" — multiply roof area by 0.2, which RHS sizes "to accommodate typical UK summer rainfall". Depth: "On a soil that drains at 5cm (2in) per hour, the rain garden would need to be 15cm (6in) deep, with an extra 5cm-10cm (2-5in) below the lowest point where excess water would leave." That 5cm/hr is the fast end of RHS's own acceptable band — "a minimum of 1.25cm (½in) per hour, but will still work with absorption rates of up to 5cm (2in) per hour" — so 15cm is a worked example at one end of the range, not a universal depth. The 48 hours is written as a planting spec, not a performance target: the bed "is planted with plants that can stand waterlogging for up to 48 hours at a time" — it says what the plants tolerate, and RHS states no drain-down time anywhere on the page. Distance: siting within 5m is not forbidden, it triggers advice — "If siting your rain garden closer than 5m (16ft) to your house, seek advice from a Geotechnical Adviser or Registered Ground Engineering Professional to avoid any damage to foundations by infiltrating water." An overflow is required either way: "Ensure that the lowest point of the rain garden allows overflow water to access a drain, or other rain garden element."
claims.detail: Verified verbatim from RHS. Sizing: "Allow the rain garden to constitute 20% of the roof area" — multiply roof area by 0.2, sized for typical UK summer rainfall. Depth: "On a soil that drains at 5cm (2in) per hour, the rain garden would need to be 15cm (6in) deep, with an extra 5cm-10cm (2-5in) below the lowest point where excess water would leave." That 15cm is tied to the fast end of the acceptable infiltration band — it is not a universal depth. The 48 hours is stated as a planting spec: the bed is "planted with plants that can stand waterlogging for up to 48 hours at a time", i.e. it describes what the plants tolerate rather than a performance guarantee that water clears in 48 hours. Distance: RHS does not flatly forbid siting within 5m; it says "If siting your rain garden closer than 5m (16ft) to your house, seek advice from a Geotechnical Adviser or Registered Ground Engineering Professional to avoid any damage to foundations by infiltrating water." It also requires an overflow: "Ensure that the lowest point of the rain garden allows overflow water to access a drain, or other rain garden element."

source.name: RHS — Rain gardens

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: RHS does not show the calculation or design storm behind the 20% figure, does not state a return period, and does not say what happens in the intense summer downpours the Met Office projects. A rain garden sized for 'typical UK summer rainfall' is not the same as one sized for a 1-in-30-year event. No source I fetched gives a domestic UK rain garden performance measurement.

claims.statement: The RHS gives a drainage threshold for rain gardens: the site should absorb water at a minimum of about 1.25cm (1/2in) per hour, and still works at rates up to 5cm (2in) per hour. To test it, dig a hole about 25cm (10in) deep, fill it with water, let it empty, then refill and time the second fill — the first soaking saturates the surrounding soil, so only the second reading means anything. If the ground drains more slowly than that, the RHS says the site is not suitable, and names very heavy clay or a high water table as cases where that "might be true". Read this as RHS's design gate for the plain unlined form — a shallow planted depression that infiltrates into the native soil — rather than a law of physics: the same page suggests working gravel or grit into less well-draining soil, and slow sites are commonly handled elsewhere with an underdrain or a lined detention design, which function but are no longer pure infiltration. Around Cambridge this matters, because the region carries substantial Gault and Oxford clay as well as free-draining chalk: the answer genuinely varies street by street and has to be tested on the spot, never assumed from a soil map.
claims.detail: This is the floor rule the brief was looking for, and it is stated plainly by RHS: "The ideal rain garden site is one that drains at a rate of a minimum of 1.25cm (1/2in) per hour, but will still work with absorption rates of up to 5cm (2in) per hour. If it takes longer, the site is not suitable. This might be true of a very heavy clay soil or where there is a high water table." The test a homeowner can run is given: "Excavate a hole about 25cm (10in) deep and fill it with water. Once empty, refill and observe the time it takes to drain." Pre-wetting matters — the second fill is the one you time, because the first saturates the surrounding soil. In practice: mark the water level, wait an hour, measure the drop. A drop of less than about 1.25cm in that hour is a fail. This is highly relevant to the Cambridge working assumption: the region carries substantial Gault and Oxford clay as well as free-draining chalk, so the answer genuinely varies street by street and must be tested, never assumed from a soil map.

source.name: RHS — Rain gardens

claims.checker_note: verified as a citation — URL live, quotes exact — but downgraded in strength: a single advisory body's suitability threshold for one design, hedged by RHS's own "might" and its own grit-amendment advice, not an absolute limit
claims.cannot_establish: RHS gives no test procedure detail — no hole diameter, no number of pre-soak fills, no instruction to repeat on different days or after wet weather, so results will vary. The 1.25-5 cm/hr band is stated without derivation, and the upper bound is unexplained. It also does not address whether a clay site can be rescued by excavating and backfilling with an engineered soil (which is standard practice in larger SuDS schemes) — so 'cannot work' should be read as 'cannot work as an infiltration rain garden on the existing soil'.
claims.wall_fell_because: The evidence supports a design gate, not a hard floor. RHS says "not suitable" — a recommendation about one specific unlined infiltration design — and hedges the cause with "might be true of". The very same page offers a way past the threshold ("If the soil is less well draining, incorporate gravel or grit"), which is incompatible with a limit that cannot be crossed. Beyond RHS, slow-draining and clay sites are routinely built as rain gardens with an underdrain, engineered soil media, or a lined detention/bioretention cell; these function, they simply stop being pure infiltration into native ground. The measurement is also too coarse to carry a floor: a hand-dug 25cm hole timed over an hour has wide variance and RHS's own threshold sentence is ambiguously worded. So below 1.25cm/hr the plain unlined depression is a poor choice and the layer must change form — that is a gradient with a design branch at the bottom, not a point where the layer cannot stand. Publish it as a strong default gate that redirects the design, not as a floor.

claims.statement: Approved Document H — the government's statutory guidance on how to satisfy the drainage requirements of the Building Regulations in England — says at paragraph 3.25 that "infiltration devices should not be built: within 5m of a building or road or in areas of unstable land... in ground where the water table reaches the bottom of the device at any time of the year", or where contamination in the runoff could pollute groundwater. Paragraph 3.23 lists infiltration devices as "soakaways, swales, infiltration basins and filter drains"; a rain garden fed by a downpipe is not named, but is functionally in that family. This is guidance, not a ban: the same document states there is "no obligation to adopt any particular solution contained in an Approved Document if you prefer to meet the relevant requirement in some other way", and it bites on building work subject to the Regulations rather than on every spade in every garden. Read it as the settled professional standard that turns the RHS's "seek advice near a building" into "don't, unless you can show why it is safe" — and note that (b) is a February test, not an August one.
claims.detail: Approved Document H (Drainage and waste disposal, 2015 edition), paragraph 3.25, states: "Infiltration drainage is not always possible. Infiltration devices should not be built: a. within 5m of a building or road or in areas of unstable land; b. in ground where the water table reaches the bottom of the device at any time of the year; c. sufficiently far from any drainage fields, drainage mounds or other soakaways so that the overall soakage capacity of the ground is not exceeded...; d. where the presence of any contamination in the runoff could result in pollution of a groundwater source or resource." Paragraph 3.23 defines infiltration devices to include "soakaways, swales, infiltration basins and filter drains" — a rain garden taking a downpipe is functionally in this family. This hardens the RHS 5m advice from 'seek advice' into 'should not'. Note point (b) is a winter test, not a summer one: the water table must be below the base at every time of year, so a hole that is dry in August but standing water in February fails. Point (d) is directly relevant to the previous room's construction-rubble ground — contaminated fill over an aquifer rules out infiltration.

source.name: HM Government — Approved Document H: Drainage and waste disposal (Building Regulations, England), 2015

claims.checker_note: verified quotation, overstated framing — text is exact and the source is live, but "hard prohibitions" must become "statutory guidance saying should not", and the reach must be narrowed from "any soakaway" to building work under the Regulations
claims.cannot_establish: Approved Document H governs building work under the Building Regulations. Whether a homeowner digging a shallow planted depression in an existing garden is legally caught by it is genuinely unclear and I could not resolve it from any fetched source — so treat the 5m and water-table rules as the correct engineering standard and a strong liability argument, not a proven legal duty for a retrofit. The document is the 2015 edition; I did not verify whether a later amendment changed paragraph 3.25. It also applies to England only.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule claims the infiltration layer "cannot stand" — a hard floor — but the evidence supports neither half as an absolute. The 5m condition is a regulatory and geotechnical precaution about wetting foundations and undermining road subgrade, not a statement that water stops soaking into soil 4.9m from a wall; AD H's own front matter permits compliance by other means, so a designer who demonstrates safety (lined sides, engineered offset, structural assessment) is not barred. The water-table condition is closer to real physics — saturated ground accepts nothing while saturated — but the AD's test is "at any time of the year", which condemns a device that infiltrates perfectly for fifty weeks and backs up for two. That is a seasonal performance failure and a compliance failure, not an impossibility. Decisively, AD H itself supplies the workaround at paragraphs 2.9 and 2.10: "Where infiltration is not possible (see paragraph 3.25), they may also be used with an impermeable barrier below the storage layer as a detention tank prior to flows discharging to a drainage system." The document that states the constraint, in the same breath, tells you the feature still works — as attenuation rather than infiltration. A condition whose consequence is "redesign it as a lined detention basin" is a fork in the design, not a floor. If a floor rule is wanted here, the only defensible one is narrower and about compliance rather than function: within 5m of a building or road, or where the winter water table reaches the base, unlined infiltration should not be relied upon and the feature must be designed as lined storage or justified by other means.

claims.statement: Water butts cannot meet a dry summer's garden demand — the constraint is storage, not rainfall. The RHS puts collection from a small shed roof at 2,500-3,500 litres a year in dry south-east England, enough to fill around 10-15 standard 240-litre butts, and more than that in wetter regions. So the supply exists; almost nobody has the storage to hold it. What a single 240-litre butt buys is establishment support for new planting and pond top-ups, not a watered garden: a genuinely useful 10mm soak over a 20m2 border takes 200 litres, since 1mm over 1m2 is 1 litre — most of a butt in one go. If the garden needs a hose to survive August, no realistic amount of storage fixes it; the planting has to change instead. (The per-tree figure of 40-60 litres a week, and the sprinkler-versus-household comparison, are not on the cited page — publish them only with their own source.)
claims.detail: RHS figures, verified: "2,500-3,500 litres of rainwater each year can be collected from the roof of a small shed - enough to fill around 10-15 standard 240-litre water butts." So the supply exists; almost nobody has the storage. Against that, RHS demand figures: "newly planted trees need around four to six full 10-litre cans of water per week in dry weather" — 40 to 60 litres per week, per tree. One full 240-litre butt therefore covers one new tree for about four to six weeks, and nothing else. Scale it: watering a 20m2 border with a genuinely useful 10mm soak takes 200 litres, since 1mm over 1m2 is 1 litre — most of a butt in one go. And RHS notes "Sprinklers can use as much water in an hour as a family of four people would normally use in two days", which puts a sprinkler at roughly a thousand litres an hour, or four butts. The honest design conclusion: butts buy you establishment support for new planting and pond top-ups, not a watered garden. If the garden needs a hose to survive August, no realistic amount of storage fixes it — the planting has to change instead.

claims.checker_note: partly verified — the supply figure is verbatim on the cited page but loses its "in dry south-east England" qualifier as quoted; the demand figures (40-60 L/week per new tree, sprinkler vs family of four) are absent from the cited source and remain unverified

RHS gives no shed roof area for that figure, so it cannot be scaled to a specific house. The 200-litre-per-20m2 figure is my own arithmetic from the mm-to-litre identity, not a quoted source.
