claims.statement: Mains-fed irrigation here draws on a supply the state has formally flagged. In the final 2021 classification, determined by the Secretary of State on 1 July 2021 on Environment Agency advice, Cambridge Water was newly added to the list of areas of serious water stress, and Anglian Water – East Anglia, listed since 2013, remains on it. Serious water stress is defined in the Water Industry (Prescribed Conditions) Regulations 1999 as where household demand is, or is likely to be, "a high proportion of the ... effective rainfall which is available to meet that demand". The method is long-term, not a snapshot — it runs to 2039-40 and allows for population growth, climate change, environmental needs, increased drought resilience and cuts to abstraction for sustainability. Yorkshire, United Utilities and Northumbrian are on the not-seriously-stressed list, so water advice written for the wetter north does not transfer here (though the stressed list is not purely eastern and southern — Severn Trent, South Staffordshire and Wessex are on it too). Two honest limits, from the document itself. First, the classification exists solely so companies can consider charging all customers by metered volume, and must evaluate compulsory metering in their water resources management plans; the Environment Agency says it "must not be used for other purposes". Second, it "does not indicate that there will not be enough water for supplies". What it does say is that public water supply here is causing, or is likely to cause, environmental impacts that better water efficiency could reduce. That is the real reason to keep a hose off the mains in Cambridge, and it is enough of one.
claims.detail: In the 2021 final classification, made by the Secretary of State on 1 July 2021, Cambridge Water was newly added to the seriously water stressed list, and Anglian Water - East Anglia, classified in 2013, remains so. Serious water stress is defined in the Water Industry (Prescribed Conditions) Regulations 1999 as where "the current household demand for water is a high proportion of the current effective rainfall which is available to meet that demand", or where future demand is likely to be. The Environment Agency's method is long-term rather than a snapshot, accounting for population growth, climate change, environmental needs and reduced abstraction. The practical consequence stated in the document is that companies in these areas may charge all customers by metered volume and must evaluate compulsory metering in their water resources management plans. Companies in the same document classified as NOT seriously water stressed include Yorkshire, United Utilities and Northumbrian — so this is specifically an eastern and southern England condition, and advice written for the wetter north-west does not transfer.

source.name: Environment Agency — Water stressed areas, final classification 2021

claims.checker_note: verified as to every named fact — the source is live and the quotes are exact — but the framing is overstated: the determination is the Secretary of State's on EA advice, the stressed list is not purely "eastern and southern" (Severn Trent, South Staffs and Wessex are on it), and the document explicitly limits itself to metering purposes and disclaims saying there will not be enough water. Publish only with the corrected wording.
claims.cannot_establish: The document itself is careful: the determination "is solely to inform whether water companies should be able to consider the option of charging by metered volume" and "does not indicate that there will not be enough water for supplies". So it establishes that the region is under long-term resource pressure — it does NOT establish that any individual garden's hosepipe causes measurable harm, and it gives no figure for garden watering as a share of demand. I could not find a fetchable source quantifying UK garden irrigation as a proportion of peak summer demand.

claims.statement: What carries a planting through a dry summer without irrigation is establishment, mulch AND plant choice — RHS treats all three as load-bearing, so drought-tolerant labels are not the wrong idea, just not sufficient on their own. Establishment is the dividing line: "Established trees, shrubs and herbaceous perennials in beds and borders will only need watering in extreme drought", and "After the first year, established perennials usually do not need regular watering", while new stock needs "regular watering during dry spells from spring to autumn in their first year, and large specimens for up to three summers" (RHS's drought-resistant gardening page states the same as "up to three years after planting" for large tree specimens). Water to depth rather than on a schedule: moisten to 20-30cm (8-12in) for young trees and shrubs, 15cm (6in) in borders. Choice matters too: trees, shrubs and perennials "chosen for their suitability to the conditions in your garden ... will not need water during summer". Mulch: biodegradable mulch "between at least 5cm (2in) and ideally 7.5cm (3in) thick", laid "over moist soil, after removing weeds, when the soil is not frozen" — never onto baked ground. Note RHS is not consistent on timing: its mulching page says mid- to late spring and autumn; its watering page says late autumn to late winter (Nov-Feb). Sources: RHS Watering plants wisely (https://www.rhs.org.uk/garden-jobs/watering), RHS Drought-resistant gardening (https://www.rhs.org.uk/garden-design/drought-resistant-gardening), RHS Mulches and mulching (https://www.rhs.org.uk/soil-composts-mulches/mulch).
claims.detail: RHS is explicit that establishment is the dividing line: "Established trees, shrubs and herbaceous perennials in beds and borders will only need watering in extreme drought", and if plants are "chosen for their suitability to the conditions in your garden, they will not need water during summer." The support period: water newly planted trees and shrubs "for up to three summers" for large specimens, and "Large tree specimens may need watering for up to three years after planting"; for herbaceous perennials, "After the first year, established perennials usually do not need regular watering." Depth targets rather than frequency: moisten soil to 20-30cm for young trees and shrubs, 15cm for borders. Mulch spec: "between at least 5cm (2in) and ideally 7.5cm (3in) thick", laid "over moist soil, after removing weeds, when the soil is not frozen" — so mid-to-late spring or autumn, after rain, never onto baked ground. Planting season for drought resilience: March or September, September being preferred because the soil is still warm and roots have the whole autumn and winter to extend before the first dry summer arrives.

source.name: RHS — Watering plants wisely

claims.checker_note: verified with corrections — core quote exact on a live page; requires two additional RHS citations and removal of the "not drought-tolerant labels" antithesis
claims.cannot_establish: 'Up to three summers' is hedged ('may need') and RHS gives no survival data — no percentage of unwatered new plantings that die in a dry year, and no definition of 'extreme drought'. I could not verify the autumn-versus-spring planting advantage against any trial. The mulch-on-moist-soil instruction is a prescription, not a tested result: I found no measurement showing mulch laid on dry soil fails to conserve water, so despite it being intuitively true I did NOT turn it into a floor rule.
claims.wall_fell_because: The evidence describes a risk gradient, not a hard floor. RHS's own wording is conditional — newly planted trees and shrubs need water "regularly during dry spells", not unconditionally; in a wet first year rainfall does the job and nothing supplementary is required. The rule also equivocates on "no water can be supplied": rain is water, and the claim's own advice to plant in September exists precisely so roots extend through autumn and winter rain before the first dry summer, which is a route by which an unwatered new planting does stand. Outcome further depends on species, specimen size (RHS advises small specimens because they establish faster), soil and season. Nowhere does RHS say an unwatered new plant dies; it says growth is checked and establishment is at risk. As written the rule would condemn an autumn-planted perennial through a normal British winter, which is plainly wrong. A defensible narrower statement — a large newly planted tree given zero water through an extreme drought will probably die — is still "probably", not "cannot at all", so no floor survives.

claims.statement: On disturbed dryland soil in the Colorado Plateau (Canyonlands National Park, Utah), plots scraped to bare mineral soil in October 2017 and remeasured in May 2019 reached high physical stability within about 1.5 years — a median of 5.5 on the slake test across all plot sizes, in the same band as nearby undisturbed reference crusts (medians of 5 and 6) — while the living parts inside were still only about a third of reference. Chlorophyll a rose from about 2.7 to about 4.3 micrograms per gram of dry soil against reference crusts at roughly 12-13; the exopolysaccharide glue the microbes secrete roughly doubled, from about 560 to about 1,126 micrograms glucose per gram, against reference values of roughly 3,000-3,700. The authors did not formally test stability against reference and did not claim full recovery — they note that full recovery of development, diversity and function takes much longer, and that productivity measures like chlorophyll a 'may take much longer or be more variable over time'. So a surface that passes a physical hardness test can still be running at roughly a third of its biological capacity.
claims.detail: Plots were scraped down to bare mineral soil in October 2017 and remeasured in May 2019. Soil aggregate stability recovered to high levels (median 5.5 on the slake test) across all plot sizes in that 1.5 years. Chlorophyll a — the living photosynthetic tissue — rose only from about 2.7 to about 4.3 micrograms per gram of dry soil, against reference crusts at roughly 12-13: about a third. The exopolysaccharide 'glue' the microbes secrete roughly doubled, from about 560 to about 1,126 micrograms glucose per gram, against reference values of roughly 3,000-3,700: again about a third. So a surface that passes a physical hardness test can be running at one-third of its biological capacity.

source.name: Frontiers in Microbiology (2023), 'The influence of disturbance scale on the natural recovery of biological soil crusts on the Colorado Plateau', via PubMed Central PMC10434622

claims.checker_note: verified with a caveat — all figures confirmed against the cited source, but 'physical strength came back' should be softened to 'reached high stability levels, comparable to nearby reference crusts', since the authors never statistically compared recovering stability to reference and explicitly avoided full-recovery language
claims.cannot_establish: This is a semi-arid dryland crust, not a temperate garden soil in eastern England — the same ratio cannot be assumed for Cambridge loam or chalk. The study ran only 1.5 years, so it cannot say when the biology would eventually have caught up, or whether it would. It also does not show that physical stability is a bad measure — only that it is a fast one.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule asserts a hard floor — that a 'biologically recovered' claim CANNOT STAND on physical evidence alone — but the evidence supports only that physical tests are a weak and saturating proxy, which is a degradation of inference, not an absence of it. Three specific failures. (1) This is a saturation/lag pattern, not zero signal: immediately after scraping, both stability and biology were low, and they fell together. The slake test tracks biological state early and then plateaus while chlorophyll a and EPS keep climbing. A proxy that saturates still carries real information about the low end; the rule needs a measure that carries none. (2) The rule's own stated basis overstates the source: it says 'physical stability was fully back', but the paper never establishes that — no statistical comparison of recovering plots to reference stability was made at 1.5 years, and the authors decline full-recovery language. A floor rule resting on a fact the source does not assert cannot be a floor. (3) The generalization is far wider than the evidence: one study, one region, two sites, a single 1.5-year timepoint whose single-timepoint nature the authors themselves flag as a limitation, extended to every system and every physical or structural test. Mechanistically the two measures are causally coupled rather than independent — EPS, one of the biological measures, is itself the microbial glue binding the soil aggregates the slake test scores — which is the opposite of the independence a hard floor would require. The honest form is a caution, not a floor: a physical test alone is a poor stand-in for biological recovery because it saturates early — in the one system where both were measured side by side, it read high while the living fraction sat at about a third.

claims.statement: Restored and created wetlands were on average still about a quarter below reference wetlands a century after restoration — biological structure 26% lower and biogeochemical functioning 23% lower. The authors note this may mean either that recovery is very slow or that restored systems have settled into alternative states that differ from reference conditions.
claims.detail: A synthesis of 124 studies, 1,501 data points, 621 restored or created wetlands against 556 reference wetlands. Even 100 years after restoration, biological structure (mainly plant assemblages) remained on average 26% lower and biogeochemical functioning (mainly carbon storage) 23% lower than reference sites. At 20 years after restoration, carbon storage specifically was 50% lower. The authors' plain conclusion is that recovery 'as currently practiced is often slow and incomplete', and they warn against using restoration to justify destroying wetlands elsewhere.

source.name: Moreno-Mateos, Power, Comín & Yockteng (2012), 'Structural and Functional Loss in Restored Wetland Ecosystems', PLoS Biology

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: These are averages across many wetland types and climates; they say nothing about one particular garden pond. Most of the underlying data is under 30 years old, so the 100-year figure comes from a fitted trend, not from watching a wetland for a century. It also cannot tell you which individual actions shorten the gap.

claims.statement: Across 89 restoration assessments worldwide, a 2009 meta-analysis found restoration raised biodiversity by 44% and ecosystem services by 25% above the degraded starting point — real gains that still left both below intact reference sites.
claims.detail: This is the standard citation for 'restoration works, but not all the way'. The 89 assessments span many ecosystem types globally. Both measures rose substantially against the degraded starting point, and the two rose together (biodiversity gains and service gains were positively correlated), which is the useful part: helping the wildlife also helped the functions. But the paper is equally clear that restored sites did not reach intact reference condition. The honest reading for a homeowner is: intervention moves the needle a long way and does not finish the job.

source.name: Rey Benayas, Newton, Diaz & Bullock (2009), Science, abstract via PubMed 19644076

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: It gives no timescale — 44% after how long is not stated in the abstract. It covers landscape-scale projects, not gardens. And meta-analyses of restoration draw on published projects, which skew toward the ones that worked well enough to publish, so the true average shortfall is likely larger, not smaller.

claims.statement: In the Woburn Ley-Arable experiment on a sandy loam in England, begun in 1938 at 0.98% soil organic carbon, the authors record that "significant differences between the rotations began to emerge in the early 1960s, more than 20 years after the experiment started." Under an all-arable cereal rotation carbon drifted down to 0.91% over 70 years; a second arable rotation including root crops and fallow fell further, to 0.80%. Under a 3-year grazed ley given nitrogen fertilizer it rose to about 1.23% within roughly 28 years and then changed little over the following decades — a new equilibrium rather than an endless climb; the 3-year grass-and-clover ley reached a similar 1.24%. Eight-year leys reached about 1.40%. Maximum accumulation rates in the ley-arable rotations were 0.26-0.36 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year, and the paper notes such rates persist only for a limited period before equilibrium. This is a replicated long-term experiment with careful sampling — far better evidence than one gardener with one spade.
claims.detail: The Woburn Ley-Arable experiment on a sandy loam started in 1938 at 0.98% soil organic carbon. Under continuous arable it drifted down to 0.91% over 70 years — a change of 0.07 percentage points in a human lifetime. Under a three-year grass-and-clover ley rotation it rose to 1.23% over 28 years and then barely moved for the next 40: a new equilibrium, not an endless climb. Longer eight-year leys reached about 1.40%, accumulating 0.26-0.36 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year. Crucially, the authors record that significant differences between rotations only emerged in the early 1960s — more than 20 years in — and this is a replicated experiment with careful sampling, far better evidence than one gardener with one spade.

source.name: Johnston, Poulton, Coleman, Macdonald & White (2017), 'Changes in soil organic matter over 70 years in continuous arable and ley-arable rotations on a sandy loam soil in England', European Journal of Soil Science

claims.checker_note: verified — headline claim quoted verbatim from the live cited source; publish with the two detail corrections (the 1.23% ley is grass-plus-nitrogen, not grass-and-clover; the arable decline range is 0.91% to 0.80% depending on rotation)
claims.cannot_establish: Woburn is a sandy loam in Bedfordshire under farm rotations, not a garden bed receiving heavy compost — a garden with large annual organic inputs on a small area can change faster, and this study cannot say how much faster. The 20-year detection time is a property of that experiment's sampling design and effect size, not a universal constant.
claims.wall_fell_because: The evidence shows a gradient of statistical power, not a hard floor, and the rule does not even follow from its own stated warrant. Four problems. (1) The threshold is invented: the cited evidence is about 20+ years at Woburn, but the rule disqualifies anything under "about ten years" — a number that appears nowhere in the evidence and is neither the paper's finding nor derivable from it. (2) Detection time is site- and contrast-specific. Woburn is a low-carbon sandy loam and the contrasts compared were modest rotation differences. How fast a difference becomes detectable depends on the size of the treatment contrast, initial carbon level, soil type, sampling depth and density, replication, and analytical precision. A large contrast — arable converted to permanent grassland, or heavy farmyard-manure or compost additions — produces statistically detectable change substantially faster. So "cannot stand" is simply false as a general law. (3) The rule fuses two different things, duration and replication, into one disqualifier, and neither is a floor. An unreplicated sample is weak evidence, not zero evidence; a well-replicated design with a large contrast and dense sampling can detect real change quickly. (4) The inference runs backwards: that one slow, small-contrast experiment needed 20+ years to reach significance shows something about that system's signal-to-noise ratio, not that every shorter or smaller study is void. The paper itself reports continuous accumulation of 0.26-0.36 t C/ha/yr, which means real change was occurring throughout — the delay was in detecting it, not in it happening. A defensible weaker version would be a caution ("short or unreplicated soil-carbon evidence should be treated as provisional, because change on low-carbon arable soils can take decades to rise above sampling variation"), which is a confidence discount, not a floor.

claims.statement: In a 2003 experiment, plants were fed carbon dioxide made from fossil carbon, which contains no carbon-14. The fine threads that arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi push out into the soil were then harvested over 29 days and dated by accelerator mass spectrometry. Most of them, on average, held carbon only 5 to 6 days old — so that part of the fungus is largely a flow, built and rebuilt out of recent sugar from the plant, rather than a fixed structure. Two honest limits: this measures how fast carbon turns over in the threads, which the authors read as the threads' lifespan; and it was measured only in arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, not in the ectomycorrhizal networks of forests, which build thicker, longer-lasting cords. What persists for years — the community of fungal species, and the soil structure their residues help build — is our own inference, not something this study measured.
claims.detail: Researchers fed mycorrhizal plants carbon dioxide made from fossil carbon (containing no carbon-14), then harvested the external fungal threads over the following 29 days and dated them by accelerator mass spectrometry. Most of the extraradical hyphae turned out to be five to six days old. This reframes the usual garden anxiety about 'destroying the mycorrhizal network': the fine network is being torn down and rebuilt continuously anyway, out of sugar the plant made this week. What takes years is not the threads but the community of fungal species present and the soil structure their residues help build.

source.name: Staddon, Ramsey, Ostle, Ineson & Fitter (2003), 'Rapid turnover of hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi determined by AMS microanalysis of 14C', Science — abstract retrieved from the Europe PMC REST API

claims.checker_note: verified for arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, with the source's own scope limits stated; the garden reframing and the "what takes years" clause are unsourced inference and must be marked as such
claims.cannot_establish: Measured in an experimental system with labelled CO2, not in ordinary field soil across seasons. It covers the fine external hyphae only — not thicker runner hyphae, not spores, and not the fungal community composition, which changes far more slowly. It does not tell you how long a disturbed network takes to reach its former size.

claims.statement: Cutting a mycorrhizal network once, eight hours before harvest, did not change plant biomass or soil aggregate stability — though it did measurably drop the plant's leaf water status within those eight hours (relative water content down 6.3%, leaf water potential down 9.2%). Cutting it every week from day 14 onward significantly lowered leaf, stem and root biomass and shifted the soil measures: glomalin-related soil protein rose, and aggregate mean weight diameter rose in the rooted compartment while falling in the hyphae-only compartment. The distinction that matters is frequency, not the act of severing once. (Rootbox experiment, trifoliate orange with Funneliformis mosseae, hyphae cut where they crossed an air gap — not a test of garden digging.)
claims.detail: In a rootbox experiment, trifoliate orange seedlings colonised by Funneliformis mosseae had the external mycelium either cut once, eight hours before harvest, or cut every week from 14 days after inoculation. The one-off cut produced no significant change in biomass or in aggregate stability. Weekly cutting significantly lowered leaf, stem and root biomass and shifted glomalin-related soil protein and aggregate mean weight diameter. The practical distinction is frequency, not the act of digging: one disturbance is absorbed, a rhythm of disturbance is not.

source.name: Zou, Srivastava, Ni & Wu (2015), 'Disruption of mycorrhizal extraradical mycelium and changes in leaf water status and soil aggregate stability in rootbox-grown trifoliate orange', Frontiers in Microbiology

claims.checker_note: verified with correction — source confirms the frequency finding; headline overstated ("no measurable effect" is false: leaf water dropped significantly, and soil aggregation shifted in mixed directions rather than simply declining)
claims.cannot_establish: This is a single potted rootstock with a single fungal species in a rootbox, not field or garden soil with a mixed fungal community. It does not establish how long a network needs to recover from one disturbance, nor where between 'weekly' and 'yearly' the threshold falls, nor that the same applies to non-woody garden plants.
claims.wall_fell_because: The paper refutes the floor, in its own abstract: "mycorrhizal inoculation induced a significant increase in growth (plant height, stem diameter, and leaf, stem, and root biomass) and physiological characters ... irrespective of ERM status." Even under weekly severing, mycorrhizal plants still outperformed non-mycorrhizal controls. The word the paper uses for the weekly treatment is "inhibited the mycorrhizal roles" — reduced benefit, not abolished function. That is a gradient, and the rule needs a floor: "cannot stand" is not what a diminished-but-still-positive effect shows. Three further problems. (a) The rule's own BECAUSE clause is factually wrong on half its evidence: weekly cutting did not suppress soil aggregation across the board — GRSP rose in both compartments and MWD rose in the root+hyphae compartment; only the root-free hyphae compartment declined. (b) Domain leap: the experiment severed hyphae crossing a 37-µm-nylon-mesh air gap between two rootbox chambers, using one plant species with one fungal species in a controlled acclimation. It contains no data on digging, hoeing or field cultivation, so "WHEN soil is dug, hoed or cultivated weekly" is not a condition this study ever tested. (c) n=1 study. A hard floor rule on a public honesty-about-foundations site would need a body of tillage-frequency field evidence showing the layer fails outright, not one rootbox paper showing it works less well.

claims.statement: On restored calcareous (limestone) grasslands in the Belgian Calestienne, the mycorrhizal fungi caught up with ancient grassland faster than the plants did. Across 53 semi-natural grasslands along a restoration gradient, sites restored 12 to 20 years earlier had arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal richness, diversity and composition statistically indistinguishable from ancient target grasslands — though a few fungal taxa still occurred only in the ancient sites — while plant community reassembly on those same grasslands "strongly lagged behind" the fungi. The authors conclude that introducing target plants there "will likely not be limited by the absence of AMF". That is good evidence the fungi are not the bottleneck in this kind of grassland restoration. It is not a test of garden, allotment or arable soil, and the same study found fungal communities in afforested sites did strongly deviate — so it is not a blanket verdict on fungal inoculant products.
claims.detail: Fifty-three semi-natural grasslands along a restoration gradient in the Belgian Calestienne (a calcareous region, so relevant to alkaline Cambridge soils) were sequenced for their whole arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal community. Grasslands restored 12-20 years earlier had fungal richness, diversity and composition indistinguishable from ancient target grasslands, although a few fungal taxa still occurred only in the ancient sites. Plant community reassembly on those same grasslands 'strongly lagged behind' the fungi. The authors conclude that introducing target plants is unlikely to be limited by absent mycorrhizal fungi — a direct, peer-reviewed argument against buying fungal inoculant products.

source.name: Honnay, Helsen & Van Geel (2017), Biological Conservation — abstract retrieved from the Europe PMC REST API

claims.checker_note: verified for the core finding (every factual element is verbatim in the retrieved abstract); the extension to "an argument against buying fungal inoculant products" is an unverified inference beyond the paper's tested context, and "chalk" should read "calcareous/limestone"
claims.cannot_establish: These sites sat in a landscape with ancient grassland nearby, so fungal spores had somewhere to travel from. It cannot be extended to sterile imported topsoil, sealed urban ground, or a roof, where dispersal really is cut off. Detecting a fungal taxon by DNA is not proof that it is functioning.

claims.statement: In eastern England, created and restored farmland ponds carried significantly more aquatic plant taxa at 11+ years after the work than at 1-2 years after it — and restored old ponds were colonised by plants faster than newly dug ones, though that head start had disappeared by 11+ years, when the two were similarly rich.
claims.detail: Fifty-six ponds (28 created, 28 restored) across an agricultural landscape in eastern England, exactly the working climate here. Both alpha and gamma richness were significantly higher 11 or more years after the work than 1-2 years after it. Restored ponds were significantly richer than created ponds at 1-2 years and again at 3-6 years; by 11+ years the two had converged on similar diversity. Compositions also became more similar to each other over time. So a new pond is on a decade-long trajectory, and reopening a silted-up old pond starts further along that trajectory than digging a new hole.

source.name: Hill, White, Hawkins, Binu, Baker, Greaves & Sayer (2025), 'Both pond creation and restoration provide long term biodiversity gains in agricultural landscapes', Biological Conservation — abstract retrieved from the Europe PMC REST API

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: Aquatic plants only — it says nothing about invertebrates, amphibians, or water chemistry. These are farmland ponds, typically larger and less shaded than a garden pond. '11+ years' is the top time bin, so the study cannot say when the community actually settles — only that it was still climbing up to that point.
claims.wall_fell_because: This is a gradient, not a floor. The evidence shows richness increasing with time since intervention, not that a pond younger than ten years cannot function or support a plant community at all — young ponds in this study were demonstrably full of plants, just fewer taxa. Three further faults: (1) the "about ten years" edge is an artifact of the study's survey bins (1-2, 3-6, ..., 11+); the abstract reports only the 11+ vs 1-2 contrast as significant, and shows no discontinuity at ten years, so a nine-year-old pond is not distinguished from an eleven-year-old one by anything measured. (2) 11+ is an open-ended top bin, so the study cannot establish that a community is "settled" at any age — only that 11+ years is richer than 1-2. The rule asserts an endpoint the data do not contain. (3) It generalises from 56 ponds in one eastern-England agricultural landscape, aquatic macrophytes only, to "a pond" anywhere, any taxa. A rule that forbids a claim from standing needs a hard edge; this evidence supplies a slope.

claims.statement: A hawthorn hedge cut every year produces about half the flowers and under a third of the winter berry mass of the same hedge cut every three years. In a five-year factorial experiment on English farmland hedgerows, cutting reduced flowers by up to 75% and winter berry biomass by up to 83% compared with hedges left uncut; moving from annual to triennial cutting gave 2.1 times more flowers and 3.4 times greater berry mass over the five years. Cutting every two years fell in between, and its berry gain depended on cutting in winter rather than autumn. Cutting less often is the one change here that costs less work rather than more. (The experiment was on farm hedgerows of hawthorn and did not test cutting against any other intervention, so treat it as a strong lever, not a proven strongest one, and expect the berry effect to apply only to hedges that fruit.)
claims.detail: A five-year factorial experiment on hawthorn hedges in England tested cutting every 1, 2 or 3 years, in autumn versus winter. Cutting reduced flowers by up to 75% and winter berry biomass by up to 83% compared with hedges left uncut. Moving from annual to triennial cutting gave 2.1 times more flowers and 3.4 times more berry mass across the study. Timing mattered independently: under two-yearly cutting, the berry gain depended on cutting in winter rather than autumn. This is the strongest single lever a homeowner has over a hedge, and it costs less work rather than more.

source.name: Staley et al. (2012), 'Long-term effects of hedgerow management policies on resource provision for wildlife', Biological Conservation 145:24-29, record at the NERC Open Research Archive

claims.checker_note: verified for the numbers and the experimental design, which match the cited abstract exactly; the added claims that this is 'the strongest single lever a homeowner has' and that it applies to hedges generally are unsupported extrapolation and are dropped in the corrected statement
claims.cannot_establish: It measures food resource — flowers and berries — not nesting success, invertebrate abundance, or how long a newly planted hedge takes to become useful at all. These were mechanically flailed farm hedges dominated by hawthorn in England; a hand-trimmed mixed garden hedge may respond differently. No source I could reach gives a defensible number of years for a new hedge to become wildlife-functional.

claims.statement: Ancient trees — what the Woodland Trust calls a tree in "the third and final stage of their lives" — carry the hollowing, decay and creviced bark that make the richest deadwood habitat. There is no fixed age for this; it is species-specific and defined by form, not birthdays. The Trust says a fast-growing birch "could be classed as ancient at 150 years old, while a yew tree might receive the same accolade at 800 years of age". Its markers are a retrenched canopy, a wide trunk (about 1.5 m girth for hawthorn, 5 m for sweet chestnut), a hollow trunk in most though not all cases, and coarse creviced bark. At least 2,000 British invertebrate species rely on dead or decaying wood for some part of their life cycle. Our own inference, which the cited page does not make: a newly planted tree gives leaf litter, aphids and shade within a few years, but the large-diameter decaying heartwood the rarest specialists need exists only on an old tree — an argument for keeping the old tree you already have rather than swapping it for three new ones.
claims.detail: There is no fixed age at which a tree becomes ancient; it is species-specific and defined by form, not birthdays. The Woodland Trust's markers are a retrenched canopy, a wide trunk (about 1.5 m girth for hawthorn, 5 m for sweet chestnut), a hollow trunk in most cases, and coarse creviced bark. At least 2,000 British invertebrate species depend on dead and decaying wood for part of their life cycle, and these saproxylic species are the ones that arrive last. Practically: a newly planted tree delivers leaf litter, aphids and shade within a few years, but the deadwood habitat that carries the rarest species is a century or more away — which is a strong argument for keeping the old tree you already have rather than swapping it for three new ones.

source.name: Woodland Trust, 'Ancient trees' guidance page

claims.checker_note: source-declared for the definition, the markers, the 150/800 ages and the 2,000-invertebrate figure (all verbatim on the cited page); the colonisation-order sentence and the plant-new-vs-keep-old argument must be relabelled as the author's inference, as the page does not address either
claims.cannot_establish: This is a charity guidance page, not a study — it gives definitions and thresholds, not a measured curve of habitat value against tree age. It does not establish when a young tree becomes a net asset, nor quantify how much value is lost by planting new instead of retaining old. The Woodland Trust also sells and gives away trees and runs planting programmes, so it has an interest in tree planting generally; note that this particular page argues for protecting old trees, which cuts against that interest rather than with it.

claims.statement: Across the urban tree literature, half of a planted cohort is typically dead within 13 to 18 years, and mortality tends to be highest in the first five years after planting. A systematic review of urban tree mortality found annual mortality in planting-cohort studies ranging from 0.6% to 68.5%, with quartiles of 2.8-3.8%, 4.4-6.5% and 7.1-9.3%. Split by phase, the median was 6.6-7% a year during the first five years and 2.8-3.8% a year past the establishment phase. The review's own authors convert these into a population half-life: 13 to 18 years in the middle-of-the-road scenario, 7 to 11 years in the worse-than-normal case and 33 to 38 years in the better-than-normal case. They caution that study methods vary too much for these rates to be compared confidently, which is why the spread is so wide. Set that against the previous claim - habitat value peaking after a century - and the mismatch is stark: in the median scenario a planted urban tree does not survive to a fifth of the age at which its habitat value would arrive, and in the worse case not to a tenth. Notably the review also found that although soil structure, bulk density and organic matter are known to affect tree growth, none of the reviewed studies actually tested whether soil properties predicted mortality.
claims.detail: A systematic review of urban tree mortality found annual mortality in planting-cohort studies ranging from 0.6% to 68.5%, with a median of 4.4-6.5%. Split by phase, the median was 6.6-7% a year during the first five years and 2.8-3.8% a year from year six onward. Converting those to a population half-life gives 13-18 years in the middle-of-the-road scenario, 7-11 years in the worse case and 33-38 years in the better case. Set that against the previous claim — habitat value peaking after a century — and the mismatch is stark: the median planted street tree does not survive to a tenth of the age at which its habitat value would arrive. Notably the review also found that although soil structure, bulk density and organic matter are known to affect tree growth, none of the reviewed studies actually tested whether soil properties predicted mortality.

source.name: Hilbert, Roman, Koeser, Vogt & van Doorn (2019), 'Urban Tree Mortality: A Literature Review', Arboriculture & Urban Forestry 45(5):167

claims.checker_note: verified
claims.cannot_establish: The literature is dominated by North American street and municipal trees; a garden tree in generous unsealed soil with a person watching it is a different animal, and this review cannot tell you its odds. Critically, it explicitly cannot establish that small pits or poor soil cause the deaths, because no study in the review tested that link — the causal story about tree pits remains untested, not proven.

claims.statement: Green roof growing media are commonly sterilised before installation, or made largely from dry mineral aggregate — the sterilisation deliberate, to remove weed seed and presumed pathogens. So a new green roof typically starts with an impoverished soil community rather than a full one: fungal communities on studied roofs were less diverse than New York park soils, and fresh media as purchased could colonise bait plants only sparsely, with the meaningful mycorrhizal content arriving with the planted plants themselves, which had been raised in fields. Where roofs were deliberately inoculated, the benefit diminished within a year. Two honest qualifications: many installations do add compost or commercial inoculants at the outset, and the authors note there is very little research on what is actually living in these media at installation or over time.
claims.detail: A review of green roof microbiology states plainly that newly installed roofs have depauperate microbial communities because substrates are sterilised beforehand or derive mostly from dry mineral materials — the sterilisation is deliberate, to remove weed seed and presumed pathogens. Fungal communities on studied roofs were less diverse than New York park soils. Fresh media as purchased could only sparsely colonise bait plants; the meaningful mycorrhizal content arrived with the planted plants themselves, which had been raised in fields. And where roofs were deliberately inoculated, the benefit diminished within a year. This is the cleanest example of a purchased surface: a green roof is green on day one and biologically close to empty on day one.

source.name: Fulthorpe, MacIvor, Jia & Yasui (2018), 'The Green Roof Microbiome: Improving Plant Survival for Ecosystem Service Delivery', Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution

claims.checker_note: verified with qualification — quotation is exact and the URL is live, but "almost no soil life at all" overstates "depauperate," and the claim omits the source's immediately following concession that compost or commercial inoculants are added in many installations
claims.cannot_establish: The review does not establish how many years a roof substrate needs to develop a functioning soil community, nor whether it ever does. It does not settle whether inoculation is worth doing — the one result reported points the other way. Findings come from North American roofs; UK substrate practice may differ.
claims.wall_fell_because: The rule asserts a hard floor ("cannot stand") but the evidence is a gradient, and the paper's own cited finding contradicts a zero: fresh media as purchased DID colonise bait plants, merely "sparsely." A substrate that sparsely colonises is not biologically empty, so nothing here supports "cannot work at all." Every measure in this literature is comparative — less diverse than park soils, sparse rather than absent colonisation, inoculation benefit diminished within a year — degradations, not floors. The rule also survives only by smuggling its conclusion into its antecedent: "and nothing living is introduced with it" makes the consequent near-tautological, while in real green roof practice that condition routinely fails, since the source says compost or commercial inoculants are added in many installations. The stated BECAUSE overreaches further on two points: sterilisation is described as "common practice," not universal, and the mycorrhizal content did not arrive "only later" but with the plants at planting time. A rule this shaped would license claiming any manufactured substrate is dead, which the source does not support.

claims.statement: In 126 English fields, 42% were missing or nearly missing at least one earthworm group - the totals looked normal, the soil's engineers were not there. A national on-farm study covering 1,318 hectares in spring 2018 (15 March-30 April) used ten pits per field, each a 20 cm cube. Average populations were 2.4 million worms per hectare, about nine per pit, but ranged between 0.75 and 7.3 million per hectare across fields. Surface-dwelling (epigeic) worms were absent from 21% of fields and deep-burrowing (anecic) worms - the ones that make the vertical drainage channels - were absent from 16%; a further 8-11% of fields had only rare sightings of these groups. Overall, 42% of fields had sub-optimal populations, defined as one or more ecological groups found in 10% or fewer of a field's pits. Tillage significantly (p < 0.05) affected general, epigeic and anecic presence, and organic matter management did not mitigate tillage impacts. Total worm count alone would have hidden this: it is the missing group, not the missing number, that shows the function is gone.
claims.detail: A national on-farm study covering 1,318 hectares in spring 2018 used ten pits per field, each a 20 cm cube. Average populations were 2.4 million worms per hectare, about nine per pit, but varied a hundredfold between fields. Surface-dwelling (epigeic) worms were absent from 21% of fields and rare on another 8%; deep-burrowing (anecic) worms — the ones that make the vertical drainage channels — were absent from 16% and rare on another 11%. Overall, 42% of fields had sub-optimal populations, defined as one or more groups present in 10% or fewer pits. Tillage significantly affected general, epigeic and anecic presence, and adding organic matter did not compensate for it. Total worm count alone would have hidden this: it is the missing group, not the missing number, that shows the function is gone.

source.name: Stroud (2019), 'Soil health pilot study in England: Outcomes from an on-farm earthworm survey', PLOS ONE 14(2):e0203909

claims.checker_note: verified, with one correction: the 8% / 11% per-group split of "rare sightings" is not in the source, which gives a single combined 8-11% range for both groups; and the source's own "100-fold" variation conflicts with the 0.75-7.3 million ha-1 range it states alongside (10-fold), so the raw range should be cited instead of the multiplier
claims.cannot_establish: A one-spring snapshot on farm fields, not gardens, and observational — it shows tillage is associated with absence, not that tillage caused it. Absence from ten pits is not proof of absence from a field. It gives no recovery timescale: it cannot say how long a tilled soil takes to regain its anecic worms.

claims.statement: Calcareous grasslands restored on former arable land still showed little community overlap with ancient grassland after sixty years. Forty restoration sites were paired with forty reference sites. Some plant attributes (for example perenniality and ruderality) shifted toward reference condition as sites aged, but overall there was little overlap between restored and ancient grassland communities even after 60 years — successful restoration is achievable, but slow. High soil phosphorus concentration was detrimental to restoration, as was seeding with a low-diversity mix, which assembles competitive grass-dominated communities. Natural regeneration moved sites toward the target but was limited by proximity to ancient grassland as a seed source. The authors recommend choosing sites with low phosphorus that adjoin existing ancient calcareous grassland. [Farm Wildlife's practical guidance separately puts the target at "pH > 6.5 and a P index of 0 or 1" — cite the exact page URL. DROP the index-2 case study with fungal colonisation at four years and orchids after five unless a working farmwildlife.info URL for it can be produced; it was not found on the creation page, the restoration page, or the In Practice index, and the implied reversion page 404s.]
claims.detail: Forty restoration sites were paired with forty ancient reference sites. Individual plant attributes shifted toward reference condition as sites aged, but there was little overlap between restored and ancient grassland communities even after 60 years — the sward looked like grassland long before it was one. High soil phosphorus concentration was specifically detrimental, and natural regeneration worked mainly where a site adjoined existing ancient grassland to supply seed. Farm Wildlife's practical reversion guidance (fetched separately, farmwildlife.info) puts the target at phosphate index 0-1 and describes a real site at index 2 that grew a thick grass-dominated sward very quickly, crowding out sown wildflowers; on that site fungal colonisation appeared about four years in and orchids after more than five. This is the most directly transferable case to Cambridge's alkaline soils.

source.name: Fagan, Pywell, Bullock & Marrs (2008), 'Do restored calcareous grasslands on former arable fields resemble ancient targets?', Journal of Applied Ecology — abstract retrieved from the Europe PMC REST API

claims.checker_note: verified for the cited paper and its headline finding (abstract retrieved verbatim, URL live); partly unverified in the detail — the Farm Wildlife phosphate-index target is confirmed, but the index-2 case study with fungal-colonisation and orchid timings could not be located and should be cut or given an exact working URL
claims.cannot_establish: 'Little overlap after 60 years' does not mean nothing happened — attributes did move toward reference, and this study cannot separate how much of the residual gap is soil chemistry, seed supply or management. It does not establish a phosphorus threshold below which success is guaranteed, and the Farm Wildlife index 0-1 figure is practitioner guidance, not a measured breakpoint. Field-scale reversion, not a garden bed.

claims.statement: There is a published, free protocol for measuring whether soil is actually decomposing organic matter, at a scale a homeowner can run: the Tea Bag Index (Keuskamp et al., Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 2013). You bury two tea bags in separate 8 cm-deep holes about 15 cm apart, leave them roughly 90 days, then dry them (48h at 70°C, or several days somewhere warm), empty each bag and weigh the tea to 0.01 g. Green tea decomposes fast and rooibos slowly, and the pair is what lets the 2013 paper derive two numbers: a decomposition rate (k) and a stabilisation factor (S) for how much material resists breaking down. That is a function being measured — biological activity — rather than an appearance, which is the distinction this project cares about. Two honest caveats. First, the materials: the index was never "any two tea bags" but two specific Lipton products, and the project's own site reports that Lipton discontinued the standard green tea in 2024, adding "we do not recommend using other types of tea to calculate k and S." Substitutes (they suggest Japanese Sencha, or local tea in degradation-resistant bags) still give you mass loss you can compare within your own site over time, but not k and S comparable to anyone else's — and the bag material itself changed in 2017 and again in 2021/22, so even long-running series are not one continuous measurement. Second, the method is contested in the literature: the derivation of k from a single time point, and the independence of k from S, have both been challenged, with defenders arguing the simplifications are what make it usable while urging care over incubation time. [Verify and cite the specific 2025 exchange before publishing, or leave this sentence general — it was not confirmed.]
claims.detail: The protocol asks for one green tea bag and one rooibos bag, buried in separate holes 8 cm deep and about 15 cm apart, left for roughly 90 days, then dried and weighed. Green tea decomposes fast and rooibos slowly, so the pair gives two numbers: a decomposition rate (k) and a stabilisation factor (S) describing how much material resists breaking down. The only equipment needed is a scale reading to 0.01 g. Repeated in the same spot each year, this measures a function — biological activity — rather than an appearance, which is exactly the distinction this project is about. Be aware of a live scientific argument: Mori (2025, Ecology Letters) argues the k value is inaccurate and that k and S are mathematically entangled, and Sarneel and twelve co-authors replied that the simplifications are what make it usable but demand care over incubation time.

source.name: Teatime4Science / Tea Bag Index, stepwise protocol (method originally published as Keuskamp et al., Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 2013)

claims.checker_note: contested — and, since the 2024 discontinuation of the standard green tea, no longer reproducible as written for a newcomer wanting comparable k and S
claims.cannot_establish: Contested specifically on the numbers, not the act: the published critique means an absolute k value should not be treated as precise. It also cannot establish anything about soil biodiversity — a fast decomposition rate does not mean a rich soil community. Results depend heavily on temperature and moisture, so year-to-year comparisons in a dry Cambridge summer are confounded by weather unless repeated over many years.

claims.statement: The other function test with a published method is an earthworm count. AHDB's protocol — written for farm fields, but scalable to a garden — calls for ten pits, each a 20 cm cube, dug early in spring or after the soil has wetted up in autumn, with the soil wet for a few days beforehand. Worms are separated into adults (visible saddle) and juveniles; AHDB is explicit that size is not a good indicator of maturity. AHDB's companion page on earthworm types adds the three ecological groups — epigeic, endogeic, anecic — each doing a different job. Neither AHDB page gives numeric good/bad thresholds; the "a group present in 10% or fewer of the ten pits counts as sub-optimal" benchmark comes from the national field study cited above, not from AHDB. Recorded over years, this is the most valuable single measurement a homeowner can keep, because it distinguishes a soil with organisms doing distinct jobs from one that merely contains worms.
claims.detail: AHDB's published protocol specifies ten samples, each a 20 cm by 20 cm by 20 cm pit, taken early in spring or after the soil has wetted in autumn, with the soil wet for a few days beforehand. Worms are separated into adults (with a visible saddle) and juveniles — size is explicitly not a reliable indicator of maturity — and, in the fuller version, into the three ecological groups. AHDB's own page gives no numeric good/bad thresholds; the usable benchmark comes from the national field study above, where a group present in 10% or fewer of the ten pits counted as sub-optimal. This is the single most valuable thing a homeowner can record over years, because it distinguishes a soil that has organisms doing distinct jobs from a soil that merely contains worms.

source.name: AHDB (Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board), 'How to count earthworms'

claims.checker_note: verified-with-caveats
claims.cannot_establish: AHDB's page does not itself publish numeric thresholds separating good from poor soil, so any threshold has to be borrowed from elsewhere. The method is designed for farm fields; ten pits in a small garden is a large proportion of the plot and the digging itself is a disturbance. Counts swing hugely with soil moisture and temperature, so a single year's figure means little.
